articles.title: Ordinal Response Elicitation for Systematic Review Screening with GPT
articles.authors: Ronald Luo; Abu Ilius Faisal; Ziya Sastimoglu; Jamal Deen
articles.abstract:
Background: Systematic reviews are crucial for evidence-based practice but are often hindered by labor-intensive methodologies. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) may help improve review efficiency and replicability.
Objective: Building on prior research, this study evaluates the impact of prompt engineering on LLM performance in automating systematic reviews, specifically examining the "zero-shot" capability for predicting article inclusion based on titles and abstracts alone. 
Methods: We reanalyzed 24,534 studies across three systematic reviews using two sets of prompts with GPT-3.5 Turbo. One set rated the suitability of a study on a scale of one to ten, while the other elicited a binary response. Both ordinal-response and binary-response prompts were assessed for accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, F1 score, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). We also evaluated Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for ordinal-response prompts and statistically validated the results using K-fold permutations and one-way analysis of variance.
Results: Ordinal prompting allowed for fine-tuning of sensitivity and specificity, proving to be a viable zero-shot inclusion prompt with ROC Area Under Curve (AUC) scores between 80-90%. Including studies rated seven or higher achieved sensitivity and specificity of ~80%, while using the mean score increased sensitivity to nearly 100%, a task not possible with earlier strategies.
Conclusion: Prompt engineering offers a scalable solution that allows researchers to target highly relevant articles or maximize sensitivity to include nearly all relevant studies if more time is available.

articles.title: How reproducible are preclinical systematic reviews? Evidence from a multi-team challenge
articles.authors: Fiona Jane Ramage; Kaitlyn Hair; Matheus Gallas-Lopes; Aileen MacLellan; Sofija Vojvodic; Maria Economou; Francesca Tinsdeall; Bruno Dutra Arbo; María Arroyo-Araujo; Alexandra Bannach-Brown
articles.abstract: Systematic reviews of preclinical data are helpful in informing experimental design and translation, yet their own reproducibility has not been evaluated. We conducted a community-led Reproducibility Challenge to address this gap. Five international teams assessed reproducibility and identified factors affecting the replication success for four published reviews involving animal models of disease. Most teams successfully reproduced the original conclusions. However, we identified important quantitative and qualitative discrepancies in replicating individual steps of the systematic reviews. Differences arose in study selection, data processing and meta-analysis, and risk of bias assessments, due largely to incomplete or ambiguous reporting in the original reviews and to restricted access to underlying data and analysis code. Our findings suggest that preclinical systematic reviews may be more robust to replication than studies assessed in initiatives from other fields, although a lack of methodological transparency remains a significant barrier to exact replication. We provide recommendations, including refinements to reporting standards, to strengthen the transparency of preclinical evidence syntheses. We demonstrate that such collaborative challenges serve as a scalable model for community-driven engagement with reproducibility and the validation of systematic review findings. Wider adoption of reporting standards and open science practices is needed to ensure that preclinical systematic reviews provide a reliable foundation for translational research.

articles.title: How and why do we study research methods? The TYPE-ME typology of methods research
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract:
Background: Methods research aims to develop, evaluate, refine, or provide guidance on research methods, support their implementation or de-implementation, or synthesize existing methods research. Many types of methods research appear in health research journals, but their labels, definitions, and boundaries remain unclear. This complicates planning, reporting, indexing, and teaching, and limits the visibility of the field. We aimed to develop, refine and pilot-test a typology for recognising, describing, and classifying methods research.

Methods: An international panel of 11 methodologists developed the typology through written feedback, structured group discussions, and iterative revision. In two testing rounds, panel members independently applied the typology to 52 methods research articles from 26 journals, generating 494 article assessments. We used the results to refine definitions and labels, add boundary notes, and document remaining disagreements.

Results: TYPE-ME defines methods research and organizes it along two cross-cutting dimensions: approach (“how?”, 15 types) and objective (“why?”, 14 types). Testing clarified difficult boundaries and led to a condensed version that distinguishes 10 types for quick orientation: theory-based methods research; simulation studies; methods research based on real data; methodological randomized studies; surveys, interviews, or focus groups; consensus studies; studies of applied methods; syntheses of methods research; guidance for applying, reporting, or assessing methods; and methodological implementation research. Detailed type descriptions, boundary notes, and examples appear in an accompanying document and at www.methods-research.org.

Conclusions: TYPE-ME offers a common reference for recognising, describing, and classifying methods research, and can support its planning, reporting, indexing, and teaching. As a living typology, it will evolve through application, user feedback, and further testing.

articles.title: Making research more reproducible: eleven paths forward
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Reproducibility has emerged as a core theme within the research reform movement, with strong engagement of meta-researchers and policy-makers. Since reproducibility is not equally relevant or feasible across research communities or disciplines, actions to improve it should be attuned to the diversity of epistemic practices present across the academic landscape. We conducted a multi-stage co-creative process with key stakeholders to formulate evidence-based and actionable recommendations aimed at increasing reproducibility across academic communities. Our iterative process yielded eleven recommendations, organised across four key areas: (1) infrastructure, standards and community, (2) incentives and policy, (3) training and skills, and (4) strengthening the evidence base. The recommendations include concrete steps for funders, publishers, research institutions, research communities and meta-researchers. They emphasise the need for context-sensitive norms and policy-making that accounts for epistemic diversity across research fields, as well as the need for stronger incentives, open practices, and dedicated support to enhance the transparency and trustworthiness of research. Improving reproducibility is a collective action problem. Isolated policies are therefore unlikely to produce substantial change. Our recommendations map where stakeholders need to act in concert and which steps each is best positioned to take; since coordination itself has no clear owner, we see large public funders as best placed to align efforts and incentives. Generative AI is expanding the capacity to produce research claims faster than the capacity to verify them, and building a stronger verification infrastructure cannot wait until the evidence base is complete.

articles.title: A scoping review of Open Science practices in corpus linguistics research
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: While many disciplines have responded to the replication crisis with calls and measures to promote Open Science/Scholarship (OS) practices, corpus linguistics (CL) has been slower to espouse these ideas. This study examines the uptake of OS practices in 907 research articles published 2020-2025 in ten international CL journals. The number of preregistered studies, replications, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses was tracked. Full-text queries were performed to estimate the number of articles with open materials, data, and code. Their (re)usability based on FAIR principles was qualitatively assessed in a stratified sample of 141 articles. Between 2020–2025, around half of studies in international CL journals were published in open access. Very few authors made use of self-archiving options. Crucial components of research, e.g. raw and annotated corpus data, annotation schemes, and analytical scripts, are rarely available. The results suggest that CL currently stands closer to the starting line than the frontier of the OS movement. The findings establish baseline prevalence estimates against which progress towards more open CL research can be measured in the future.

articles.title: Learning behaviors through verbal instructions facilitates conflict resolution
articles.authors: Francois Remy Foerster; Nicolas Bourguignon; Philippine Lemoine; Daxun Zhu; Senne Braem; Salvatore Lo Bue
articles.abstract: The cognitive and neurobiological principles of instruction-based learning in humans have been a topic of interest and intensive research for over a decade. Much has been learned about their place and importance in driving adaptive behavior, but this line of work has mostly been based on the presupposition that behaviors are learned through verbal communication. Many other behaviors however are also learned through nonverbal means, and it is still unclear whether nonverbally instructed behaviors qualitatively differ from those instructed verbally. We set out to address this issue by looking at the effect of verbal versus nonverbal instructions on the processing of instruction-based task conflict. Using a between-subject design (N = 192), we show that congruency effects, the hallmark of conflicting behaviors, endure when task rules are nonverbally instructed, but are selectively reduced when task instructions are verbal. Furthermore, we show that verbal instructions promote conflict resolution across stimulus formats. This finding confirms the putatively superior status of language in learning new behaviors, inviting close consideration of its place in human adaptive behavior from the cognitive and neurobiological viewpoint.

articles.title: Human-Supervised LLM-Assisted Mapping of Educational Research at Scale: A Mathematics Education Demonstration
articles.authors: Xia Yang; Haoyi Wang; Zachary Hawes
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for large-scale research synthesis, but their use in educational content analysis requires workflows that are reliable, auditable, and researcher-defined. This study develops and evaluates a human-supervised, multi-model LLM workflow for educational research mapping. Using mathematics education as a demonstration field, we annotated 4,940 abstracts published between 2001 and 2025. We developed and pilot-calibrated a hierarchical five-module coding framework before applying it to the full corpus. The framework coded each article’s analytic focus, whether mathematical content or processes (MCP) were foregrounded, research method, and sociocultural or individual-characteristic labels (ISC); for records coded as empirical and MCP-present, it also coded the primary mathematical area or practice. Two primary LLMs independently applied the framework; a third model addressed disagreement cases, followed by human audit and adjudication. Agreement between the two primary LLMs was strong across major modules (κ = .748 - .892). Human audit showed high alignment for model-agreed cases (κ = .777 - .974), whereas cases requiring auxiliary-model majority resolution showed lower and more variable agreement with human labels (κ = .600 - .791). Thus, model disagreement identified boundary cases requiring human review. The final labels supported descriptive field mapping: educator-focused research became the largest analytic-focus category, attention to sociocultural and individual characteristics increased, and overlap between empirical mathematics-focused work and ISC-coded work remained limited. LLM-assisted research synthesis is most trustworthy when implemented as an auditable workflow rather than as a one-step classification procedure.

articles.title: AI-Faces by Illinois: A Database of AI-Generated Faces Depicting Children
articles.authors: Tim Wei-Ting Chao; Junyi Mei; Iris Tianyi Shang; Enrique Macias; Zara Mkrtychian; Danyi Zhang; Sara A Oh; Jasmin Serrano Rodriguez; Brenda Corina Straka; Michael Rizzo
articles.abstract: Faces serve as gateways of impression formation during human interactions and are widely used as stimuli throughout psychological research. To source these stimuli, researchers often rely on established databases of photographs of adults’ and children’s faces or public image repositories like Google Images. Although these resources have proven valuable, there are important limitations, especially for research using images of children. This manuscript introduces a novel alternative to those databases: AI-Faces by Illinois, a database of 1,152 photorealistic, AI-generated images depicting child faces that is freely available for non-commercial use (OSF link to images and norming data: https://osf.io/vurm5/; CC-BY-NC-4.0 license). These images vary systematically by perceived age (3, 6, 10, 15 years), gender (boy, girl), race/ethnicity (Black, East Asian, Latine, Middle Eastern/North African, Native American, Pacific Islander, South Asian, White), and emotional expression (10 smiling, 4 angry, 4 frowning images per group). Two norming studies (Study 1: N = 1,261, Study 2: N = 131) revealed that adults rated the AI-generated images as equally real as the photographs of children from existing databases and perceived them in line with their prompted age, gender, race/ethnicity, and emotion. The images also elicited perceptual biases similar to those documented in research using real faces, supporting their ecological validity. This manuscript highlights the methodological advantages and new ethical considerations of using AI-generated faces of children in psychological research.

articles.title: Friends and strangers engage in distinct regimes of body motion synchrony during conversation
articles.authors: Mark Allen Thornton; Emma Templeton; Lindsey Tepfer; Thalia Wheatley
articles.abstract: When people talk, their bodies often move together, usually unnoticed. Researchers have studied this synchrony as one behavior. We show that it is several, and that they resolve into two distinct regimes: one for friends and one for strangers. To do so, we analyzed 387 conversations between friends and strangers using markerless pose estimation. We identify three separable forms of body motion synchrony (quantity, directional, and pseudo-synchrony) and largely explain them through four mechanisms (turn-taking, conservation of motion, entrainment, and station keeping). Both the forms and mechanisms of synchrony differ between friends and strangers. Friends synchronize in strong, simple way, moving as a single embodied system (“co-enaction"). Strangers synchronize in a more heterogenous regime, navigating a set of norms (“regulation”). These findings suggest that body motion synchrony is best understood not as single behavior but as paralinguistic scaffolding, its form shaped by the conversation – and relationship – it supports.

articles.title: Peer work interventions for young people navigating hospital services: A systematic review
articles.authors: Pip Buckingham; Alessandra Chinsen; Lou Kerley; Tim Cronin; Kenneth Pang
articles.abstract: Peer workers are people with relevant lived experience working in formalised peer roles, with peer worker programs holding promise for improving patient outcomes. Despite this, no previous reviews have investigated peer worker programs for young people (10-24 years) in hospital services. This rapid review and meta-synthesis aimed to describe characteristics of such programs, and synthesise evidence on feasibility, acceptability, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for empirical studies published between January 1, 2015 and May 2, 2025 and a second search was conducted. Seventeen studies were included. There was significant heterogeneity in terms of intervention characteristics, targeted health issues, and peer roles. Most young people and service providers deemed interventions to be feasible and acceptable. Peer roles provided social support and role modelling to facilitate health-related learning, self-management and participant comfort. Key barriers included technical issues (e.g., virtual delivery), non-cohesive group dynamics, poor understanding of peer roles among clinicians, and irrelevant or non-tailored program content. Facilitators included comprehensive training and supervision for peer workers and flexible, adolescent-centred program delivery. Qualitative reports highlighted improvements in psychosocial wellbeing, while quantitative evidence was limited or mixed. Although more high-quality research is necessary to determine effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, this review provides preliminary evidence that with careful design and implementation, peer worker programs may improve care experiences and wellbeing for young people receiving care in hospital settings.

articles.title: A single mechanism underlies the forgetting of meaning and form
articles.authors: Lyulei Zhang; Adam F Osth; Lachlan Dunn
articles.abstract: Forgetting is often assumed to preserve the meaning of experience while rendering surface forms inaccessible, an assumption used to explain the greater persistence of false than true memories for semantically related experience. Here, we tested a novel prediction of global-matching models: false memories driven by form relatedness should also persist over delay. Across two experiments using the Deese-Roeideger-McDermott paradigm, participants studied semantic and structural (orthographic/phonological) associates, and were tested after 45 seconds or 2 days. False recognition persisted while true recognition declined irrespective of whether memories were elicited by semantic or form relatedness. A global-matching model captured these patterns through a single forgetting mechanism that reduces general memory quality across content types. The same mechanism also captured the study-time effect, opposite to delay, by strengthening memory quality. These findings challenge dual-process accounts of forgetting, instead suggest a single mechanism governs forgetting of meaning and form.

articles.title: Open science in a contentious field: How transparent is research on social media and adolescent mental health?
articles.authors: Isabelle Galet-Lalande; Justine Blackwell; Tom Elis Hardwicke
articles.abstract: The impact of social media on adolescent mental health is a topic of heated debate. In contexts such as these, where evidence is contested and policy stakes are high, research transparency is especially important. Transparent research practices facilitate independent scrutiny and informed decision-making. The present study aimed to assess the adoption of transparent research practices in studies investigating the impact of social media on adolescent mental health. A corpus of 235 eligible empirical articles was identified via a collaborative review maintained by prominent researchers in the field. Articles were coded for eight transparency indicators. Results indicated that while open access, funding statements and conflict of interest statements were relatively common (≥74%), preregistration, data sharing, materials sharing, analysis script sharing, and use of reporting guidelines were rare (≤14%). This widespread lack of transparency undermines the credibility of evidence in this contentious policy-relevant domain.

articles.title: Cognitive resources can be intentionally released when processed information becomes irrelevant: Insights from the primacy effect in working memory
articles.authors: Vencislav Popov
articles.abstract: Processing information depletes a limited cognitive resource. This resource can recover passively over time, but an open question remains: if resources are spent to process information that soon becomes irrelevant, are these resources immediately released? I present an analysis of the Source of Activation Confusion (SAC) model of human memory and its ability to explain the primacy effect in working memory – the tendency for items at the beginning of a list to be better remembered than those in the middle or end. The SAC model attributes the primacy effect to a limited resource pool that is depleted during the encoding of each item into memory, with resource recovery happening passively over time. The model's core mechanisms are challenged by two experiments that reveal the primacy effect can be reset with the application of a forget signal, suggesting resource recovery is not entirely passive. This means that either the passive resource recovery assumption needs to be reformulated, or that the primacy effect is not a result of resource depletion. Given the broad range of other findings the model can explain, abandoning it is premature. Instead, I propose that in addition to recovering passively over time, memory resources can be manually released when the information encoded with them is no longer relevant. This reformulation is important because it significantly limits the range of possible substrates for the proposed resource. I discuss implications for related theories and phenomena such as ego depletion.

articles.title: How and when to implement self-efficacy interventions to maximize the benefits of virtual reality exposure therapy for fear of heights
articles.authors: Kayleigh Piovesan; Julia Klenke; Armin Zlomuzica
articles.abstract: Strategies aimed to enhance self-efficacy (SE), such as mastery experiences and verbal persuasion may promote exposure therapy. Here, we evaluated the effects of two strategies to boost SE administered during and/or after virtual reality exposure therapy (VRET) for fear of heights. Height-fearful participants (N = 83) were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: VRET alone, VRET combined with SE enhancement via positive performance feedback during VRET, VRET combined with post-exposure SE via mastery experience activation and evaluation, or VRET combining both SE enhancement strategies. Subjective, behavioral, and psychophysiological indices of height fear and general SE were assessed from pre- to post-intervention and at 3-month follow-up. Across conditions, height fear and avoidance decreased while behavioral approach increased with effects largely maintained at follow-up. Participants receiving post-exposure mastery experience activation and evaluation showed the strongest reductions in subjective fear during the behavioral approach test and in anxiety expectancies. Decrease in subjective height avoidance was also stronger compared to the condition that received SE enhancement during VRET. Notably, participants receiving positive performance feedback during VRET showed the least improvement (across several outcome measures). Our results indicate that post-exposure activation and evaluation of mastery experiences is suitable to further promote VRET outcome in height fear. Conversely, applying positive performance feedback during VRET seems ineffective and leads to diminished exposure treatment benefit. These findings provide novel perspectives on the potential use of SE enhancement as a supplementary strategy to augment exposure therapy. This study was preregistered on ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT05824884).

articles.title: Social media reveals population dynamics of dysphoric dreaming
articles.authors: Remington Mallett; Laura Sowin; Michelle Carr
articles.abstract: Nightmares disrupt sleep health and predict future psychiatric diagnoses, yet reliable population estimates and their fluctuations over time are difficult to obtain. Here, we set out to test if a digital surveillance approach could be used to observe reliable estimates of nightmare frequency and dysphoric dreaming in the general population from social media posts. English-language posts from r/Dreams, a subreddit where users share their dreams, were analyzed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count to quantify nightmare frequency and anxious dreaming from text. An interrupted time series analysis was used to show that both nightmare frequency and dysphoric dreaming increased immediately following the World Health Organization's declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic. This observation mirrors a large body of existing work that used more traditional methods. This "digital dream surveillance" approach might offer the field of sleep medicine a low-cost and real-time system for monitoring population sleep health.

articles.title: Towards a community driven framework for standardized open data in psychoneuroendocrinology: A Delphi consensus study
articles.authors: Maria Meier; Milou S. C. Sep; Thomaz Bastiaanssen; Emma Clephas; Conny W.E.M. Quaedflieg; Jakub Rajcani; Robert Richer; Bence Szaszkó; Susanne Vogel; Stella Voulgaropoulou
articles.abstract: In psychoneuroendocrinology (PNE), data is valuable due to its high clinical and health-related relevance and resource-intensive data collection yet sharing it openly alongside publications remains uncommon. If shared, data remain highly fragmented and non-standardized, which hinders data reuse and integration across studies. To address this, we formed a consortium and, as a first step, conducted this study using a modified Delphi approach across two survey rounds to inform about important considerations regarding data structure, metadata, subject-level variables, and implementation requirements before a data standard for PNE may be developed. The panel in the final round consisted of 50 responders from the field of PNE. In two online survey rounds, respondents rated their agreement with 84 statements anonymously on a 5-point Likert scale. Consensus (> 70% [dis]agreement) was achieved for 80 items. The results highlight a broad agreement within the PNE community on the need for, and key components of, a standardized data structure, including a balance between flexibility and standardization to allow for adaptability across many use cases as well as comparability. Developing and establishing a standard for PNE data will be a central next step to foster transparency, sustainable use of resources, and the translational potential of our work.

articles.title: Measuring U.S. and Kenyan children’s vocabularies using object, photograph, cartoon, and line drawing stimuli
articles.authors: Rebecca Zhu; Maya Martinez-Krams; Joab Ochieng Arieda; Tabitha Nduku; Judith Fan; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: Early childhood assessments typically involve picture stimuli. As these assessments spread worldwide, researchers make an implicit assumption: that children across contexts understand pictures in the same way, at the same developmental timepoint. What if this assumption does not hold for some or all kinds of pictures? In the present research, preregistered samples of 128 3- to 7-year-olds from Kisumu, Kenya (Experiment 1) and 64 3- to 4-year-olds from the San Francisco Bay Area, U.S.A. (Experiment 2) participated in a vocabulary assessment in four formats (i.e., objects, photographs, cartoons, black-and-white line drawings). Preregistered analyses showed that children from both contexts performed similarly across object, photograph, and cartoon formats, though additional exploratory analyses suggested that Kisumu children may perform less accurately in the line drawing format, at least for ambiguous stimuli. Moreover, exploratory error analyses revealed that the children from Kisumu made different kinds of errors in the object format than in the picture formats, whereas the children from the San Francisco Bay Area made more similar kinds of errors across object and picture formats. These findings tentatively bring more confidence to the existing use of photograph- and cartoon-based assessments in global contexts, though more research is necessary to replicate the current findings, and to determine in exactly which contexts picture-based assessments are appropriate or inappropriate.

articles.title: Same Tool, Different Work: Patterns of Generative AI Use and Academic Outcomes
articles.authors: Christos Stamatoulis; Lavinia Pyrovetsi; Christos Mourikis; Asmitha Ponnam; Irene Karayianni
articles.abstract: Most research on students’ GenAI use relies on frequency. Yet frequency captures exposure, not how students use GenAI. This study examined whether patterns of use are more informative for outcomes than frequency. Exploratory factor analysis of items developed inductively from pilot data identified two dimensions: evaluative integration (EI, use to support understanding), and low-verification uptake (LVU, shortcut use). Survey responses from 157 undergraduates were used to test associations with performance and indirect associations through academic self-efficacy (ASE), with frequency included for comparison. EI was positively associated with performance, whereas LVU was negatively associated with it. EI showed a significant indirect association through ASE and no remaining direct association; LVU showed both a significant indirect association and a remaining direct negative association. Frequency predicted neither performance nor ASE. In a separate model, frequency strengthened the positive association between EI and ASE, but the interaction was nonsignificant when the EI and LVU interactions were estimated jointly. No moderation was found for LVU. How students engage with GenAI may therefore be more informative for academic outcomes than frequency alone. The findings support further development of measures of student-GenAI interaction and testing of pedagogical approaches that promote evaluative integration.

articles.title: The BRIMMER test: The bounds of the Standard Deviation under constraints
articles.authors: Ian Hussey; Lukas Jung; Lakena Kouatche Gill Wilfried; Jamie Cummins
articles.abstract: Reported summary statistics are not free to vary independently of one another. The sample size, the mean, and a scale''s minimum and maximum possible values jointly constrain the values that the sample standard deviation (SD) can take. A reported SD that falls outside these bounds is impossible, and signals an error or worse. Because such checks require only the numbers printed in an article, they are practical tools for error detection and trustworthiness assessment even when the underlying data are unavailable. The mathematics involved is nearly a century old but badly scattered. We document at least eight literatures that independently derived, and repeatedly rediscovered, partial versions of the same results, including the little-known fact that Popoviciu''s 1935 paper already contained the sharp odd-n bound usually credited to later authors. We organize these results into a single framework of nested constraints, from the scale limits alone through sample size, mean, integer-valued data, and reported internal consistency (Cronbach''s alpha). Along the way we sharpen several published bounds and derive novel ones, including the first that use a reported reliability coefficient. We name the resulting checks BRIM and BRIMMER (Bounds-Related Inconsistency of Means, and of Means and Errors Reported), by analogy with the granularity tests GRIM and GRIMMER. Both are implemented, with rounding handled explicitly and validation against exhaustive enumeration, in the R package {strait} and in a point-and-click web application (https://errors.shinyapps.io/brimmer).

articles.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between problematic social media use and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms: A comment on Nagata et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Marika Melin; Bo Melin; Gustav Nilsonne
articles.abstract: In a recent study, Nagata et al. concluded prospective within-individual associations between problematic social media use (PSMU) and ADHD symptoms. In the present reanalyses, we report discrepant increasing and decreasing effects of PSMU on subsequent change in ADHD symptoms, and vice versa, depending on the model used to analyze data. Meta-analytic aggregations of these divergent effects did not differ significantly from zero. Hence, we conclude that the findings by Nagata et al. may have been spurious and their conclusions premature. It is important to bear in mind that correlations, including cross-lagged effects, in observational data may be spurious in order not to overinterpret findings. For increased analytic rigor, we recommend researchers to fit, as we did here, alternative models to data to verify whether results are robust under different justifiable analytical strategies.

articles.title: Mindfulness Promotes Adaptive Meaning-Making about Difficult Experiences in Introductory Physics: Evidence from Two Preregistered Randomized Controlled Trials
articles.authors: Brian Galla; Tessa Benson-Greenwald; Avital Pelakh; Michael James Tumminia; Tyree Langley; Carol M Greco; Melanie Good; Eric Kuo; Timothy Nokes-Malach
articles.abstract: Two field experiments with psychologically threatened undergraduates in introductory physics tested whether mindfulness promotes adaptive meaning-making about learning setbacks (Experiment 1) and unpleasant learning emotions (Experiment 2). Participants were randomly assigned to receive five consecutive days of 20-minute audio guided mindfulness training or to a no-training audiobook control (Experiment 1) or an active relaxation training (Experiment 2). In Experiment 1 (N=149), students completed experience sampling and longitudinal surveys assessing interpretations of difficult physics experiences. In Experiment 2 (N=303), students completed daily diaries of interpretations of negative physics emotions for 15 consecutive weekdays before, during, and after training. In both experiments, preregistered analyses showed that mindfulness students reported more adaptive interpretations, and in Experiment 2, meaning-making changes mediated improvements in both challenge-type stress appraisals and physics motivation. Though mindfulness is about non-elaborative observation of the present, our findings suggest its practice can be used to internalize adaptive meaning-making about learning struggles.

articles.title: The cost of scrutiny: subclinical social anxiety and performance context reshape frontal-midline theta network reconfigurations during probabilistic learning
articles.authors: Hanjie Liu; Melle J. W. van der Molen
articles.abstract: Social anxiety is reliably characterized by biases toward avoidance and aversive learning. Frontal-midline theta (FM-theta) oscillations have been implicated as a key neural mechanism underlying these learning biases. Here we combined a dynamic network neuroscience approach with computational modeling to investigate how FM-theta oscillatory activity coordinates large-scale functional network interactions on a trial-to-trial basis during feedback-guided learning. Additionally, we examined how these neural dynamics are altered in social anxiety across different social contexts. A sample of 146 human participants (129 female, mean age = 20.4 years) with varying levels of social anxiety completed a probabilistic selection task while performing alone and under scrutiny. Using non-negative matrix factorization, we identified two functional neural subgraphs supported by FM-theta. Fronto-parietal connectivity increased following aversive outcomes and scaled with positive prediction errors, consistent with error-monitoring and belief-updating. Fronto-occipital connectivity scaled with prediction errors when performing alone but not under scrutiny, indicative of context-sensitive disruption of belief-updating. Participants with elevated social anxiety showed increased fronto-occipital connectivity, as well as stronger subgraph coupling, indexing cross-network integration. This latter effect facilitated learning of simple stimulus-reward associations, but hampered learning of difficult stimulus-reward associations. Together, these findings reveal that social anxiety amplifies fronto-occipital FM-theta connectivity and cross-network integration, facilitating learning under low demand while hampering learning under high demand.

articles.title: Stressed out! Not working out? Relationship between momentary stress and physical (in)activity across different time lags: An Ecological Momentary Assessment study
articles.authors: Melanie Bamert; Jennifer Inauen; Alea Ruf
articles.abstract:
Background: Stress is frequently cited as a barrier to physical activity, yet evidence from daily life remains inconclusive and may depend on the specific stress aspect (perceived stress, physiology), physical (in)activity indicator (e.g., steps, vigorous activity), and temporal window examined. This study investigated associations between multiple momentary stress aspects and subsequent physical (in)activity across several time lags in daily life.
Methods: Seventy-six adults in the weight loss maintenance phase who reported difficulties maintaining a balanced diet participated in a 7-day ecological momentary assessment study. Participants completed hourly smartphone surveys assessing momentary perceived stress and perceived safety and continuously wore a chest-mounted sensor to derive vagally-mediated heart rate variability (vmHRV), steps, light physical activity (LPA), moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), and sedentary behaviour (SB). Multilevel two-part models estimated within-person associations between each stress aspect and the subsequent occurrence and amount of physical (in)activity at 10-, 30-, 60-, and 120-minute lags.
Results: Within-person associations between momentary stress indicators and subsequent physical (in)activity were predominantly small and non-significant. When significant associations emerged, higher momentary stress was positively related to the amount of subsequent physical activity, particularly for steps. Significant associations for the occurrence of physical (in)activity were largely restricted to vmHRV, indicating that activation of stress-related physiology was related to a higher probability of engaging in physical activity. Results showed heterogeneity across time lags and physical activity indicators but were overall consistent across the three stress aspects in terms of the direction of the associations.
Conclusions: The findings highlight that associations between momentary stress and physical (in)activity in daily life were generally small and specific to the temporal resolution, but when significant, showed a consistent directional pattern across stress aspects. Higher momentary stress was followed by short-term increases in physical activity. While vmHRV largely converged with subjective stress indicators, it also revealed additional associations, highlighting complementary information across stress measures. Together, these findings emphasize the value of multimodal stress assessments and fine-grained, time-lagged analyses for capturing stress–physical activity dynamics in everyday life.

articles.title: Item-dropping to improve in-sample Cronbach's alpha can harm true reliability: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles.authors: Ze Freeman; Ian Hussey
articles.abstract: Cronbach's alpha is the most commonly reported metric of reliability in psychological measurement, and statistical software encourages a common post hoc revision: dropping the item whose removal most improves in-sample alpha. A Monte Carlo simulation examined what this practice does to true reliability, varying items per scale (5 to 40) and sample size (20 to 1,000), with item pools generated from a loading distribution fitted to 3,783 factor loadings from real psychological scales. Two strategies, always dropping the nominated item or dropping only when in-sample alpha improves, were evaluated against the population alpha and true reliability of the retained items. The bias in the reported alpha itself was modest, overstating true reliability only in short scales at small samples and understating it elsewhere. The decision was another matter: at the smallest scale and sample size, dropping reduced true reliability in 46.7% of the replications in which the conditional rule acted, despite requiring an apparent improvement, and almost the entire apparent gain was selection optimism. Stricter decision rules helped only in large samples: with N of 200 or more, acting only on apparent gains above .02 kept the probability of harming the scale at or below 7%, whereas at N = 20 no threshold examined made the decision safe. Because this risk depends on scale length and sample size, given loadings typical of trait scales, it is knowable before data are collected, whereas nothing inside the alpha-if-item-removed table distinguishes a genuinely weak item from a sampling artefact.

articles.title: Very little data tampering is needed to produce statistically significant results: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles.authors: Ian Hussey
articles.abstract: Simulation studies to date have examined the impact of Questionable Research Practices on the false positive rate of common statistical inference tests (e.g., Stefan & Schonbrödt, 2023), but not the impact of unquestionably undesirable research practices, such as fabrication and falsification. While any result can be obtained through sufficient fabrication or falsification, we have little insight into how much of either is needed to generate statistically significant results under a null hypothesis. This article therefore simulates data generated under the true null hypothesis and alters, deletes, or invents one data point at a time, targeting the data points that most oppose the desired result, and re-running the test after every change until it is significant in the intended direction. Six tampering strategies (dropping cases, switching condition labels, re-pairing values, duplicating, fabricating, and replacing cases) are applied to three common tests: the independent *t*-test, Pearson *r* correlation, and the Chi-square test for a 2x2 contingency table. Results demonstrate that, in small samples, only a small absolute number of tampers are typically needed to obtain significant results. In large samples, although the absolute number of tampers needed grows, the proportion of the sample needing to be tampered with to obtain significance falls rapidly. The strategies that alter no recorded value, and so are plausibly hardest to detect, are among the most effective. Critically, unjustifiably deleting inconvenient data points, which researchers rate as far more defensible than invention, is no less dangerous than outright fabrication: both manufacture false positives from null data reliably, and at comparable and very small cost (e.g., median tampers of 5-10% at moderate sample sizes across tests). Fabricating and falsifying results therefore requires a worryingly small amount of actual data tampering.

articles.title: Relationships between salivary oxytocin levels in infants, age and caregiving practices involving close proximity
articles.authors: Nicole Nadine Lønfeldt; Velisar Manea; Victoria Southgate
articles.abstract:
Oxytocin has been linked to social cognitive development. Salivary oxytocin has been found to decrease from five months to seven years, coinciding with declining attention to eyes. Oxytocin is stimulated by close interpersonal contact. As infants grow, they spend less time in close proximity to their caregivers, which may result in decreased levels of oxytocin.
Thus, in a sample of infants between eight and 21 months (n = 204), we estimated the relationship between age and salivary oxytocin levels, while controlling for potential confounders (gender, birth mode, birth with synthetic oxytocin) and explored the contribution of caregiving factors that involve close caregiver- infant contact (co-sleeping and breastfeeding) to the variation in oxytocin levels. Oxytocin concentrations in saliva were estimated with enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Correlations and a hierarchical multiple regression were conducted.
Bivariate and multivariate analyses did not support relationships between salivary oxytocin levels and age, co-sleeping or breastfeeding.
Our findings do not support the idea that infant salivary oxytocin levels decrease in response to infants growing older, gaining more independence, and moving physically away from caregivers as they stop breast and bottle feeding. Future studies may investigate these parent behaviors closer to saliva collection, using behavioral observation and measuring oxytocin reactivity.

articles.title: Effect of meditation across scales: Integrating metabolism, circadian rhythm and epigenetic mechanisms
articles.authors: Palkin Arora; Vaibhav Tripathi
articles.abstract:
Meditation has long been studied for its ability to enhance mental, social, and emotional
well-being and reshape brain networks. This review presents an integrated perspective that
meditation is not only a form of mental training but also a phenomenon with measurable
physiological and molecular correlates.
Emerging findings reveal that meditation modulates stress-induced markers, cerebral
metabolic changes, hormonal rhythms, and changes in gene expression and epigenetic regulation
across cellular pathways in humans. This review proposes an integrative multiscale model in
which meditation is shown to contribute to the coordination between neural activity and
peripheral rhythms, thereby promoting adaptive homeostasis. This multi-scale perspective
provides a biological framework for understanding how meditation influences processes across
the brain and body.

articles.title: Semantic Network Sharing in Human Versus LLM Discussion Groups
articles.authors: Yoshiko Arima
articles.abstract: Using a corpus of 51 mock-jury discussion groups, we analyzed the discussion process of human groups and then compared it with that of large language model (LLM) groups in an exploratory analysis. The task was a hidden profile task, solvable only by combining information distributed across members. We examined solution-path attainment and the sharedness of the word-level semantic network (the cross-member edge ratio: the proportion of edges linking words introduced by different members) in relation to the information-sharing process. Human discussion progressed from individual to group-level sharing: an information-sharing phase in which intra-individual semantic networks remained (cross-member edge ratio .34), followed by an information-integration phase in which network links became shared across members (.54), and a decision phase (.66). In LLM groups calibrated to human behavioral statistics, this three-phase structure was radically compressed, lacking the human allocation of time. Under a memory constraint, however, the individual-to-group sharing shift observed in humans emerged. A stepwise prompt ladder reproduced the reported collapse of LLM collective reasoning and identified the constraints that avert it. Moreover, the association between the sharedness of the semantic network and solution-path attainment found in human groups (ρ = +.52, n = 50) was not observed in LLM groups (n = 8 per condition). These differences are interpreted as showing the contrast between human groups, which come to share a semantic network gradually through discussion, and LLM groups, which share a knowledge structure from the outset.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Mental Health Support Tool, Not a Therapist: Implications for Young People, Families and Schools
articles.authors: John Olusola Ojo
articles.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of how young people respond to emotional distress. This research commentary examines why young people may turn to AI chatbots for mental health support, the potential benefits and risks, and how families, schools and communities can respond. Immediate access, perceived privacy and discomfort discussing emotional difficulties may help explain why some young people use chatbots, particularly when professional support feels unavailable or difficult to access. However, general-purpose AI systems were not designed to provide mental health care, and emerging evidence raises concerns about misleading advice, sycophantic responses, emotional dependence and the potential reinforcement of distorted or delusional beliefs in vulnerable users. AI cannot observe a young person’s physical condition, conduct a comprehensive clinical risk assessment or ensure that appropriate safeguarding action follows. It may help young people organise their thoughts, prepare for a conversation or identify questions to discuss with a trusted adult or professional, but it cannot replace human connection, professional judgement or accountable care. This commentary proposes a balanced and precautionary response that supports young people in using AI safely while maintaining clear pathways to appropriate human support.

articles.title: Does facial expression processing require attention? A multi-lab replication of Eimer et al. (2003)
articles.authors: Ziyi Wang; Alejandro Estudillo; Ala Yankouskaya; Nazanin S. Andalibi; Amy Bland; Chris Robert Harrison Brown; Elisabeth Fonteneau; Donovan G. Govan; Marine Granjon; Tijl Grootswagers
articles.abstract: How the brain processes facial expressions and whether this process requires focal attention have been central topics of neurophysiological research on face processing. In a seminal study, using scalp-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs), Eimer, Holmes, and McGlone (2003) found that emotional and neutral faces were differently processed in the brain as early as 160 ms after stimulus onset. Importantly, these ERP differences disappeared when attention was directed away from the face stimuli, suggesting the necessity of focal attention in facial expression processing. These results have greatly motivated further research in the field. Yet, subsequent research did not always agree with these findings, and the study was never directly replicated. Hence, this study has been selected by #EEGManyLabs, a global and multi-laboratory replication project, for a high-powered direct replication across multiple laboratories (N = 41 in each laboratory). We hypothesize the replication of the original positive findings, including the ERP effects differentiating emotional and neutral faces and their dependence on focal attention. To address the debate on facial expression processing and the role of N170, we will also take this opportunity to reassess key negative findings of the original study, namely no difference between emotional and neutral facial expressions in N170 and no ERP differences among the six facial expressions. Replication or revision of these findings will confirm the necessity of focal attention in emotional face processing and the postulated biomarkers of basic emotion processing. This study will provide a reproducible benchmark on face processing.

articles.title: Emoticon variation: Noses and rotations do not alter meaning, but mouths and mirrorings do
articles.authors: Dominic Thompson; Shuping Ling
articles.abstract: Emoticons can visually differ in various minor ways. This includes presence or absence of an element, like the 'nose' or 'tear' in the :-) and :'( emoticons, differences in orientation, as in the :) versus (: emoticons, or a change to an element, such as the 'eyes' in the :) versus ;) emoticons. It is unclear which types of variation impact meaning or whether there is consistency in the types of variation that have the most effect on meaning. We present a study investigating how emoticon variations are perceived and interpreted in a range of contexts, including positive, negative, and sarcastic. Given that an established function of emoticons is to clarify message intent, and research suggests non-native speakers may use emoticons in a compensatory way, we also compare the perceptions and interpretations of native (n = 151) and non-native (n = 119) speakers of English in each context type. Utilising emoticons that were produced by participants in earlier research, a series of ratings and emoticon selections reveal patterns of contextual use, interpretation, and perceptions of meaning equivalence. Results reveal that specific visual variations, including the nose element or rotation of an emoticon, have little impact on meaning, while other variations, such as mouthshape or mirroring an emoticon, do alter meaning. The scale of visual change does not correlate with meaning change. Results also indicate native and non-native speakers pattern very closely in their overall use and interpretation, suggesting emoticons can be useful in facilitating cross-cultural or cross-linguistic conversations. However, there are important exceptions with more subtle emoticon variations and in more semantically complex contexts. This suggests the nuances of emoticon usage within a language community take more time to acquire.

articles.title: Estimand or estimator? Comparing vowel overlap measures against a known ground truth
articles.authors: Grant M Berry
articles.abstract: Many scalar indices quantify acoustic category separation—the Pillai trace, Bhattacharyya distance, and the overlap coefficient—yet seldom are they computed on the same data. Disagreements are read as differences of functional but are often differences of estimator. Phontrast, a reproducible, open-source R toolkit, computes measures from one token-level table over a shared kernel density estimation backbone; a positive-control simulation with known Bayes-optimal truth separates each measure's estimand from its estimator. Location-only and Gaussian-family measures are provably unresponsive to higher-moment separation—possibility, not prevalence. Two results are empirical: (1) every estimator inflates with dimensionality at fixed sample size, whereas at two dimensions the kernel estimators understate population values by 29% at 500 tokens per category; and (2) halving or doubling the bandwidth moves a kernel estimate by up to 0.98 of its [0, 1] scale. Two public vowel datasets demonstrate the toolkit rather than deliver phonological findings: in thirteen dimensions (MFCCs), the Bhattacharyya functional tracks overlap at r = −.951, ρ = −.989 under a matched kernel but −.710, −.849 in closed form. Crucially, the gap is the estimator, not the functional. No single functional dominates; Jensen–Shannon distance is foregrounded as a distribution-free metric that delivers an interpretable quantity.

articles.title: A movement-suppression perspective of cognitive effort during listening
articles.authors: Bjorn Herrmann
articles.abstract: Cognitive effort shapes how well speech is understood under difficult conditions, yet how listeners regulate it remains poorly understood. Here, I review an overlooked motor dimension: effortful listening reduces gaze, saccades, blinks, and head movements. This movement suppression is not a simple proxy for effort, however, because stillness also marks inward disengagement. I argue that movement suppression instead reflects a listener's broader attentional and behavioral state, and propose a framework distinguishing casual, focused, and disengaged listening. I outline a neuro-functional architecture linking auditory, cognitive, and motor systems, and discuss how, within the focused mode, suppressing movement may aid comprehension. Treating movement as part of the listening state unites systems usually studied apart and casts effort as a perception–action process.

articles.title: Reinforcement learning underlies social connection and memory in a friendship decision-making task
articles.authors: Courtney A. Jimenez; Meghan L Meyer
articles.abstract: Who we choose to befriend can impact many of our own life outcomes, from social capital to wellbeing. Here we find that reinforcement learning principles can characterize friendship decision-making and predict social connection and memory for a potential friend. Participants completed a novel friendship decision-making paradigm in which they observed video clips from the reality TV show, The Valley, depicting a clique of friends navigating friendship with a specific character, Kristen. The clips were normed to vary in the reward value of friendship with Kristen. For each scene, participants decided whether they would want to be friends with Kristen and how connected they felt to her. One day later, they completed surprise memory tests and individual-difference measures. The reward, expected value, and prediction error of a scene about Kristen predicted participants’ feelings of connection to her. Individual differences relevant to friendship formation—concern over relationship acceptance and social support receipt—corresponded with differences in exploratory versus exploitative friendship decision-making (inverse temperature) and flexibility in learning about Kristen (learning rate). Finally, memory showed a negativity bias. Participants more accurately recalled scenes characterized by lower friendship reward and larger negative friendship prediction errors. Together, these findings suggest that friendship formation can be viewed as a learning problem: people continuously update expectations about friendship with others, and those updates shape both social connection and memory. Computational principles that help us learn about rewards in the world may also help shape who we fold into our social world.

articles.title: A guide to evaluating LLM-based extraction and judgement tools
articles.authors: Jamie Cummins
articles.abstract: Researchers have begun to delegate extraction and judgement research tasks to tools built on large language models (LLMs), including the annotation of text, screening of papers, extraction of numerical values, and identification of supporting passages. Existing guidance establishes that these tools should be validated, documented, and tested for robustness. Researchers still need practical guidance, however, on how precisely different tools can be most appropriately evaluated. This paper provides a step-by-step workflow for evaluating such tools. This involves firstly defining the tool’s output, identifying the desired comparator, and specifying what would count as satisfactory performance – from these decisions, the appropriate analyses and requirements for comparison can be determined and conducted. I provide a worked example of this evaluation approach based on a simulated systematic review extraction-and-judgement tool.

articles.title: Are Temperament and Personality Traits Sibling Constructs or Twins? Toward a Lifespan Science of Personality Development
articles.authors: Katherine M. Lawson; Whitney R. Ringwald; Rebecca Shiner; Richard Robins
articles.abstract: Temperament and personality traits both refer to relatively stable individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, but they are often studied in isolation from each other. Consequently, there are vast bodies of research exploring the nature, development, and consequences of temperament and personality traits, with little integration between areas. The present study examines the overlap vs. distinctness of temperament and personality traits, with the goal of promoting greater integration. First, we review past theory and research on their connections. Then, we apply 10 criteria from Lawson and Robins’ (2021) sibling constructs framework, supplemented by recently developed methods from large language models, to understand associations at the construct and measurement levels — aiming to orient researchers away from black-or-white thinking that has divided the two fields and toward embracing the complex overlap that characterizes the relationship between these domains. Based on our analyses, we argue that temperament and personality traits show substantial overlap at the construct level, differing mainly in how they are measured. We provide recommendations to unify these unnecessarily disparate literatures, paving the way toward a genuine, integrated science of personality development across the lifespan.

articles.title: Reward, Affiliative, and Dominance Smiles are Categorized More Accurately when Defined in Morphological than Socio-Functional Terms
articles.authors: Paweł Malinowski; Monika Wróbel
articles.abstract:
Little is known about the role that perceivers’ conceptual knowledge of the social and morphological aspects of facial expressions plays in emotion recognition. Here, we examine how smile conceptualization and dynamics impact the categorization of reward, affiliative, and dominance smiles based on the Simulation of Smiles Model. In Study 1 (n = 192), Polish participants read definitions of smiles formulated in either morphological or socio-functional terms. Next, they viewed dynamic or static expressions of these smiles and rated the extent to which each expression portrayed a reward, affiliative, and dominance smile. As predicted and consistent with previous studies, affiliative smiles were categorized more accurately when presented in dynamic than in static form. However, contrary to our expectations, the categorization was more accurate when smiles were defined in morphological than socio-functional terms. Studies 2 (n = 196) and 3 (n = 265) replicated the advantage of morphological over socio-functional conceptualizations in UK-based samples but did not unambiguously support the role of dynamics in smile categorization. Together, our findings suggest that the impact of expression dynamics on smile categorization may be more complex than previously assumed and point to the role of smile conceptualization in this process.

Keywords: smile, facial expression, emotion categorization, facial dynamics, positive emotion

articles.title: Environmental Influences using Linked External Data in ABCD: A Review of the First Decade
articles.authors: Carlos Cardenas-Iniguez; Shermaine Abad; Michell M. Hernandez Flores3; Erin Thompson; Thomas Elliott Floyd; Aaron Reuben; Ka I Ip; Marybel Robledo Gonzalez; Kelly Shen; Nardos Iyob
articles.abstract: Environmental contextual factors, including neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built environments, and environmental exposures, exert complex and multifaceted influences on neurodevelopmental outcomes. Characterizing these influences requires linking high-resolution geocoded residential data to information about neighborhoods, built and natural environments, exposures, and policies.  We synthesize a decade of Linked External Data Environment and Policy (LED-E&P) research within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM (ABCD) Study – a longitudinal cohort of ~11,800 U.S. youth, organized around the Adolescent Neural Urbanome, a framework that moves beyond aggregate socioeconomic proxies to directly measured environmental features.  We first describe an overview of the LED-E&P working group, describe the geographical coverage of the ABCD Study dataset, and then summarize key findings across neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built and urban environments, air pollution, greenspace, and macro-level state policies. The evidence consistently shows that adolescent development is shaped by cumulative environmental influences.  Across these findings, three themes recur: these influences reflect social and structural drivers of health rather than differences in children or communities; both risk and protective factors shape outcomes; and developmental timing and study design determine what can be concluded. Moving forward, continued refinement of residential geocoding and exposure methods, integration with biological data, and translation to intervention science will advance understanding of modifiable environmental influences. This work enhances our ability to characterize developmental environments and identify modifiable targets to promote healthy development across adolescence and beyond.

articles.title: Human or AI? An Interpretable Method for Auditing  Free-Text Data in Online Psychological Research
articles.authors: Joanna Kuc; Anthony Hills; Greg Cooper; Mahmud Elahi Akhter; Talia Tseriotou; Maria Liakata; Daniel Robert Lametti; Jeremy I Skipper
articles.abstract: Online psychological studies increasingly rely on free-text responses, but the availability of generative AI creates new challenges for evaluating the authenticity and integrity of data pertaining to human introspection. We present an interpretable text-analysis workflow for identifying linguistic cues associated with perceived AI authorship in digital journal entries. Across a two-week journalling study, 251 participants submitted 2,808 text entries, which were independently labelled by human annotators as human-written, AI-generated or invalid, and compared with classifications from a commercial AI-detection tool. We extracted 127 transparent features capturing length, semantic coherence, stylistic consistency, readability, natural-language-inference-based consistency, lexical overlap and Linguistic Inquiry Word Count 2022 psycholinguistic categories. On a high-confidence subset defined by convergence between human judgements and automated detection, interpretable classifiers strongly distinguished entries perceived as human from those perceived as AI-generated. A decision tree achieved 95.3% accuracy using a small set of auditable rules based on verb rate, syllable count, article use and sentence count, while a linear SVM identified 18.6% of entries as ambiguous cases suitable for human review. Entries perceived as AI-generated were longer, more coherent, more stylistically uniform and more formally structured, whereas entries perceived as human showed greater present focus, self-reference and stylistic variability. These findings provide a transparent framework for auditing possible AI mediation in remote psychological text data, while showing how interpretable models can support human review rather than replace it.

articles.title: Workplace Spirituality and Academic Achievement in Business Schools: The Mediating and Moderating Roles of Self-Efficacy
articles.authors: Sunil Kumar
articles.abstract:
Purpose — Academic achievement is shaped not only by students' cognitive capabilities but also by the institutional and psychological environments that support their learning and developmental trajectories. Although workplace spirituality has been extensively associated with positive individual and organizational outcomes in corporate settings, its influence on students' academic achievement and the underlying psychological mechanisms in higher education remain under-theorized and empirically underexplored. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and Psychological Capital (PsyCap) Theory, this study examines the impact of workplace spirituality on academic achievement by investigating the dual role of self-efficacy as both a mediator and a moderator among business school students.
Design/methodology/approach — Primary survey data were gathered from a sample of 230 postgraduate and undergraduate students enrolled across QS-ranked business schools in India using validated, multi-item measurement scales. The proposed conceptual and structural framework was evaluated using R (Version 4.5.3) and variance-based Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) utilizing the `seminr` package with 5,000 bootstrap re-samples.
Findings — The empirical results demonstrate that workplace spirituality exerts a robust, positive influence on both self-efficacy (β = 0.841, p < 0.001, f2 = 2.490) and academic achievement (β = 0.307, p = 0.018, f2 = 0.074). Self-efficacy is likewise positively and significantly associated with academic achievement (β = 0.493, p < 0.001, f2 = 0.178). Mediation analysis confirms that self-efficacy partially mediates the relationship between workplace spirituality and academic achievement, accounting for 56.68% of the total effect (indirect β = 0.416, p < 0.001; total β = 0.734, p < 0.001). In contrast, the hypothesised moderating role of self-efficacy on the spirituality–achievement relationship is not supported (β = -0.050, p = 0.108). The overall structural model demonstrates substantial explanatory power, accounting for 70.7% of the variance in self-efficacy (R2 = 0.707, Adjusted R2 = 0.712) and 60.8% of the variance in academic achievement (R2 = 0.608, Adjusted R2 = 0.604).
Originality/value — This study advances higher education management literature by extending the paradigm of workplace spirituality from traditional corporate organizational settings to business school environments. It demystifies the "black box" linking spiritual, meaningful institutional climates with objective and subjective student outcomes, proving that workplace spirituality functions primarily as an essential socio-contextual antecedent that activates students' intrinsic efficacy beliefs.

articles.title: Psychometric Properties of the Highly Sensitive Child Scale and Its Role in Socio-Emotional and Behavioral Development: Evidence from Japanese Adolescent Samples
articles.authors: Shuhei Iimura; Kosuke Yano; Chieko Kibe; Sofie Weyn; Michael Pluess
articles.abstract: Environmental sensitivity, defined as the capacity to perceive and process information from both supportive and adverse environmental experiences, plays an important role in socio-emotional and behavioral development. However, existing research has predominantly focused on childhood, leaving a gap in our understanding of environmental sensitivity during adolescence. To bridge this gap, we conducted three studies using self-report data from 2,375 Japanese adolescents aged 10–14 years and their mothers. First, we aimed to provide a comprehensive description of adolescent sensory processing sensitivity (referred to as trait sensitivity) by applying the 21-item Highly Sensitive Child scale to Japanese adolescents (Studies 1 and 2). Second, using three-wave longitudinal data, we examined how trait sensitivity interacts with various environmental contexts (i.e., negative/positive parenting and peer relationships) to predict adolescents’ socio-emotional and behavioral development (Study 3). Results showed that adolescent trait sensitivity was characterized by a general factor reflecting sensitivity to a broad range of negative and positive stimuli, as well as two specific domains: Ease of Excitation–Low Sensory Threshold and Aesthetic Sensitivity (i.e., bifactor model). Trait sensitivity was positively correlated with other temperament and personality traits, including negative emotionality, behavioral inhibition, neuroticism, and openness. Trait sensitivity and environmental factors independently predicted internalizing and externalizing problems, as well as prosocial behavior. Notably, trait sensitivity was a significant positive predictor of both internalizing problems and prosocial behavior. These findings suggest partial continuity in the structure and developmental functions of trait sensitivity from childhood to adolescence.

articles.title: From RI-CLPM to panelGVAR: Evaluating Stationarity in Network Modeling of Panel Data
articles.authors: Sacha Epskamp; Hyungjun Park; Xinkai Du; Nadyanna M. Majeed; Adela-Maria Isvoranu
articles.abstract:
The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) and the panel graphical vector-autoregression model (panelGVAR) are two popular frameworks for multivariate panel data. These models differ along two dimensions, and we contribute new methodology on both. The first dimension is stationarity: the panelGVAR constrains all parameters to be equal over time and treats the first wave as endogenous, whereas the RI-CLPM, as commonly specified, leaves every parameter wave-specific. Our first contribution is a pipeline of nested models: a guarded decision tree that tests one stationarity constraint at a time and releases those that fail. The second dimension is the parameterization: our second contribution integrates the GGMs into the RI-CLPM, yielding the random-intercept cross-lagged panel network model (RI-CLPN), which standard SEM software cannot specify. Both are implemented in the R package psychonetrics. Two simulation studies evaluate the
per-constraint verdicts under likelihood-ratio, AIC, and BIC criteria and network recovery under mean and variance non-stationarity. They show which violations the pipeline detects, and what ignoring them costs when a panelGVAR is fitted directly. A tutorial and two empirical examples illustrate the pipeline.

articles.title: Brief and simultaneous assessment of delay, probability, and joint delay–probability discounting: Initial validation of the three-for-one discounting task in tobacco use [preprint]
articles.authors: Jeff S. Stein; Haylee Downey; Justin Charles Strickland; Allison Tegge
articles.abstract:
Abstract
While delay discounting (DD) is a reliable marker of tobacco use, far less is known about probability discounting (PD) or how delay and risk jointly influence decision-making. To allow simultaneous assessment of DD, PD, and their interaction, we developed the three-for-one (TFO) discounting task. In 36 trials (<3 minutes), the TFO task estimates Effective Delay 50 (ED50) across a range of reward probabilities, allowing both empirical analysis of how risk impacts DD and quantitative modeling to derive independent DD and PD rates (k, h). Adults (n=134) reporting current- or never-cigarette smoking completed the TFO task, standalone DD and PD tasks, and a risk-numeracy scale (measuring understanding of risk/probability). The current vs. never-smoking group showed lower ED50 (higher DD) for certain/near-certain rewards (ps≤.021), but not riskier rewards. TFO-derived DD and PD rates showed evidence of known-groups validity (sensitivity to smoking-related DD differences, p=.002), discriminant validity (small correlation between DD and PD, r=.11), and convergent validity (moderate-to-strong correspondence with standalone tasks, ps<.001). The never-smoking group showed higher between-task correspondence in DD (p=.001); however, this effect was better accounted for by a moderating role of risk numeracy, evident in both DD and PD (ps<.001). Collectively, the TFO task showed that risk attenuates smoking-related group differences in DD and provided generally accurate assessment of DD and PD rates. Accuracy may be lower in participants with lower risk numeracy, but this does not impact sensitivity to known group differences in DD. Future work should explore additional validation approaches while evaluating methods to mitigate numeracy-related effects.

articles.title: Bounded Psychological Change: Why Identity Preservation Constrains Experimental Effect Sizes
articles.authors: Erich H. Witte; Frank Zenker
articles.abstract: Experimental psychological studies consistently report small-to-medium effect sizes, with meta-analyses showing modal effects around Cohen’s d = 0.35 and the majority falling below d = 0.50. While these “smallish” effects are traditionally blamed on methodological deficits—such as low statistical power, publication bias, unreliable measures, and weak manipulations—this paper argues for a theoretically grounded constraint on the maximum expectable effect size. If human experimental participants are identity-preserving systems that naturally resist experimental task demands, these stable, modest effects can be understood as features of a system designed to preserve self-coherence. Drawing on the dynamics of assimilation and accommodation, we propose two axioms: a limited adaptation budget and the constraint that accommodation cannot exceed assimilation without destabilizing identity. Combined with a simple linear averaging assumption, these axioms yield a maximum standardized effect size of d = 0.50 as an upper bound for experimentally induced behavioral changes—on the assumption that ethically permissible manipulations in identity-relevant domains shift the average participant no more than one-half (z-standardized) standard deviation from the control baseline. This theoretically motivated explanation fits remarkably well with empirical meta-analytic evidence, yields falsifiable predictions, highlights the role of shared meaning spaces, and problematizes the conditions under which experimental and control groups can be meaningfully compared. We provide practical guidelines for designing studies that respect the bounded nature of identity-relevant change and for interpreting effect sizes as proportions of a domain-specific maximum.

articles.title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
articles.authors: Charlotte Riedl; Tao Burga; Erola Pons; Patricia Groß; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

articles.title: Unpacking Human Decision Strategies during AI-aided Decision-making
articles.authors: Haoming Sun; Chao Zhang; Linghan Zhang; Chris Snijders
articles.abstract: Interventions aimed at improving appropriate reliance on AI have had mixed effectiveness. We argue that this may be due to the lack of attention to individual differences in human decision strategies, combined with overconfidence in relying on the results of aggregate-level analyses. We approach this issue in a set of three studies. In Study 1, we design a set of decision strategies grounded in self- and AI-confidence to provide a robust first-order approximation of what individual strategies can be. We use simulation to assess the conditions under which these strategies are identifiable.
