Across two experiments (N = 173), we found that 1) reward rate estimates were more accurate for frequently sampled options and 2) confidence in estimation accuracy was unaffected by the sampling frequency. Importantly, when frequently sampled options had objectively poor reward rates, participants shifted their preference toward the infrequently sampled option, suggesting that frequent sampling improved their ability to identify the better option. These results suggest that frequency bias reflects a “rational” use of frequently sampled information rather than an irrational distortion of reward-rate estimation or confidence.

articles.title: Angular Discrepancy and Personality Functioning Across Interpersonal Circumplex Surfaces
articles.authors: Kimberly J. Gilbert; Christopher James Hopwood
articles.abstract: Multisurface interpersonal assessment (MSIA) compares interpersonal circumplex (IPC) profiles across surfaces such as problems, sensitivities, values, and efficacies. A core premise of MSIA is that cross-surface discrepancy, the degree to which interpersonal themes align or diverge across these surfaces, carries clinical meaning beyond the elevation of any single surface, yet this assumption has rarely been tested directly. The present study operationalized cross-surface discrepancy as the angular distance between surface peaks and examined its association with personality functioning in 1,101 community adults. Greater discrepancy between problems and efficacies (r = -.47) and problems and values (r = -.37) predicted higher levels of personality functioning and explained incremental variance beyond surface elevations (change in R² = .034 and .044). Follow-up analyses suggested that people whose primary problems involved being too cold had higher personality functioning if they had values and efficacies in non-cold regions of the IPC. Associations between personality functioning and problems-sensitivities discrepancy were mostly explained by shared interpersonal dysfunction, and non-problem pairs showed negligible effects. These findings offer initial evidence that people who tend to have problems being too cold have higher levels of personality functioning to the degree they value and can engage in non-cold interpersonal behaviors.

articles.title: Affective Abstraction and Emotion Differentiation Across Development
articles.authors: Miłka S. Waniak; Chantal A. Valdivia-Moreno; Ajay Satpute; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: To master a culture’s categorical systems, growing minds must learn both to identify abstract similarities that bind two individual instances into a common category (e.g., recognizing what makes Scooby and Snoopy both “dogs”) and to differentiate instances that belong to different categories (e.g., calling Garfield a “cat” rather than a “dog”). Research has charted how children learn to “lump” and “split” categories in the cognitive literature, but we know much less about how emotion categories develop. Here, we administered laboratory tasks assessing affective abstraction (i.e., the ability to match two images that induce similar affective experiences) and emotion differentiation (i.e., how specifically one categorizes one’s emotions as distinct) to a cross-sectional sample of participants in the USA aged 10-25 (50.62% women). Affective abstraction scores were largely uncorrelated with age, but the ability to match cross-category stimuli of the same valence (e.g., a negative-affect-inducing house and a negative-affect-inducing animal) increased with age. Interestingly, affective abstraction and emotion differentiation scores were positively associated, especially in youth participants. Thus, abstraction and differentiation are not merely opposites of each other (i.e., it’s not the case that people either tend to chronically “lump” emotion categories or chronically “split” emotion categories). Instead, there may be shared cognitive processes that allow individuals to construct emotion categories that are both nuanced and general enough to conform to societal norms, and this covariance is most pronounced in youth. These results shed new light on the development of emotion categorization.

articles.title: AI Overviews Reduce Search Result Engagement & May Influence Attitude Polarization
articles.authors: Saloni Dash; Yiwei Xu; Lei Cai; Sterling Williams-Ceci; Wang Liao; Emma Spiro
articles.abstract: AI-generated overviews (AIOs) increasingly appear at the top of search result pages, making them the first, and potentially only, content users encounter during search. Despite their widespread adoption, their impact on information seeking, processing, and downstream attitudes remains critically underexplored. Across two preregistered experiments (N = 2,797), we randomly assigned participants to view AIOs on one of four contested topics manipulated to be attitude-congruent, attitude-incongruent, or balanced (only Study 2) relative to their prior attitudes. Participants who viewed an AIO, irrespective of content, were significantly less likely to engage with subsequent search results than control (no AIO). Participants perceived attitude-incongruent AIOs as more biased and weaker than attitude-congruent AIOs. Despite this, attitude-incongruent AIOs reduced attitude polarization relative to attitude-congruent AIOs in Study 1, but not in Study 2 (although directionally consistent). Taken together, these findings suggest that AIOs significantly influence information seeking and processing and raise critical concerns for democratic deliberation.

articles.title: How Social Context Shapes Perceived Identity Overlap:  Evidence from Christian Democrats
articles.authors: Trystan Loustau; Liane Young
articles.abstract: Why do some people perceive two social identities as fitting together while others see them as largely distinct? We propose that these perceptions are shaped, in part, by the social environments in which people live. We tested this model using Christian Democrats, whose religious and political identities often violate prevailing partisan stereotypes. Two observational studies (Ns = 505 and 484) showed that local political (Democratic voting margins) and religious (Christian prevalence) contexts predicted perceived support for Christian and Democratic identities. Specifically, living in more Democratic counties was associated with greater perceived support for Democrats and lower perceived support for Christians, whereas living in more Christian counties was generally associated with greater perceived support for Christians and lower perceived support for Democrats. In turn, greater perceived support for either identity was associated with perceiving Christian and Democratic identities as more overlapping. Consistent with this model, a preregistered experiment (N = 769) demonstrated that increasing perceived support for Christians increased perceived overlap between Christian and Democratic identities. Across studies, greater perceived overlap was selectively associated with warmer evaluations of Christian and Republican targets, suggesting that when people perceive their identities as not fitting together, they may reaffirm one identity (e.g., Democrat) by distancing themselves from the competing identity (e.g., Christian) and salient outgroup members (e.g., Republicans). Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of identity overlap are shaped by social environments and identify perceived social support as one mechanism through which social environments influence these perceptions.

articles.title: Increasing Governmental Efficacy Beliefs Drives Support for Congestion Pricing Policy
articles.authors: Danielle Goldwert; Anandita Sabherwal; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles.abstract: Congestion pricing charges drivers a fee to enter high-traffic areas, reducing congestion and travel times while generating revenue for public transit and lowering air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Despite its effectiveness, the policy remains contentious because it imposes immediate, salient personal costs in exchange for benefits that are less tangible, delayed, and distributed across both individuals (e.g., shorter, more reliable trips) and society (e.g., cleaner air, safer streets, and improved public transit). This asymmetry between how costs and benefits are experienced poses a challenge to public support, which is essential for both the adoption and long-term durability of the policy. Across two large-scale experiments conducted in New York State (N = 15,014) and Washington, D.C. (N = 4,030), we tested 24 psychologically informed interventions designed to increase support for congestion pricing. Increasing governmental outcome efficacy beliefs, by emphasizing that the policy enables government to deliver meaningful public benefits, emerged as the most effective strategy, increasing support for congestion pricing by 30%, while also improving perceptions of the policy's effectiveness and fairness. These effects were robust across intervention delivery modes that varied in participant engagement and did not differ by political affiliation. Together, these findings identify policy-specific outcome efficacy as a scalable and politically robust communication strategy for building public support for sustainable transportation policies.

articles.title: Shared Neurobiological and Computational Mechanisms of Psychedelic, Contemplative, and Fasting-Induced Mystical Experience
articles.authors: Alex Jinich-Diamant
articles.abstract: Psychedelics, contemplative practice, and fasting are physiologically unrelated interventions that nevertheless converge, across cultures and centuries, on a common experiential endpoint: the mystical state. Here I propose that this convergence reflects shared disruption of a single computational architecture, the precision-weighted predictive hierarchy, through three mechanistically distinct but functionally equivalent routes. Serotonergic psychedelics sensitize layer 5 pyramidal neurons and disinhibit higher-order thalamic nuclei, relaxing the gain on top-down priors; open-monitoring meditation shifts thalamocortical coupling geometry toward diffuse, matrix-type connectivity, elevating cortical entropy; and caloric restriction attenuates the metabolic machinery sustaining high-level attractor states, destabilizing the default mode network from below. All three routes terminate in a transient near-critical regime characterized by relaxed priors, scale-free cortical dynamics, and expanded degrees of freedom in the brain's generative model, conditions I identify as the neurobiological substrate of mystical experience. Critically, the depth of this state, not its pharmacological or procedural occasion, is the primary predictor of lasting therapeutic benefit, implicating conscious experience itself as the mechanistic agent of change. I further argue that near-critical dynamics may constitute the conditions under which field-theoretic and quantum-coherent contributions to consciousness become empirically detectable. This framework generates testable predictions across molecular, circuit, and phenomenological levels, and positions the neuroscience of mystical states as a tractable frontier for understanding how the brain constructs, maintains, and fundamentally reorganizes its model of reality.

articles.title: Beyond Color: A Constructivist Account of Chromatic Stimuli as Multidimensional Physiological and Psychological Events
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: Color science has spent most of its history explaining one thing: the conscious sensation of hue, saturation, and brightness. Yet beside that success sits a growing list of inconvenient findings. Examples include ambiguous colors (one photograph seen as white-and-gold by some and blue-and-black by others); memory colors (a gray banana that looks faintly yellow); color before form (newly sighted patients who see color before objects); imagined or dreamed colors (chromatic experiences generated without light or eyes); aphantasia (people who cannot summon a color in imagination); synesthesia (a printed letter flooded with color); and large, stable individual differences in the colors people report. These are not marginal curiosities or isolated anomalies. They are the ordinary output of a system that the percept-centered framework leaves out. A chromatic stimulus does not simply produce a color percept; it initiates a broad physiological and psychological event, of which the percept is only one part. That percept is constructed at the moment of seeing by memory, language, attention, affect, and culture, and it shapes them in turn, a reciprocal determinism of percept and event. I develop this framework at three levels, as two nested theories: a new theory of color contained within a constructivist model of the entire chromatic event. The account retains trichromatic and some opponent-process theory rather than replacing them, but extends them by predicting phenomena the traditional framework treats as noise. Chief among these are the individual differences that, on this view, become the primary evidence for how color is constructed.

articles.title: Geographically aggregated psychological traits from linguistic analysis of Twitter data predict U.S. voter realignment since 2016
articles.authors: Michael Stewart Cohen; Mehak Sachdeva; Zening Duan
articles.abstract:
The 2016 U.S. Presidential election heralded the beginning of a political realignment in American politics. A key question for understanding this realignment is whether the Republican party’s shift towards right-wing populism was driven by Donald Trump’s candidacy, versus Trump’s political success being driven by dynamics in the electorate that predated his political
rise. Individual surveys have commonly been used to address such questions, but there are many limitations to that method, including the cost of data collection and the need for accurate self-reflection on psychological questionnaires. We instead addressed this question by examining a corpus of Twitter posts written between July 2009 and February 2015, aggregated by U.S. county. The geographic distribution of psychological traits (personality, empathy, and moral foundations) was estimated by applying to the aggregated Twitter data lexica quantifying how strongly individual words predict psychological traits. The aggregate personality measures were then used to predict vote share for Donald Trump from 2016 to 2024, controlling for a baseline of prior Republican support. Low agreeableness predicts greater support for Trump, a novel result relative to other geographically aggregated data but consistent with prior survey findings relating this trait to right-wing populism. Low empathic concern and the degree to which tweets reference unfairness and defilement also predict shifts towards Trump. Our analysis suggests that people in geographic regions that shifted rightward beginning in 2016 were already expressing emotions consistent with Donald Trump’s messaging in their social media postings before his political rise.

articles.title: Effects of inoculation interventions on impressions of mock political candidates
articles.authors: Michael Stewart Cohen; Jean Decety
articles.abstract: Inoculation interventions have been a major focus of recent research attempting to combat the influence of disinformation in our society. However, no prior work has examined whether these interventions specifically reduce the impact of unproven or false accusations against politicians, which is a major vector by which disinformation can influence voting behavior in democracies. Here we demonstrate, through 11 studies, that interventions designed to increase awareness of manipulative messaging, such as the use of emotionally-charged language, can reduce the impact of derogatory accusations on impressions of novel mock political candidates. Individuals who viewed video or gamified inoculations showed a reduced impact of accusations on subjective ratings for all candidates about whom accusations of misconduct were made, relative to those who did not receive the inoculation. These effects were strongest when the truth status was ambiguous, but there is also some beneficial impact even when an accusation is clearly refuted, i.e., a reduction in Continued Influence Effects. Overall, these findings indicate that inoculation interventions that train citizens to be aware of manipulative techniques can effectively reduce the impact of unproven derogatory accusations against politicians.

articles.title: The latent geometry of dream content
articles.authors: Daniele Gatti; Tomaso Vecchi; Pietro Pietrini; Emiliano Ricciardi; Giulio Bernardi; Luca Rinaldi
articles.abstract: Dreams provide a potential unique window into human cognition, yet it remains unclear whether dream content reflects structured representational organization or largely idiosyncratic expression. Here, we analyze a large-scale dataset of dream narratives (21,607 reports) using a transformer language model to construct a high-dimensional representational space of dreams, in which each report is mapped onto a vector. We ask whether this space is structured, and if so, how different sources of information are organized within it. We find that dream content exhibits a structured latent geometry: dreams produced by different individuals, as well as by individuals of different genders, occupy systematically distinct regions of this space, particularly in more abstract semantic representations. Temporal information is also embedded in this geometry: the similarity between dreams decreases gradually as the temporal distance between them increases, revealing a continuous encoding of historical proximity, although this effect mainly reflects changes in language use and narrative conventions over time. Finally, similarity among independent descriptions of dreamers predicts similarity in their dream content, linking person-level characteristics to the organization of dream representations. Together, these results show that dreams are not random constructions but structured expressions of latent cognitive organization, in which personal, demographic and historical dimensions are systematically embedded across multiple representational levels. By making this structure explicit, the present approach provides a general computational framework for mapping the organization of internal experience.

articles.title: Pathways to Autistic Burnout: A Qualitative Study of French Autistic Adults' Experiences
articles.authors: Capucine Rebours; Jeanne Kruck
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Autistic burnout—a state of chronic exhaustion with functional loss and increased sensory sensitivity—has been identified as a significant yet underexplored phenomenon. While emerging research has documented potential contributors in Anglophone contexts, little is known about how autistic individuals in diverse institutional settings describe pathways to burnout. This study examined how French autistic adults identify and articulate factors contributing to their experiences of autistic burnout.
Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 67 French autistic adults (48 women, 11 men, 8 non-binary/agender/genderfluid; mean age 37.7 years; mean age at diagnosis 35.2 years). Interviews explored perceived contributors to burnout and were analyzed using qualitative content analysis with an abductive approach.
Results: Participants described burnout as emerging from cumulative exposure to unaccommodating environments rather than discrete triggering events. Key contributors included persistent sensory overload, social demands requiring sustained self-monitoring, camouflaging, and systemic barriers to recognition and support. Participants emphasized how chronic adaptation progressively depleted resources, with life transitions or micro-disruptions functioning as tipping points within already fragile equilibriums. Gendered experiences, particularly late diagnosis linked to gender-biased diagnostic frameworks, intensified burnout pathways for women and gender-diverse individuals.
Conclusion: Autistic burnout reflects sustained adaptation to environments misaligned with autistic needs rather than individual deficit. Findings underscore the need for multilevel interventions addressing environmental barriers, reducing camouflaging pressures, and ensuring timely, accessible diagnostic and support systems. France's distinctive institutional landscape—marked by psychoanalytic legacies and diagnostic delays—may shape how universal burnout mechanisms manifest.

articles.title: Spatial and featural cue weighting in children’s developing object representations
articles.authors: Vladislav Ayzenberg; Olivia Maltz; Samoni Nag; Amy Krivoshik; Stella F. Lourenco
articles.abstract: To accurately represent an object, observers must individuate it from surrounding objects and classify it with the appropriate category or identity. Adults flexibly weight different visual cues when perceiving objects, but less is known about whether, and how, the weighting of visual object information changes over development. The current study examined how and why children weight spatial (e.g., left/right location) and featural (e.g., color) cues during object perception. In Experiment 1, we tested whether 12-month-old infants and 4-year-old children encoded spatial and featural properties of objects, and, importantly, how children weighted these cues when they were pitted against each other. Infants learned and used relative spatial position more reliably than featural information. By contrast, preschoolers encoded both types of information but weighted featural information more heavily when the cues conflicted. In Experiment 2, we used computational models to test whether different visual objectives—individuation versus classification—are sufficient to produce these patterns of cue weighting. Models trained to individuate objects weighted spatial information more than features, whereas models trained to classify object weighted featural information more than space. These findings suggest that developmental changes in spatial and featural weighting may reflect, in part, changes in the visual objectives that guide object perception.

articles.title: Perceived error climate in primary school classrooms: A multidimensional perspective
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: The way teachers address errors in the classroom plays a crucial role in shaping how students experience their errors, regulate their learning processes, and ultimately learn from them. To capture these dynamics, the concept of the perceived error climate has been introduced, describing the extent to which errors are positively perceived and treated as constructive learning opportunities by teachers and students. Prior research with secondary school students conceptualized the error climate as comprising eight subdimensions organized under a single higher-order factor (Steuer et al., 2013). However, this structure has not yet been confirmed in younger students, and a single second-order factor may not provide a sufficiently differentiated representation of the construct. To address these deficits, we examined the structure of the perceived error climate in primary school classrooms and proposed a novel second-order structure distinguishing between emotional and instructional support following errors. The study drew on a sample of N = 2,628 third- and fourth-grade students from 187 classrooms across two domains (maths and German as a first language). Using multilevel multigroup confirmatory factor analyses, we examined the structure of the perceived error climate at both the individual and the classroom level. Results supported the proposed structure of eight subdimensions loading onto the two second-order factors of emotional and instructional support following errors. These second-order factors were positively related to students’ individual adaptive affective-motivational and adaptive action-related reactions to errors, respectively. Overall, the findings demonstrate that primary school students already perceive the error climate as a multifaceted classroom feature and that these distinctions are relevant for students’ engagement with their own errors.

articles.title: Mind wandering and executive functions: A conceptual replication of Kam & Handy (2014)
articles.authors: Mana Fazel; Esmée Verwijk; Hilde Geurts; Filip Van Opstal
articles.abstract:
Mind wandering – a spontaneous shift in attention away from a task – has been consistently
associated with impaired cognitive task performance, often attributed to disruptions in
executive functioning. In this study, we conducted three experiments to replicate and extend
previous work (Kam & Handy, 2014) by examining how mind wandering interacts with three
core executive functions: Inhibition (Experiment 1: Sustained Attention to Response Task, n
= 54), updating (Experiment 2: Random n-back Task, n = 52) and shifting (Experiment 3:
Number-Letter Task, n = 54). If mind wandering is closely related to executive functioning, it
was expected that mind wandering would impair performance on trials requiring these
functions, reflected in lower accuracy and increased reaction time variability. Our findings
did not confirm this: Mind wandering was associated with a general negative effect on
performance, rather than specifically impairing executive functioning. Accuracy was lower
on executive than non-executive trials in the inhibition and shifting tasks, but these effects
were not attenuated by mind wandering. In the updating task, where executive and non-
executive trials were matched in difficulty, mind wandering reduced accuracy in both
executive and non-executive trials. Variability in reaction time was found to be higher during
mind wandering in the inhibition and updating tasks, with evidence against such an effect in
the shifting task. These findings suggest that the observed performance decrements may be
more closely tied to task demands than to executive functions per se.

articles.title: Revisiting the Relation Between Statistical Learning and Literacy: Reliable Measures of Sensitivity to Bigram Frequency Predict Spelling but not Reading Skill
articles.authors: Haoyu Zhou; Fabienne Chetail; Louisa Bogaerts
articles.abstract: Our language environment is rich in statistical structure. It is therefore natural to hypothesize that statistical learning (SL) —the ability to detect regularities in the environmental input— contributes to the efficient processing of written text and supports literacy skills. Some prior studies reported correlations between SL as a general ability and reading, while others found null effects. We propose that this link may be better revealed by measuring individuals’ learning of orthographic statistical patterns, a type of regularity more directly relevant to literacy. This study examined how sensitivity to bigram frequency in participants’ first language (L1, French) and the ability to learn novel bigrams through exposure relate to literacy outcomes. The measures showed moderate to good reliability (L1 sensitivity: r = .60; novel orthographic learning: r = .84) and were significantly associated with spelling, but not reading. Notably, sensitivity to bigram frequency was not significantly associated with orthographic learning performance and did not mediate the link between orthographic learning and spelling. These findings suggest that different aspects of sensitivity to existing and newly acquired orthographic patterns independently support spelling abilities in French, without extending to reading performance.

articles.title: Claims about vaccine interventions in low-income countries require data from low-income countries: a commentary on Liu et al. (2024)
articles.authors: Henrike Maria Jungeblut; Shaheed Azaad
articles.abstract: Liu et al. (2024) recently published a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on vaccine promotion interventions. One key finding highlighted in the study’s abstract is that strategies that increased access to vaccines were especially effective in lower-income countries and those with limited healthcare access. Here, we raise two issues that call this finding into question. First, Liu et al.’s dataset contains no studies in which access interventions are implemented in low- or even middle-income countries, meaning that any claims about the efficacy of access interventions in these regions are extrapolated from a pattern so far observed only in high-income countries. Second, the interaction effect supporting this conclusion appears to be an artifact of the authors’ selecting a model that systematically excluded the largest non-access intervention effects in low- and middle-income countries.

articles.title: Statistical Reasoning regarding Possible Adverse Outcomes of Vaccination
articles.authors: Alexander C. Walker; Jeremy David Gretton; Ethan Andrew Meyers; Alexandra Mary van der Valk; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Derek J. Koehler
articles.abstract: The present research examines how individuals evaluate evidence for a causal link between a vaccine and an adverse outcome, focusing on two key statistical considerations: the background incidence (or base rate) of the outcome in the absence of vaccination and the number of adverse outcomes assessed. Participants repeatedly judged the strength of evidence that a vaccine had caused an adverse outcome as information accumulated. Providing base rate information reduced perceived evidence strength and concerns about vaccine safety, particularly when the observed number of adverse events matched rather than exceeded population expectations. These effects were more pronounced among more numerate individuals. Explicitly translating base rate information into expected case counts further reduced perceived risk when the number of adverse events matched population expectations, including among less numerate participants. Conversely, explaining how monitoring many outcomes increases the likelihood of false positives had little impact on participants’ judgments. Together, these findings show how individuals’ numerical abilities interact with the presentation of statistical information to shape vaccine-related judgments, highlighting effective strategies for improving risk assessment.

articles.title: Far out: How to achieve extreme results without really trying
articles.authors: Joachim Krueger; Benjamin R. Aizenberg
articles.abstract:
Extremism – political or otherwise – presupposes the presence of extreme, unusual, unexpected, or
outlying numerical values on some scale, and likewise, extreme judgments about such values.
Political extremism is the paradigmatic domain in which pertinent psychological dynamics play out.
Extremism is commonly considered undesirable, and to explain it, it is routine to invoke similarly
undesirable psychological constructs, as amply demonstrated in many chapters in this volume. In
this chapter, we show that fundamental perceptual, statistical, and behavioral mechanisms can
produce extreme results no one foresaw, intended, or desired. We further show that extreme results
can occur without the contribution of comparative perceptual or judgmental processes.

articles.title: Ways Students’ Reasoning about and Experiences with the School Climate Shape Satisfaction and Belonging: Evidence from a Mixed Methods Investigation
articles.authors: Jordan Ashton Booker; Shane McCarty; Alicia Mitchell; Chloe L Johnson; Madison Mitchell; Kyle Pacque
articles.abstract: Our objective was to expand insights about supports and stressors shaping high school students’ adjustment. Using an ecological framework, we considered how indicators of the school climate, different cohorts and group memberships, and meaning making from students could each be informative of students’ high school adjustment. We used a concurrent embedded mixed methods design to capture students’ appraisals of the school climate and recollected challenges at school. We recruited students from an Ohio, USA high school and conducted a quantitative survey about the school climate (i.e., support, structure, schoolwide behaviors) from students ages 13 to 18 years (n = 1,157, 51.6% girls; 51.2% White; 25.9% Black). Students also provided open-ended responses about recent school challenges. We investigated the content of these responses for themes about typical happenings with peers and faculty, about resources and policies around the school, and about personal concerns students held. Students’ whose survey reports emphasized more prosocial prevalence, lower bullying prevalence, and better school structure and support also reported greater feelings of belonging with and satisfaction at school. Notably, more junior students and girls were less likely to endorse these patterns, hinting at greater challenges given grade level and gender. Students’ open-ended responses about school challenges often emphasized concerns about the school structure and responsiveness from others: concerns about bullying and fighting; frustrations with faculty decisions and policy; and worries about peer pressure and social conflicts. Students also spoke to concerns of discrimination and marginalization as part of open-ended responses. Findings highlighted the importance of a highly structured and responsive school climate for students. Findings also highlighted targets for better anticipating and intervening with what could be heightened challenges for groups of students with diminished status in the school.

articles.title: Sex and Ethnicity Disparities in Autism Diagnosis: Population-Level Findings from Linked Health and Education Data
articles.authors: Evie Shore; Robin Evans; Matthew Warburton; Faisal Mushtaq; Lydia Gunning; Megan Louise Wood; Mark Mon-Williams
articles.abstract: There is limited robust population level evidence on the widely reported disparities in autism diagnosis by sex and ethnicity. Universal measures of school readiness, particularly the domains measuring social and emotional development, have been proposed as early indicators of developmental need, but whether the disparities in formal diagnoses across demographic groups are reflected in these population-level measures remains unclear. This study examined how sex, ethnicity, and their intersection were associated with the frequency and timing of childhood autism diagnoses and whether school readiness measures were associated with subsequent diagnosis across demographic groups. Linked health and education records for 55,054 children from a Northwest District of England were analysed using Poisson regression. Children from minoritised ethnic backgrounds and females were less like to receive an autism diagnosis and experienced significantly longer times to diagnosis than males and White British children. South Asian heritage females showed the greatest disadvantage. These patterns were not reflected across distributions of school readiness scores, suggesting diagnostic disparities by sex and ethnicity may reflect structural inequalities within identification pathways rather than true differences in underlying need. Developmental differences are evident and measurable by age five across demographics, highlighting the opportunity for earlier identification and support.

articles.title: Capacity Limits in Cognitive Processing Reflect the Curse of Generalization
articles.authors: Steven M Frankland; Raja Marjieh; Marco Nurisso; Joseph Fluegemann; Taylor Webb; Giovanni Petri; Richard L. Lewis; Jonathan D. Cohen
articles.abstract:
The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrast
to the near limitless capability of others. While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amounts
of information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: for
example the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that can
be performed at once. Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science,
and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited. We argue
that this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization—how effectively existing
representations can be used in novel settings—and how many distinct representations can
be processed in parallel. Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization
— a characteristically human cognitive strength — come at the expense of surprisingly
strict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristic
human weakness. We refer to this as the “curse of generalization.” We formulate this first in
information-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network model
of classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity. This tension
offers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena — from performance on the tasks on
which we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly — as well
as the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalization
capabilities comparable to humans.

articles.title: Overreaction and Underreaction: How Information Display Impacts Expectation Formation
articles.authors: Jenny Zhou; Jian-Qiao Zhu; Jake Spicer; Yitong Lin; Nick Chater; Adam N Sanborn
articles.abstract: Forecasting from a stream of past observations is a routine judgment task in organizations and markets, and a large literature holds that people systematically overreact when doing so, placing excessive weight on recent observations. Prominent models of expectation formation, grounded in mechanisms such as increased salience for recent signals and limited memory for past information, have predicted overreaction as a near-universal behavioral pattern, successfully capturing prior empirical findings. Here we identify boundary conditions on overreaction in expectation formation. Reanalyzing prior data in which participants viewed the full history of past realizations as a line graph, we confirm that while overreaction is most prevalent, it also varies systematically with task context, diminishing under high persistence and even reversing into underreaction as the process approaches a random walk. To test whether information display format shapes these patterns, we conducted two new experiments in which past realizations were presented sequentially, with only the most recent observation displayed (ruling out visual extrapolation). This design should, under either salience- or memory-based theories, elicit maximal overreaction. However, we find that participants instead exhibited reduced overreaction and, under high persistence, pronounced underreaction. These results establish information display format as a key moderator of forecast bias direction: reducing available history not only attenuates overreaction but can reverse its direction entirely, posing a novel challenge to prevailing theories of expectation formation.

articles.title: Musical Hedonia in Children: The Child-directed extended  Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (eBMRQc)
articles.authors: Francesca Cantoni; Laura Ferreri; Zoé Mandernach; Aude Bulland; Erika Godde; Anna Fiveash; Barbara Tillmann
articles.abstract:
Musical reward is a multidimensional construct, extensively studied in adults using the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (BMRQ) and its extended version (eBMRQ). However, no validated tool currently allows children to report their own musical reward experience directly, rather than through parental proxy. We developed the eBMRQc, a child-directed adaptation of the eBMRQ comprising six items, one per subscale (Social Reward, Musical Seeking, Emotional Evocation, Mood Regulation, Sensory-Motor, Musical Absorption). In Experiment 1, 98 adults completed the adult and child versions, revealing significant correlations between corresponding total scores and subscales, as well as similar relationships with musical and dance training. In Experiment 2, 140 children (mean age 8.5 years) completed the eBMRQc using a child-adapted visual response scale, and performed a beat-alignment task. Children understood the questions, and showed variability across subscales. eBMRQc scores were unrelated to beat-alignment performance, suggesting that links 
between musical reward and rhythmic ability may depend on additional factors. Findings show feasibility and conceptual validity of the eBMRQc as a self-report questionnaire of musical reward in elementary school-aged children. The eBMRQc may also be used as a brief assessment tool for adults and open new avenues for studying musical reward development and its relationships with individual differences.

articles.title: Stigma, medical gaslighting, and heterosexism: barriers to accessing healthcare and diagnosis in LGBTQ+ people with endometriosis symptoms
articles.authors: Ellen Frost; Sophie Höfels; Madeleine Pownall; Daryl Brian O'Connor
articles.abstract: On average it takes around 9 years to get an endometriosis diagnosis, but there is limited research that explores why this delay occurs for LGBTQ+ people who may have unique healthcare needs. 133 LGBTQ+ people with endometriosis symptoms answered open-ended text questions via an online questionnaire. Using qualitative content analysis, 23 barriers were identified. Medical gaslighting, limited diagnosis and treatment options, and the normalisation of symptoms were most frequently mentioned. Seven barriers were LGBTQ+ specific, including assumptions made about patients’ sexuality and the healthcare needs of people in same-sex relationships. The Social Ecological Model demonstrated that barriers occurred across the domains, with the majority categorised at the interpersonal level. Therefore, interventions to reduce the delay should not only target patients’ ability to access care but also consider focusing on the wider social structures that influence interactions in healthcare settings. Wider implications for LGBTQ+ sensitive endometriosis care are discussed.

articles.title: Investing in cooperation
articles.authors: Julien Lie-Panis; Christian Hilbe
articles.abstract: People do not just cooperate—they invest in becoming better cooperators. Partners learn to manage conflict, professionals train for specialized roles, and newcomers acquire the practices of their communities. Unlike cooperative acts, which directly benefit others, these efforts shape the individual, lowering their future cooperation costs. Why do people make such investments? Using a mathematical model and evolutionary simulations, we show that cooperation investments serve a dual function. First, they build cooperative capacity, enabling cooperation where it would otherwise be too costly. Second, when investments are observable and sufficiently demanding, they can honestly signal cooperative intent. When someone takes the time to work through personal conflict or learn a community's language, they do more than build capacity—they reveal an intention to cooperate.

articles.title: A Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial of Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy in Five Spanish-Speaking Countries
articles.authors: Jonathan Sandberg; Shayne Anderson; María Calatrava; Paul S. Greenman; Marie France Lafontaine; Dania Andrade-Urbina; Alessandra Sambuceti-Lewis; Alfonso Osorio; María A. Cueli-Naranjo; Patrick Steffen
articles.abstract:
Objective: Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy (EFCT) is an evidence-based approach to treating couple relationship distress (Spengler et al., 2024), however the evidence comes primarily from English-speaking samples drawn from the U.S. and Canada. This randomized controlled trial (pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov, ID: blinded for review) aimed to investigate the efficacy of EFCT delivered in Spanish compared to waitlist controls in Argentina, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico, and Spain. 
Method: 140 individuals in 70 heterosexual couples were randomized to EFCT or wait-list control conditions. Treatment consisted of 18-20 sessions of EFCT provided by 17 community-based therapists with advanced training in EFCT. Primary outcomes were dyadic adjustment, relationship satisfaction, attachment anxiety, and attachment avoidance. Measures were administered at pretest, posttest, and at several points throughout the intervention period. Linear mixed models were used to examine whether the trajectory of outcome differed across treatment and control conditions. 
Results: Consistent with hypotheses, individuals in the treatment condition experienced significantly greater improvement in dyadic adjustment (dGMA=1.09), relationship satisfaction (dGMA = .72), and greater decreases in attachment avoidance (dGMA= -.31). No significant differences were evident for attachment anxiety. 
Conclusion: Our findings suggest that EFCT provided by community-based therapists in Spanish-speaking countries is effective in improving dyadic adjustment and relationship satisfaction, with small decreases in attachment avoidance. 

Public Health significance statement: This article presents the primary outcomes of the first randomized controlled trial of Emotionally Focused Couple Therapy (EFCT) in Spanish. This 5-nation study demonstrates that couples who engaged in EFCT reported increased dyadic adjustment and relationship satisfaction and reduced attachment avoidance, with gains in the treatment groups enhanced over the control. This study is the first wide-scale, international, translational study of an empirically supported model of couple therapy with front-line therapists in a community setting. The study also provides support for the plausibility and efficacy of training therapists, in a wide variety of natural settings, to be effective in EFCT. Because decades of research have shown that couple level distress is related to a wide variety of mental and physical health problems, as well as work satisfaction and productivity, translational research highlighting effective and accessible therapy models for reducing couple distress is of practical value.

articles.title: Green against the machine: natural environments modulate agency-related behavioval and physiological responses under technostress
articles.authors: Simone Di Plinio; Claudia Greco; David Perpetuini; Massimo De Acetis; Miriam D'Ignazio; Arcangelo Merla; Daniela Cardone; Sjoerd Ebisch
articles.abstract: Most people live in densely urbanized environments with limited access to nature. At the same time, digital technologies increasingly shape everyday life and cognition but may also induce technostress, particularly when users experience malfunction, intrusions, and reduced sense of agency. This study examined whether exposure to a natural green environment, compared with a built urban (gray) environment, modulates psychophysiological responses to technostress. Fifty-two healthy adults were assigned to either a green (park/garden-like) or gray (built urban) environment. Before and after two outdoor walking sessions in the assigned environment, participants completed a word-selection task manipulating technology-induced stress and sense of agency. High-resolution infrared thermal imaging was used as a contact-free method to monitor facial temperature dynamics, providing indirect indices of peripheral autonomic regulation during task performance. High technostress reduced task accuracy and increased perceived stress. Under the condition combining high technostress and reduced agency, perceived stress decreased following green, but not gray, exposure. Facial thermal responses, particularly in the nose-tip and perioral regions, also differed between the green and gray groups under stressful task conditions, indicating that environmental exposure modulated peripheral physiological responses associated with technostress. Heart rate variability showed no consistent effects. Our results suggest that brief exposure to natural green environments may reduce vulnerability to technostress by attenuating subjective stress and modulating peripheral physiological responses. These findings contribute to the growing literature on restorative environments, human–technology interaction, and psychophysiological resilience.

articles.title: Auditory and Visual Rhythms Shape Infant Attention in Infant-Directed Singing and Speech
articles.authors: Rafael Román-Caballero; Maya Psaris; Betania Yvette Georlette; Mohammadreza Edalati; Barbara Tillmann; Sahar Moghimi; Naiqi G Xiao; Juan Lupiáñez; Laurel Trainor
articles.abstract: Early in life, infants are exposed to richly structured audiovisual signals during interactions with caregivers. Although infant-directed speech and singing effectively capture attention, it remains unclear how rhythmic cues across auditory and visual modalities shape the temporal dynamics of infant attention. To address this question, the natural temporal coupling between modalities in infant-directed singing and speech was disrupted by selectively preserving rhythmic information in either the auditory or visual dimension of the recordings while altering the other modality (auditory rhythm-only and visual rhythm-only conditions, respectively). Twelve-month-old infants showed rhythmic modulation of oculomotor behavior, with eye-tracking measures revealing systematic reorientations towards the eyes at the occurrence of auditory (strong beats and stressed syllables) and visual (head-nod) rhythmic cues, albeit in complementary ways. Synchronization was weaker and more reactive in the auditory rhythm-only condition than in the visual rhythm-only condition. However, when auditory and visual rhythmic cues were presented together in the original videos, eye-looking alignment adjusted to the faster tempo defined by the auditory rhythms, which occurred at a higher rate than the visual rhythms. These findings suggest complementary roles for each modality: visual rhythmic cues may act as an attentional elicitor, establishing reliable oculomotor synchronization, whereas auditory rhythms modulate the tempo of that alignment, serving a temporal tuning function. Our results highlight the dynamic nature of infant attention across different forms of infant-directed communication and the increased attention infants allocate to caregivers’ eyes at critical moments. This reallocation of attention toward the eyes may support learning of social and communicative meaning.

articles.title: Measuring Autistic Burnout: Psychometric Properties of the Autistic Burnout Severity Items in French
articles.authors: Capucine Rebours; Patrick Raynal; Jeanne Kruck
articles.abstract: Autistic burnout is increasingly recognized in the literature, yet no validated French-language measure existed. This study examined the psychometric properties of a French adaptation of the Autistic Burnout Severity Items (ABSI-Fr) in a sample of autistic adults with lived experience of burnout (N = 393, drawn from a larger sample of 484). Exploratory factor analysis (polychoric correlations, minres extraction, Promax rotation) identified a six-factor, 26-item structure spanning exhaustion, social withdrawal, memory, cognitive slowing, autistic self-awareness, and emotional/somatic distress, differing from the original four-factor ABSI and from existing measures of autistic burnout. Internal consistency was satisfactory (α = .694-.867; ω = .646-.809), and a Schmid-Leiman transformation supported a hierarchical structure justifying both total and subscale scores (ωH = .762, ECV = .47, PUC = .852). The total score correlated significantly with depression, anxiety, general burnout, camouflaging, and alexithymia, albeit modestly, and was not significantly associated with autistic traits (AQ-10). The structure replicated closely in the full sample (N = 484). These findings provide the first evidence for a reliable, multidimensional measure of autistic burnout in French, offering French-speaking clinicians and autistic communities a tool to name and assess this experience; diagnostic thresholds are addressed in a companion paper.

articles.title: Greater Reporting of Internal Than External Misinformation in Repeated Events Reflects Increased Familiarity and Suggestibility
articles.authors: Eva Rubínová; Aida Rincon Chong; Medhasvy Surapaneni
articles.abstract: Many events that people experience and share with others are instances of repeated events—unique instantiations of sequences of experiences with a similar underlying structure. In four experiments (each N = 128), we examined the impact of misinformation on reporting of one target instance of a repeated event; Experiments 3 and 4 additionally involved single-event conditions. Misinformation was delivered via a post-event narrative and was either internal, i.e., originating in a non-target instance of the repeated event, or external, i.e., originating outside of the repeated event. Memory was measured across free and cued recall to explore changes associated with increasing retrieval support, and in a recognition tests, where participants’ task was to select the original item from a range of options. Due to higher item familiarity and match to a general event context, we expected higher rates of endorsement and lower discriminability for internal than external misinformation. A synthesis of data across repeated-event conditions of all experiments supported our predictions: in contrast to external misinformation, exposure to internal misinformation resulted in higher rates of endorsement, lower discriminability, and overconfidence. These findings reflect two underlying processes: greater baseline accessibility of internal misinformation independent of post-event suggestion (a familiarity bias) and amplified suggestibility following exposure to internal misinformation (a suggestibility gain). There were no differences between internal and external misinformation in recognition, likely due to an overload of familiar items presented in the test. We discuss implications of our findings for theoretical understanding of repeated event memory and applied interviewing settings.

articles.title: How does the Outdoor Play and Learning (OPAL) whole school playtime programme affect children’s play? Mixed-methods insights from two English primary schools.
articles.authors: Helen Frances Dodd; Rachel Jane Nesbit; Brooke Elizabeth Oliver; Bryony Longdon; Sophie Jonsson; Lily FitzGibbon
articles.abstract: This study examined how the Outdoor Play and Learning (OPAL) programme affects school playtime quality and explores what impacts it might have on children and schools. A pre-post quasi-experimental mixed method design was used. The research was conducted with two primary schools in deprived areas of England. Observations of play, child report questionnaires and qualitative interviews with school staff were conducted. Across measures and schools there was evidence for increased playtime quality: there were significant increases in loose parts play; children reported engaging in more nature play; children engaged in more adventurous play, although high adventure remained rare; and negative affect during playtime decreased (although it was only statistically significant at one school). School staff reported that OPAL had positively affected children’s behaviour, their social and emotional development, and inclusion. Limitations include the pre-post design and the absence of a control comparator.

articles.title: Developmental differences in probabilistic reinforcement learning reflect strategy engagement rather than parameter changes
articles.authors: Kristina Pultsina; Galina Kozunova; Boris Chernyshev; Prokofiev Andrey; Anna Rytikova; Tatiana Stroganova
articles.abstract: Theoretical accounts of decision-making distinguish between two reinforcement-learning strategies: a model-based system that supports goal-directed choices through internal representations of action–outcome contingencies, and a model-free system that updates action values based on recent rewards, often approximating a win–stay/lose–shift (WSLS) pattern. While previous studies have characterized these mechanisms, their developmental trajectory remains unclear. Prevailing accounts attribute adolescents’ poorer performance in probabilistic learning to increased exploration and overestimation of environmental volatility, based on Bayesian models assuming a shared model-based strategy across age groups but differing latent parameters. Such approaches may overlook model-free contributions and individual variability, particularly during adolescence. Here, 36 adolescents and 67 adults completed a probabilistic reinforcement-learning task with binary choices and asymmetric reward contingencies (70:30), presented in sequential blocks to dissociate learning strategies. Individual behavior was fit with competing models: (I) a random baseline, (II) a WSLS heuristic, and (III) a hierarchical reinforcement-learning model implementing Bayesian adaptive learning. The results showed that both strategies contributed to behavior in each group, but in different proportions: model-based strategy was evident in only a subset of adolescents and became predominant in adults. Critically, individuals classified as model-based showed comparable latent parameters (e.g., learning rate, model strength, inverse temperature, precision) across age groups, and WSLS behavior also did not differ between adolescents and adults. Adolescents exhibiting model-based behavior had higher IQ but did not differ in age from their peers. Our findings indicate that in stable probabilistic environments, developmental differences in decision-making between adolescents and adults reflect variability in the engagement of model-based versus model-free strategies rather than differences in underlying computational parameters, with both groups behaving similarly when using the same strategy.

articles.title: Development and validation of a Scale of Non-Material Motives for Voluntarily Reducing Consumption Scale  (NMVRC Scale)
articles.authors: Andrea Velandia-Morales; Luis Mundi López; Chiara Ambrosio; Josefa Ruiz; Guillermo B. Willis; Eva Moreno-Bella
articles.abstract:
Currently, overconsumption resources are accelerating climate change and driving ecological degradation, therefore reducing consumption levels has become a critical need and a global challenge. In response, several lifestyles that aim to reduce consumption have emerged, one of the most important being material voluntary simplicity, understood as the voluntary reduction of consumption because of specific personal, social or environmental concerns. However, existing scales mix consumption patterns with preferences, values ​​and attitudes, leaving aside such specific concerns that motivate the adoption of a voluntary simplistic lifestyle. This has several implications, including the difficulty of differentiating this lifestyle from other types of anticonsumption (e.g., frugalism or minimalism). Through three studies (Ntotal = 854), this research aims to solve this limitation, developing a scale that focuses on non-material motives (such as social, personal and environmental reasons) that precede voluntary simplicity in order to investigate more deeply the subsequent consequences of this lifestyle. The first two studies were used to perform exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and to test evidence of convergent and divergent validity. The third study replicates the results in the general population. The results showed a scale with high internal consistency to measure the non-material reasons underlying the adoption of a voluntary simplistic lifestyle. NMVRC Scale was positively related to sustainable consumption, frugalism, and minimalism, but the correlations were not high, providing evidence of the distinctions between these constructs. This scale is a step forward in building a body of research that allows studying both the antecedents and the effects of voluntary simplicity on consumption.
Keywords: Voluntary simplicity, Consumption Behavior, Minimalism, Materialism, Psychometric properties

articles.title: Integrating interests, personality, character strengths, and person-job fit in relation to work outcomes
articles.authors: Fabian Gander; Livio Blaser; Rahel Tscharner; Lisa Wagner
articles.abstract: Vocational interests, personality traits, and character strengths overlap, but their shared versus domain-specific links to work outcomes – and the role of person-job fit – remain unclear because these frameworks have rarely been examined together. In this study, N = 259 working adults (79% women; ages 20–73) rated their RIASEC interests, FFM personality traits, and VIA character strengths and the extent to which each attribute was demanded by their jobs. Profile correlations between person attributes and perceived job demands were used as indices of perceived person-job fit. Outcomes were job satisfaction, work engagement, and self-rated performance. At both the person and perceived job-demand levels, all three frameworks (vocational interests, personality traits, character strengths) showed associations with the work outcomes, although their relative contributions differed. Commonality analyses indicated substantial overlap among the three frameworks, alongside smaller domain-specific contributions. Across all three frameworks, person attributes and perceived job demands showed stronger associations with work outcomes than profile similarity, whose incremental contribution beyond person and environment characteristics was small. These findings suggest that character strengths complement established vocational-interest and personality frameworks by providing additional information about work-related individual differences, while profile similarity contributes comparatively little beyond person attributes and perceived job demands.

articles.title: Scoping Review of Paramedic Practice Approaches to Supporting Autistic Patients.
articles.authors: Charlton Quitoriano; Darren Hedley; Claire M Brown
articles.abstract:
Background
Paramedics are often the first point of professional contact for autistic people during acute medical, behavioural, and mental health crises, yet encounter them in unfamiliar, time-pressured settings and with limited autism-specific guidance. Autistic people have elevated rates of co-occurring health and mental health conditions and substantially higher emergency service contact, but the nature and evidence base of paramedic practice with this population has not been systematically mapped, particularly within the Australian policy and practice context.
Method
We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Seven databases were searched from inception to 20 April 2026, alongside grey-literature searching of repositories (Overton, Trove) and targeted searching of Australian ambulance services, peak professional bodies, and autism organisations. Empirical studies were eligible if they involved paramedics or pre-hospital EMS providers and addressed autism as a distinct population or named subgroup. Data were charted and synthesised narratively; grey-literature sources were charted separately.
Results
Ten empirical studies (published 2013–2024) met inclusion criteria: seven from the United States, one from Canada, and two from Australia, with none identified from the United Kingdom or Europe. Studies were heterogeneous in design and paramedics were rarely the primary participant group; no study recruited autistic adults directly. Across studies, paramedics reported limited autism-specific knowledge and training, with training evaluations largely restricted to immediate self-reported change. Clinical tools such as communication boards and sensory kits were perceived as useful, though evaluated primarily through provider report. Grey-literature searching identified limited and fragmented autism-specific guidance; where autism appeared in Australian clinical practice guidelines, it was situated almost exclusively within behavioural-disturbance frameworks, and no Australian ambulance service had a dedicated, co-produced autism strategy comparable to examples identified in the United Kingdom.
Discussion
The evidence base on paramedic practice with autistic people is small, heterogeneous, geographically concentrated, and largely absent of autistic voices, with mental health and suicide-related presentations particularly underexamined. Australia's nationally registered paramedicine system offers a potential lever for systemic, neuroaffirming reorientation of practice that is not reducible to increased training volume alone. Co-produced research, clinical tools, and care pathways, evaluated against observed practice and autistic-reported experience, are priorities for future work.

articles.title: Evaluation of replication success: A statistical perspective and extended analysis of the SCORE data
articles.authors: Robbie Cornelis Maria van Aert; Marcel A. L. M. van Assen; Ruben Lopez-Nicolas
articles.abstract: Replications are more and more conducted in multiple research fields. A recent large-scale replication project, Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project, replicated 274 effects from research on business, economics, education, political science, psychology, and sociology. An open question remains how replication success can best be assessed. Thirteen methods for assessing replication success were applied in the SCORE project. The first goal of this paper is studying the statistical properties of replication success methods by a numerical study tailored to the characteristics of the SCORE data. The results of the numerical study show that replication success methods are unable to reliably draw a conclusion about replication success for typical sample sizes of the original study and replication. Hence, there is often insufficient information in one original study and one replication for drawing definite conclusions. The second goal of this paper is taking a novel perspective on the SCORE data by estimating the effect size of an original study and replication. Meta-analysis methods that correct for potential bias in the original study yielded close to unbiased estimates when synthesizing the original study and replication. The reanalysis of the SCORE data revealed that meta-analytic estimates were substantially closer to the effect size of the replication compared to the original study. The null hypothesis of no effect was rejected by the meta-analysis methods in 59.2% to 81.3% of the pairs of an original study and replication. We recommend researchers to make sure that methods for analyzing replicability have favorable statistical properties for the data at hand before applying these methods.

articles.title: Pervasive negativity and fragmentation across the architecture of the self-concept – a marker of transdiagnostic mental health risk in adolescence
articles.authors: Alice Roe; Kirsty Griffiths; Siobhan Gormley; Jason Stretton; Tim Dalgleish
articles.abstract:
Background
Differences in the affective organisation of the self-concept are a transdiagnostic marker of mental health problems in adults. Adolescence is a critical period for the development of the self-concept but we know little about the self-concept’s affective organisation during this critical developmental window. This study examined the architecture of the adolescent self-concept across five domains, focusing on four critical metrics: overall negativity; positive and negative redundancy (use of the same descriptive content across self-domains); and compartmentalization (the extent to which negative and positive content is segregated). 
Method
Adolescents at high (n=202, Mage = 17.16, SD = 0.62, 84.2% female, 2% other, 73.3% White British) and low (n=117, Mage = 17.08, SD = 0.57, 77.8% female, 71.8% White British) risk of affective disorder completed an Adolescent Self-Structure Task – a card-sorting task in which they were asked to characterise five pre-defined self-domains with respect to a set of positive and negative trait attributes. 
Results
Compared to those at low risk, adolescents at transdiagnostic risk of affective disorder used a greater proportion of negative trait words to characterise their overall self-concept, showed greater negative redundancy and compartmentalization, and reduced positive redundancy across self-domains. They also characterised their ‘Core Self’ in more negative terms.
Conclusions
Findings demonstrate how the organisation of an emerging sense of self during adolescence may constitute a transdiagnostic vulnerability factor for poor mental health. Efforts to improve positive self-evaluations across different domains may be effective in improving adolescent mental health.

articles.title: Shortening affect scales for ambulatory assessment: A comparison of different IRT-based approaches
articles.authors: Gudrun Eisele; Esther Ulitzsch; Milla Pihlajamäki; Inez Myin-Germeys; Jindra Bakker; Olivia J Kirtley; Aleksandra Monika Lachowicz; Wim Van Den Noortgate; Stefan Schneider
articles.abstract: Researchers often seek to measure affective experiences in daily life. Consequently, measures of positive and negative affect frequently take up large parts of ambulatory questionnaires. Optimizing questionnaire content and length is crucial in intensive ambulatory studies. In the current study, we developed and tested approaches to shortening ambulatory affect questionnaires. Specifically, we sought to build a preliminary item bank of 14 positive and 20 negative affect items calibrated with a graded response model using data from 14 individual ambulatory assessment studies (N = 3,818). We then compared different IRT-based strategies for shortening affect questionnaires to 2-4 items in simulation studies. Results indicate that computerized adaptive testing, but also simpler, (semi-) static item selection strategies achieve higher precision with the same number of items compared to random selection. We give concrete recommendations and highlight encountered issues and avenues for further refinement of the item bank.

articles.title: Interpretation biases in child and youth depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Luisa Marie Mayr; Elske Salemink; Allison Waters; Belinda Platt
articles.abstract: Cognitive theories posit that interpretation biases (IBs), the tendency to interpret emotionally ambiguous information negatively, contribute to the development and maintenance of depression. While adult meta-analyses report a moderate association between IBs and depression, evidence in populations under 18 remains inconsistent. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to (1) estimate the first overall cross-sectional effect size between IBs and child and youth depression and to summarize (2) longitudinal and (3) experimental findings from randomized controlled studies. Eligible studies included healthy and depressed participants (including comorbid conditions) younger than 18, assessed depression and IBs, and were published in English with full-text availability. A literature search in PubMed, Web of Science, PsycInfo and ProQuest Dissertations in March 2025 identified 30 eligible studies. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB2 tool for randomized studies and an adapted Downs and Black checklist for non-randomized studies. Overall study quality was acceptable, albeit with variability (M = 67.75%, SD = 12.1). A random-effects meta-analysis of 22 cross-sectional effect sizes (N = 4763) yielded a moderate overall correlation (r = .34, 95%-CI = [.27; .42], p < .001), similar to adult findings when accounting for methodological differences. Limited longitudinal (4 studies, N = 616) and experimental evidence (3 studies, N = 239) highlight the need for further research. Included studies only examined participants aged above 7 with largely low depressive symptoms, limiting generalizability. Future research should therefore examine younger and more severely depressed populations and employ validated measures of IBs in children to better characterize developmental trajectories.

articles.title: Emotion regulation predicts responses to interpersonal moral disagreements
articles.authors: Yi Zhang; Chelsea Helion; Leor M Hackel
articles.abstract: Moral disagreements are common in interpersonal relationships, yet people vary widely in how they respond to them–from avoiding interaction and keeping silent, to finding common ground, persuading others, or updating belief. The present work examines whether emotion regulation (ER) can systematically predict how individuals choose among these responses when facing disagreements. Across three online studies (total N = 892), participants reported their likelihood of using eleven response strategies in hypothetical disagreement scenarios. Response strategies formed meaningful clusters that reflect different regulatory approaches: disengaging from disagreement, attempting to resolve it, or accommodating opposing views. In turn, these response categories were systematically predicted by individual differences in trait ER (e.g., reappraisal, avoidance) as well as situation-specific appraisals of the moral, relational, and social stakes of disagreement. Together, these findings indicate that ER provides a useful lens for understanding interpersonal moral disagreements.

articles.title: A Comparison of Single and Multiple Diffusion Process Models of Continuous-Outcome Decision Making
articles.authors: Philip L. Smith; Paul Michael Garrett; Daniel Feuerriegel; Jane Yook; Simon Lilburn
articles.abstract: Continuous-outcome decision tasks, in which responses are made on continuous scales, are increasingly used to characterize the processes involved in speeded decision making. These tasks yield entire distributions of response errors rather than just error proportions. Two diffusion process models of continuous-outcome decisions have recently been proposed, the circular diffusion model (CDM), and the spatially continuous diffusion model (SCDM), which generalize the two main classes of diffusion process models of two-choice decisions to continuous spaces. The CDM, which generalizes the two-boundary Wiener model, assumes evidence is accumulated by a two-dimensional Wiener process with a vector-valued drift rate on the interior of a disk, whose bounding circle represents the decision criterion. The SCDM, which generalizes the class of multiple accumulator models, assumes evidence is accumulated by a Gaussian random process with a function-valued drift rate to a criterion. We compared the ability of the models to account for the distributions of errors and response times on three perceptual tasks: color identification, Landolt rings, and triangle orientation, in which the difficulty of the task was manipulated by varying the exposure duration. Despite some differences in their predicted joint distributions of errors and response times, both models provided good accounts of performance in all three tasks. Our findings reinforce and extend findings from two-choice studies showing that diffusive evidence processes and not model architecture is the main determinant of successful model performance, and show the theoretical unity of diffusion models across different domains.

articles.title: Low-dose cannabigerol (CBG) has different effects on sustained and divided attention in rats
articles.authors: Peter Joseph McLaughlin; Lily M Bement; Laney R. Burns; Gemma M. DeSanzo; Katarina L. Lords; Amber McKay; Shali A. Slater
articles.abstract:
Rationale: Cannabigerol (CBG), a non-intoxicating cannabinoid with high affinity for alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and antagonist activity at 5-HT1A receptors, has been suggested to enhance certain cognitive domains. Better-known alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and guanfacine treat attention deficits, and CBG should produce similar effects to these.
Objectives: This study examined whether low doses of CBG, clonidine, and guanfacine could improve performance on rodent models of sustained and divided attention, while assessing sedation as a potential confound.
Methods: Twenty-four adult female and male Long-Evans rats were trained on a signal-detection task assessing sustained attention, combined with an auditory distractor task to assess divided attention. In three experiments, rats received systemic injections of clonidine (0.005–0.08 mg/kg), CBG (0.3–10.0 mg/kg), or guanfacine (0.1–0.4 mg/kg).
Results: Clonidine impaired both sustained and divided attention at higher doses, accompanied by sedation and reduced responding. CBG produced a significant dose X task interaction: divided attention was enhanced at 0.3 and 3.0 mg/kg, while sustained attention was mildly impaired, an effect limited to the shortest (100 ms) stimulus duration. Guanfacine did not affect sustained attention but impaired divided attention starting at 0.2 mg/kg. Neither CBG nor guanfacine produced sedation.
Conclusions: Low-dose CBG selectively enhances divided attention while mildly impairing sustained attention, a dissociation not explained by sedation or overt motor effects, and distinct from the alpha-2 agonists tested. These findings support continued investigation of CBG's therapeutic potential for attention deficit.

articles.title: Examining the Influence of Perceived Authority and Expertise on Overimitation in Children and Adults
articles.authors: Ella McCormick; Michaela Dresel; Emily Burdett; Louise Mackie; Frankie T. K. Fong
articles.abstract: This study is aimed at examining how perceived authority and expertise play in tantum to influence overimitation and knowledge transmission. We will adapt a previous two-phase paradigm (Mackie et al., 2025) and use a classic puzzlebox (Horner & Whiten, 2005) to examine the influence of perceived authority and expertise on imitative behavior, set up in a pretend context of visiting a toy factory to learn about toys. Five- to 10-year-old children and young adults will observe a non-expert-authority figure (a toy factory boss) and an expert figure (a toy maker) demonstrate efficient and less-efficient methods for operating the classic puzzlebox. This will be followed by a transmission phase in which participants teach a third party how to operate the same puzzlebox. We will also explore whether each irrelevant action type will be imitated at different rate, which promises to offer novel insights into children’s and adults’ high-fidelity imitation.

articles.title: Mapping motivations for livestream viewing to gambling
articles.authors: Raymond Wu; Luke Clark
articles.abstract: Prior research shows that people who watch gambling and gambling-like content on streaming platforms display an elevated risk of gambling problems. Here, we leverage the literature on motivations as a dominant framework for understanding engagement in addictive behaviors to test how watching gambling is linked to problematic gambling. We pooled data across three online surveys and selected 544 adults who have experience with both gambling streams and gambling. Participants were assessed for their motivations to watch gambling streams, motivations to gamble, and problem gambling severity. We further assessed the frequency of past-year engagement in different types of gambling/gambling-like streams and gambling/gambling-like activities. Structural equation modelling showed that motivations to watch gambling streams were positively associated with the same motivations to gamble (enhancement, coping, and social), suggesting that people watch gambling streams for the same gratifications they receive from gambling.
