The account is not proposed as a replacement for belief-state, internal-model, predictive-coding, or active-inference approaches, but as a cross-domain feasibility argument: latent-state representations support control, learning, and evaluation only when task-relevant hidden distinctions are detectable from observations and stabilizable or actionable. Cognition, from this view, depends on latent state estimates that render behavior, learning, and evaluation well-defined under uncertainty.

articles.title: AI–Human Support Profiles Among Sustained Users of Conversational AI for Emotional Support in China: A Latent Profile Analysis
articles.authors: Rong Fu; Jiasheng Huang
articles.abstract:
Background: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for emotional support. Among sustained users, AI may become an enduring part of their broader support ecology rather than a one-off or short-term coping strategy, yet little is known about how AI and human support are configured within this population.
Objective: This study aimed to identify AI–human support profiles among sustained users of conversational AI for emotional support in China and compare their AI use, satisfaction, psychological distress, and positive well-being.
Methods: In this cross-sectional study, 484 individuals who had used conversational AI for emotional support at least once per week for more than 1 continuous month were recruited online between February and March 2026, with sustained use verified through uploaded conversation screenshots. Latent profile analysis was conducted using perceived emotional support and emotional closeness from AI and human sources, and differences in AI use, satisfaction, and psychological outcomes were compared across profiles.
Results: Participants were on average 23.62 years old (SD 4.24), and 59.3% (287/484) were women. A 3-profile solution was retained (entropy=0.824): human-anchored integrated (221/484, 45.7%), AI–human divergent (167/484, 34.5%), and AI-compensatory (96/484, 19.8%). The profiles were characterized by strong human resources with substantial AI support, greater perceived support from AI than from humans despite greater human closeness, and moderate AI support with near-floor human support, respectively. Profile differences were larger for human support and closeness (partial η²=.878 and .868) than for AI support and closeness (partial η²=.058 and .010). General-purpose AI systems predominated, and no significant profile differences existed in system type or most use behaviors. Significant profile differences existed in total AI use time (P=.019) and satisfaction (P=.013), with the AI–human divergent profile using AI longer but reporting lower satisfaction than the human-anchored integrated profile. No significant differences existed in depression, anxiety, perceived stress, or loneliness (all P≥.050). Significant differences existed in life satisfaction (P=.008) and subjective happiness (P<.001), with the human-anchored integrated profile reporting the highest positive well-being.
Conclusions: These findings highlight heterogeneity in how AI and human support are configured within sustained users’ broader support ecologies and suggest that human-anchored integration is associated with more favorable positive well-being, despite broadly similar AI use behaviors and psychological symptom levels across profiles.

articles.title: Straight-line behavior: conforming to design in a practice environment
articles.authors: Jordan Gutterman; Gillian Gold; Peter Brusilovsky; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles.abstract: Practice is an important component of computer science education, and online learning platforms increasingly provide students with large collections of programming examples and activities. How do students navigate among available practice opportunities when choosing what to work on next? Using interaction data from 247 students across three undergraduate computer science courses, we investigate the tendency for students to select the next programming activity as presented in the system, conforming to the implied sequence presented by a learning interface, which we call “straight-line behavior.” Students become less likely to follow the displayed sequence as a session progresses, while they are slightly more likely to continue in sequence following programming practice activities than example-based activities. Finally, students with more straight-line behavior also complete larger portions of the available programming curriculum. These findings suggest that both the organization of learning opportunities within educational interfaces and the decisions of how to structure curricula might contribute to their learning experiences. While adherence to displayed learning sequences may be an overlooked dimension of student behavior in computer science learning environments, it may offer opportunities for designing systems to account for differences in how students navigate programming practice.

articles.title: Why You Switch Matters: Failure-Triggered Switching Between Different Problem Types is More Related to Programming Performance than General Switching
articles.authors: Pragati Maheshwary; Gillian Gold; Jordan Barria-Pineda; Peter Brusilovsky; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles.abstract: The increasing adoption of self-directed programming practice environments creates new opportunities to examine how learners regulate their use of instructional supports and how these decisions influence learning outcomes. In this study, we analyze fine-grained log data from 115 students enrolled in an introductory programming course to investigate learners’ preferences and transitions between scaffolded tasks (e.g., tracing and code completion problems), code writing tasks, and worked examples. Using problem-level regression analyses, we investigate how prior knowledge, recent performance, and use of examples relate to learners’ regulatory decisions and subsequent performance outcomes. We found that higher prior knowledge was associated with higher success rates and productive struggle. Additionally, students with higher pretest scores were also slightly more likely to transition between task types. In general, switching behavior was symmetric: students were equally likely to move from code writing to scaffolded tasks as from scaffolded tasks to coding. However, failure on the prior problem significantly increased the likelihood of switching, and failure-triggered switching was positively associated with success, suggesting that why learners switch matters more than whether they switch task types. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating both learner characteristics and recent performance signals into self-regulated sequencing decisions. Productive practice may depend not only on the completed problems, but also on how learners adapt in response to failure, providing suggestions for programming environments that support strategic sequencing.

articles.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Promote Metacognition? Evidence from a Three-Level Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Xiuya Li; Xiaowen Liu; Lei Heya; Haibo Yang
articles.abstract: With the rapid advancement of digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from early intelligent tutoring systems to contemporary generative AI. Although AI features—such as personalization, adaptability, and instant feedback—have the potential to facilitate learners’ metacognition, empirical findings regarding the effectiveness of AI remain inconclusive. To address this gap, the present study employed a three-level meta-analysis of 54 studies (k = 121; N = 7,431) to examine the effects of AI interventions on metacognition. The results revealed a significant positive effect of AI on metacognition (Hedges’ g = 0.624, SE = 0.099, p < .001, 95% CI [0.431, 0.817]). Moderator analyses demonstrated that the control condition, intervention duration, and data source significantly moderated this effect, whereas other study, methodological, participant, and AI characteristics did not. These findings quantify the overall impact of AI on metacognition and identify key boundary conditions, thereby providing valuable insights for future research and educational practice.

articles.title: Profiling the Chinese Participants in Psychological Science: Non-WEIRD but Not Representative
articles.authors: Lei Yue; Zhangweiwei; Chunxiao Wang; Xi-Nian Zuo; Hu Chuan-Peng
articles.abstract: Psychological science aims at understanding the human mind and behavior, but it primarily relies on participants from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic regions, i.e., the WEIRD problem. This lack of diversity and representativeness of participants compromises the generalizability of psychological science. To address this issue, large-scale international collaborative projects have been initiated, and more data have been collected from non-WEIRD regions. However, it is unknown whether participants from non-WEIRD regions can represent their local population. In this preregistered report, we depicted the demographic profile of Chinese participants reported in 1, 000 empirical studies (n = 554, 794) published in five mainstream Chinese psychological journals and in 27 large-scale international collaborative projects (n = 29, 006, accounting for 2.12% of all participants). We found that age and sex were the most reported demographic variables, and other aspects of participants were less reported. The available demographic information revealed that Chinese participants were not representative of the population: most were young, well-educated, and resided in East China. Also, Chinese participants in large-scale international collaborative projects are less representative than those from Chinese journals in terms of geographical distributions. The demographic profile of Chinese participants in psychology is similar to their counterparts in many other countries and regions, suggesting the globalization of young and highly educated participants in psychological science. Together, our findings indicate that problems of representativeness are deeply entrenched in global psychological science and require coordinated cross-sector efforts.

articles.title: A General Neural Network Approach for Fitting and Comparing Attentional Decision-Making Models
articles.authors: Bingsong Zhao; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: Attentional decision models (ADMs), including attention-modulated decision models and joint models of attention and decision making, are important tools for studying the cognitive processes underlying decision formation. However, these models often cannot be fit or compared using likelihood-based methods. Building on simulation-based and machine-learning approaches, this paper develops and tests an end-to-end neural network framework for parameter estimation and model comparison, tailored to the high-dimensional, multimodal structure of attentional decision data.  In attentional drift diffusion models where likelihood-based fitting is feasible, we compared machine-learning methods to likelihood-based methods on parameter recovery, model recovery, and empirical data fitting. The machine-learning approach performed as well or better than the likelihood-based approach. The two methods yielded highly consistent conclusions for real participants on these tasks. In more complex models where likelihood-based methods are inapplicable, the machine-learning approach still achieved high accuracy in parameter recovery and model recovery. Moreover, we compared different feature-extraction strategies and network architectures and found that even the simplest were sufficient for reliable estimation and comparison with large-scale simulation data. Overall, our approach provides practical methodological tools that facilitate the advancement of attentional decision models and the development of associated theories.

articles.title: Outgroup Representation in Close Networks Shows a Nonlinear Association With Mental Well-Being
articles.authors: Trystan Loustau; Stylianos Syropoulos; Andrea Mah; BoKyung Park; Ezra Markowitz; Tatishe Nteta; Joel Ginn; Brian Lickel; Liane Young; Se Min Suh
articles.abstract: Building on research linking social diversity to well-being, we examined how racial outgroup representation in individuals’ close social networks relates to mental well-being during two periods of heightened societal stress: the COVID-19 pandemic and a polarized election period. Across two large, nationally representative datasets (N = 4,955), we observed a curvilinear relationship: moderate racial outgroup representation was linked to the lowest levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms, whereas both low and high outgroup representation were associated with worse outcomes. These associations were observed even after accounting for ingroup representation, outgroup dispersion, network size, and key demographic covariates. We then examined maladaptive and adaptive coping strategies and perceived social cohesion as candidate pathways. Moderate outgroup representation was consistently associated with lower maladaptive coping, whereas associations with adaptive coping were weaker and inconsistent. Data were consistent with an indirect linear effect of outgroup representation on well-being through increased perceived social cohesion, suggesting that although perceived social cohesion does not account for the observed curvilinear pattern, it is an important correlate of outgroup representation. Together, these findings emphasize that social network diversity has a nonlinear association with well-being and that targeting maladaptive coping may be particularly useful for promoting well-being in diverse contexts.

articles.title: Transcranial Pulse Stimulation (TPS) as a Treatment for Cognitive Disorders in Aging: A Protocol for a Systematic Review
articles.authors: Kayla Wiechens; Anna Engesser; Gabriella Ryan; Joseph M. Gullett
articles.abstract: In an aging population with limited standard pharmacological treatment methods for cognitive disorders, the importance of non-invasive brain stimulation techniques – particularly Transcranial Pulse Stimulation (TPS) – is ever increasing. Though research on TPS in the treatment of cognitive disorders is present, there are currently no systematic reviews that focus solely on the use of TPS in cognitive disorders of aging. The primary objective of this literature review is to determine what cognitive disorders of aging have been studied with TPS as a treatment, and to narratively summarize what is known about the effectiveness of TPS treatment on neurocognitive performance and neuroimaging metrics. The study protocol will follow PRISMA-P guidelines and the completed review will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase and Scopus will be searched to find peer-reviewed primary literature. Included literature will focus on the use of TPS in the treatment of at least one cognitive disorder of aging, with the relevant population defined as adults 50 years old or older. Searching and screening will be organized in Covidence and both screening and data extraction will be completed by at least two independent reviewers. Data will be synthesized narratively, with a focus on general themes and patterns, accounting for expected heterogeneity. Primary outcomes will include cognitive disorder treated (e.g. Alzheimer’s disease, dementia, Mild Cognitive Impairment, etc.), treatment protocol (number of sessions, length of treatment, etc.), outcome measures split into cognitive performance measures and neuroimaging measures, reported side effects/adverse events and relevant results. Any additionally relevant outcomes will be considered as part of narrative completeness. No ethics approval is needed, and findings will be published in a peer-reviewed journal(s). This protocol is registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251246424).

articles.title: Conscious Awareness of the Decision to Stop is Distinct from the Perception of the Stop Signal
articles.authors: Lalchhandama; Don Wallace Freeman Dcruz; Sumitash Jana
articles.abstract: Although we constantly make and inhibit movements, it remains unresolved if we are consciously aware of the underlying decisions. Such investigations are confounded by the possibility that self-reports of these decisions may be retrospectively inferred from the movement. Instead, questions regarding conscious awareness may be better addressed during response inhibition where there is no overt movement. Here, using the anticipatory response inhibition task, we tested if participants could report the time when they decided to stop, and if it was distinct from the time when they perceived the stop signal. In study 1, following stop trials, participants reported when they decided to stop. The reported decision time preceded stop signal reaction time (SSRT), an estimate of the time taken to stop, by ~93ms and was positively correlated with SSRT. This suggested that participants could reliably report this decision. In study 2, participants reported when they perceived the stop signal. Perception time preceded SSRT by ~163ms and was positively correlated with SSRT. Thus, despite no difference in SSRT, the difference between perception time and decision time from SSRT were distinct suggesting that the two timings are separable mental events. In study 3, participants either reported the decision time or perception time. We replicated that the two timings were distinct despite no difference in SSRT - perception time and decision time preceded SSRT by ~138ms and ~57ms, respectively. This suggests that the decision to stop is a consciously accessible mental event which is distinct from the perception of the stop signal.

articles.title: Decomposing subject retrieval: Diverging interference profiles for agreement and thematic dependencies in English
articles.authors: Matthew Kogan; Matthew Wagers
articles.abstract: The resolution of long-distance dependencies is mediated by both grammatical knowledge and domain-general working memory systems. Much previous work has investigated how and whether such memory operations are fine-tuned to the grammatical requirements of various linguistic dependencies. The present study recenters this issue in the context of two subject-verb dependencies with distinct grammatical functions: agreement, involving the checking of matching morphosyntactic features, and thematic binding, involving the fulfilment of argument-structure requirements. In one speeded acceptability judgment experiment and three self-paced reading experiments, we examine the online and offline profiles of dependency resolution for agreement and thematic binding in English. Experimental items in each experiment utilized ditransitive alternations to introduce several distractors intervening between the subject-verb dependency. Our results indicate that agreement is highly susceptible to interference from distractors which are syntactically dissimilar to the retrieval target but morphologically compatible with the retrieval probe. However, thematic binding is more restrictive, with interference only arising from distractors maximally similar to the retrieval target. Together, these results motivate a view of subject-verb dependency resolution in which the distinct grammatical functions of agreement and thematic binding yield distinct retrieval operations, despite targeting an identical constituent. We discuss the consequences of these interference profiles for models of cue-based retrieval and interference, whereby subject retrieval is decomposed into multiple retrievals relativized to the features most reliable for executing distinct grammatical functions.

articles.title: Perceived Changes in Religious Cognitive Dissonance and Mental Health Among Former Members of High-Demand Religions: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles.authors: David Bridger Lisonbee; Sam Hardy; Yehudis Keller; Daryl R. Van Tongeren; Julie J. Exline
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Recent advances in Cognitive Dissonance theory have clarified its broad applications and its mental health consequences when dissonance remains unresolved. However, this theory has rarely been tested quantitatively in the context of religious transitions, a major non-normative life event associated with negative mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a cross-sectional sample of 1,206 religious dones, or individuals who leave religion and do not plan to return, we extend cognitive dissonance theory by testing the conditions under which unresolved dissonance relates to perceived mental health. Participants retrospectively reported belief–behavior inconsistency and related discomfort before and after leaving, as well as current depression, anxiety, and perceived post-traumatic growth (PTG).
Results: Participants reported perceiving significant reductions in dissonance following deidentification. Greater reductions in inconsistency were associated with lower depression and anxiety, while perceived growth operated through reduced discomfort about that inconsistency. Religious demand moderated the association between discomfort and perceived growth.
Conclusion: These findings suggest that cognitive dissonance may both motivate major non-normative life events and shape their psychological consequences. For some individuals, leaving religion may improve mental health not simply because they leave, but because leaving allows them to reduce dissonance and live in greater alignment with their beliefs.

articles.title: Study planning is better served by Monte Carlo simulation than AI-generated participants
articles.authors: Jamie Cummins
articles.abstract: 'Silicon samples' – synthetic data generated by large language models prompted with demographic profiles – have been proposed as a useful method for planning human subjects research by providing useful effect size estimates. Monte Carlo simulation addresses the same planning problem from the opposite direction: the researcher specifies a data-generating process, then asks what follows. Monte Carlo simulation thus allow assumptions made about data-generating processes to be transparent and inspectable. Silicon samples by contrast bury these assumptions. In this article, I argue that this inscrutability, and consequences arising from it, makes silicon samples unsuitable for motivating study planning through effect size estimation. I conclude that researchers remain best-off sticking to Monte Carlo simulation for these purposes.

articles.title: Attachment-Informed Leadership (AIL):  A New Leadership Framework based on Attachment Theory and Social Neuroscience
articles.authors: Pascal Vrticka; Jonathan Wolf-Phillips
articles.abstract: Leadership research has produced a large and still-growing catalogue of styles, among them transformational, authentic and servant leadership, but no biologically grounded principle from which those styles might be derived or organised. We propose that attachment, understood through contemporary social neuroscience, can serve as that principle. Human beings do not regulate the demands of a challenging environment as isolated individuals but relationally, treating the resources of trusted others as functionally continuous with their own, and attachment is the mechanism through which this relational management of a finite bioenergetic budget is organised under stress. The leader-follower relationship is structurally suited to operate as an attachment relationship, and the quality of leadership depends substantially on how reliably a leader fills that role. We develop this claim into an attachment-informed leadership (AIL) framework, following a single line of reasoning from social connection and health, through social allostasis, to attachment and caregiving, and extending it into predictive regulation, interpersonal synchrony and the transfer of caregiving capacities from parenting to leadership. Read in these terms, leadership is first and foremost an attachment-based relationship in which the leader's central task is to become a reliable attachment figure for those they lead.

articles.title: Nurturing Understanding, Resilience, and Trust Using Relationship Enrichment:  A Single-Session Intervention Trial for Rural Youth
articles.authors: Erica Szkody; Ian Sotomayor; Atina Manvelian; Amanda Smock; Jessica L. Schleider
articles.abstract: Background: Adolescents in rural communities face significant geographic, cultural, and economic barriers to accessing mental health care, and depression treatments are often expensive, time-consuming, and inaccessible, leading many youth to drop out of treatment prematurely. Moreover, most evidence-based depression interventions fail to target relational difficulties, a fundamental, well-established depression risk factor in rural communities that increases susceptibility to depression and suicidal ideation. Method: This study had two aims: first, to iteratively co-design and tailor a single-session relationship competence intervention that was feasible, acceptable, and engaging for at-risk rural youth with elevated depressive symptoms using a human-centered design approach (n = 7; 85.7% Black; 57.1% Female); second, to test whether the resulting SSI improved relationship and communication knowledge, perceived change, and relationship learning, and reduced depressive symptoms at 3-month follow-up, using a randomized controlled trial (n = 440; 50.2% White; 31.4% Women). Results: Youth randomized to the SSI exhibited significantly lower depressive symptoms at follow-up than youth in the control condition, though both groups improved significantly overall. All participants reported similar gains in secondary outcomes (e.g., interpersonal skills) and rated the program as highly acceptable. Discussion: A relationship-focused SSI may offer a brief, scalable approach to improving depressive symptoms in rural adolescents over time by targeting relational difficulties as a modifiable risk factor. Recruitment challenges, including extensive exclusions for suspected fraudulent or bot-generated responses, limited the eligible rural sample size and constrain generalizability; future work should explore recruitment strategies embedded within trusted community settings.

articles.title: Evaluation of an Online Intervention to Promote Hearing Protective Behavior in Young People
articles.authors: Tjeerd Idger de Zeeuw; Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Lisanne de Regt; Marieke Pronk; Peter Verboon; catherine bolman
articles.abstract:
Objective
The present study evaluated the effectiveness of a new online behavioral intervention (Listening type Check) as an extension to an online hearing test, to increase safe ear- and headphone use and change the underlying psychological factors in persons 16-21 years old.

Design
An intensive longitudinal study with experimental design, using the experience sampling method, measured listening behavior and psychological factors two weeks before and after doing an online hearing test plus Listening type Check (intervention) or hearing test alone (control). Additionally, a process evaluation was performed.

Study Sample
Persons aged 16 to 21 years living in the Netherlands and using head- or earphones for at least one hour per week. Participants (n=54) were on average 17 years old, 57% was male, and 90% theoretically educated. 

Results
Participants in the two weeks pre-intervention, used ear- or headphones for about 6 days a week, 2 hours a day, mostly choosing a sound volume around 60% (on 0 – 100% scale). A loud volume (i.e. ≥60% when <18 years) was used for 40 minutes a day. These behaviors and underlying psychological factors did not change in the two weeks after doing the intervention.

Conclusions
Participation in a new online behavioral intervention plus online hearing test did not increase safe ear- and headphone use or change underlying psychological factors. Participants were primarily theoretically educated and exhibited relatively safe listening behavior at baseline, which may explain the absence of an intervention effect. A new effect study with vocationally educated participants is recommended.

articles.title: When Symptoms Don’t Add Up: Addressing Poor Symptom Validity in Forensic Interviews
articles.authors: Daniël H. J. van Helvoort; Brechje Dandachi-FitzGerald; Henry Otgaar; Chijs van Nieuwenhuizen; Harald Merckelbach
articles.abstract: Validity tests are widely used to detect distorted symptom presentation but offer little guidance on why such distortions occur. In an explorative qualitative study, we examined how forensic inpatients (n = 36) described antecedents of their response patterns during a collaborative feedback interview. Patients were classified as inattentive responders (n = 8), overreporters (n = 7), underreporters (n = 14), or comparison patients (n = 7) based on stand-alone validity measures administered during routine assessment. Transcripts were primarily coded on 11 literature-derived antecedent themes. Inattentive responders emphasized comprehension/scale-use problems, attention lapses, and disengagement. Overreporters described emotion-processing difficulties, needs for social attention, external incentives, and comprehension issues. Underreporters referred to self-presentational concerns, stigma, reactance-related disengagement, forensic stakes, autonomy/control motives, and mistrust/fear of disclosure. Accounts often highlighted modifiable treatment targets (e.g., interoception, stigma, mistrust, reactance). Overall, collaborative discussion of poor validity may inform case formulation and treatment planning in high-stakes forensic settings.

articles.title: Affective Valence and Temporal Framing: A Unified Generative Model of the Temporal Structure of Emotion
articles.authors: Manon JOB; Ben White; Mahault Albarracin
articles.abstract: Emotions are temporally structured: regret concerns what has happened, anxiety what will happen, joy what is happening now. Three strands of the active-inference literature each formalise one temporal face of affect: backward valence as the negative rate of change of variational free energy (Joffily and Coricelli 2013), present valence as reward prediction error (Pattisapu et al. 2025), and forward valence as the affective charge of policy revision (Hesp et al. 2021). Yet none alone spans the full temporal range, unifies these quantities into a taxonomy of emotion, or models how an agent actively selects the temporal orientation that dominates its own affect. We develop a single factored generative model in which a hidden temporal-frame state (past/present/future) redistributes precision across horizons, so that framing emerges from expected-free-energy minimisation. We motivate the architecture from the psychology of mental time travel, understood as the graded, cost-bounded regulation of how deeply memories and plans are unrolled, and show that a single depth regulator with two temporal faces reproduces the classical split between rumination (past-directed) and worry (future-directed). Affect here is a readout layer over a task-specific generative model, and the three channels are general operators on its inference dynamics. Driven by real experience-sampling sequences, the full model predicts next-moment affect out of sample better than linear autoregressive baselines, roughly doubling one-step skill where affect is volatile (held-out R² = 0.19 vs 0.09); the lead replicates in an independent second sample. On a static gamble it recovers the standard happiness equation (n = 14,803 held out) where each predecessor channel alone falls short, reaching that ceiling without expected value as a regressor: the forward channel supplies it by construction, a +30% gain over a reward-prediction-error channel. The same integration then supports capabilities the single-channel accounts lack: a latent temporal-frame state that tracks an independently measured symptom it is never shown (r = 0.17); counterfactual emotions with a behavioural signature a reward-only model cannot produce (regret drives choice-switching over and above one's own outcome, t = 10.4, replicated in a second dataset); and a mood layer whose diathesis-stress prediction holds in independent data, where a baseline vulnerability trait both lowers mood and amplifies affective stress-reactivity (vulnerability × stress, t = 4.2), a conjunction that in simulation collapses into a self-sustaining low-mood attractor. Throughout, we separate predictive claims (the channel integration) from generative ones (counterfactual and hedonic-asymmetry mechanisms).

articles.title: Understanding Young Adults' Behaviors and Beliefs Towards Loud Sound:  A Qualitative Study
articles.authors: Tjeerd Idger de Zeeuw; Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Anneloes Baan; Lisanne de Regt; catherine bolman
articles.abstract: Young adults are frequently exposed to recreational noise, yet hearing protective behaviors (HPBs) remain uncommon. This qualitative study explored psychological determinants related to safe headphone use, earplug use in amplified music settings, and hearing protection at work. Ten semi-structured focus groups were conducted with 87 Dutch participants aged 12–25 years. Data were analyzed using content analysis following the Reproducible Open Coding Kit and the Framework Method. Across all three HPBs, awareness, behavioral cues, perceived threat susceptibility, and perceived threat severity emerged as promising intervention targets. For earplug use in amplified music settings, perceived barriers and descriptive norms were additional targets, whereas descriptive and injunctive norms were particularly relevant for hearing protection at work. These findings provide guidance for developing interventions to promote hearing protective behaviors in adolescents and young adults and highlight the importance of tailoring intervention strategies to specific hearing protective behaviors.

articles.title: Characterizing the causes, dynamics, and consequences of choice deferral
articles.authors: Yi-Hsin Su; Xiamin Leng; Amitai Shenhav
articles.abstract: The fact that people often avoid making decisions is well known, and past research has helped to identify some of the conditions and reasons for doing so. For instance, people may forgo choices between bad options because they prefer not to end up with one of those options. It is much less clear when and why people avoid choosing in cases where they eventually will have to make a given decision. To study such instances of choice deferral, we presented participants with a series of choices, and for each choice they were allowed to either choose immediately or defer the decision until later in the experiment. Across six experiments and three choice domains (choices among consumer goods, artwork, and political candidates), we find that the strongest predictor of choice deferral is the overall value of a given set of options, with relative value (i.e., how hard it is to identify the best option) counterintuitively playing a smaller role. We show that the influence of overall value on choice deferral can be accounted for by a dynamic decision model according to which participants appraise the option set relative to a criterion before deciding whether to choose or defer, comparing this to a previous model whereby participants make such a decision based on a predetermined decision time limit. We further reveal that the influence of overall value on choice deferral is determined by how congruent options are with a given choice goal (choose-best or choose-worst) rather than simply how bad those options are. Collectively, our findings shed new light on how people decide to put off the inevitable.

articles.title: Partisan by proxy: Ingroup favoritism biases how humans train and interact with AI
articles.authors: Lauren Treiman; Chien-Ju Ho; Wouter Kool
articles.abstract: The success of human-AI teams depends on humans' willingness to cooperate with artificial intelligence (AI), yet little is known about whether the social group membership people associate with AI shapes this cooperation. Across three preregistered experiments using a two-player public goods game, we tested whether ingroup favoritism, operationalized through political affiliation, influences how people train and cooperate with AI. When training AI, participants taught it to be more cooperative when it would interact with members of their own political party than with members of the opposing party (Experiment 1). When playing alongside trained AIs, participants were more cooperative when paired with AI trained by their political ingroup (Experiment 2), even when they could observe that both AIs were equally cooperative (Experiment 3). These findings reveal that people shape and evaluate AI based on social group membership, extending ingroup favoritism to artificial agents that have no group membership of their own.

articles.title: Is the late positive potential (LPP) related to memory consolidation?
articles.authors: Hannah Piccirilli; Eric C Fields
articles.abstract: The late positive potential (LPP) is the component of the event-related potential (ERP) most consistently modulated by the emotional properties of stimuli. This component has been investigated in many studies, but little is known about the cognitive mechanism it reflects. In this study, we tested a model suggesting that the LPP reflects processes related to memory encoding and consolidation. To investigate this, we recorded EEG while participants read a series of neutral and negative words. Memory was then tested at both short (10-15 minutes) and long (12+ hours, including a period sleep) delays. We predicted that LPP amplitude would be positively correlated with memory, and that this relationship would be stronger after a delay (reflecting a relationship between LPP amplitude and memory consolidation). Consistent with our predictions, we found that LPP amplitude predicted memory in the delayed memory test, but not the immediate memory test. In addition, memory for negative items, compared to neutral items, declined less across the delay, and LPP amplitude mediated this effect of emotion on memory decay.

articles.title: Debugging Online Research: A Guide for Detecting Fraudulent Respondents
articles.authors: Ian Matthew Raugh; Megan Davies; Simone D'Amico; Vincent Paquin; John Torous; Manuela Ferrari
articles.abstract: Online research is increasingly popular to reach under-represented populations and expand research samples; however, it is also vulnerable to fraud in the form of “bots” (automated respondents, e.g., Large Language Models) and humans, such as completing a survey multiple times or when they are not eligible. Often, “infiltration” by such fraudulent responses is only noted and addressed after data collection has started. Here we present a classification process consisting of automated and manual detection techniques (“flags”) with practical suggestions for customization and implementation in other research contexts, grounded in the literature and our own experiences in a large online survey of video gaming behaviours. Using this protocol, we screened out 7638 likely fraudulent responses out of 8474 (90.13%). Among the flags implemented, those related to participant address, overall survey speed, and pattern of responses in “batches” provided the best performance. Ultimately, we recommend using multiple routes and layers to detect possibly fraudulent responses rather than reliance on any one or two indicators. By proactively considering how to detect and respond to fraud, researchers can have greater confidence in the integrity of their data, preserve limited resources, and minimize burden from post hoc fraud identification.

articles.title: Remembering more than the eye beholds: the effects of emotional content and mental health symptoms on boundary extension in adolescence
articles.authors: Alice Roe; Siobhan Gormley; Tim Dalgleish
articles.abstract: Boundary extension is a frequently observed phenomenon whereby an individual reports remembering more of a scene than they actually saw. Studies with adults have shown that the magnitude of boundary extension differs for scenes of emotional content and between individuals with varying mental health status. We provide the first investigation of boundary extension for emotional scenes in adolescents. Adolescents at high (n=200, Mage= 17.13, SD=.61, 83% female, 2% other) and low (n=119, Mage=17.04, SD=.55, 78.2% female) risk of affective disorders (depression, anxiety, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder) completed a Camera Distance Task with positive, negative, and neutral images containing both human and non-human central objects. Across all participants, the boundaries of positive and negative images were extended more than those of neutral images. While images containing human central objects were extended less overall than those containing objects, the effect of valence was greater for scenes with humans. Effects did not differ as a function of mental health risk status or disorder-specific symptoms. Results suggest that it is the valence and content of stimuli that influence boundary extension in adolescents, irrespective of mental health status.

articles.title: Who is highly distressed and impaired by climate change?  Cross-national cut-scores and a brief screener for population research
articles.authors: Johanna Hepp; Jana Urbild; Sean Patrick Lane
articles.abstract: Climate change is increasingly acknowledged as a source of emotional distress and functional impairment. To advance the identification of individuals most affected, we developed and validated cut-scores and brief screener items for the Climate Change Distress and Impairment Scale (CC-DIS). Using data from four prior studies (N = 1,699), we applied cluster and graded response analyses to derive empirical thresholds for emotional distress (cut-score ≥70) and functional impairment (cut-score ≥ 25), which we then validated in four representative samples from the US (n = 1,129), UK (n = 928), South Africa (n = 1,042), and Australia (n = 887). Across countries, 12–15% of participants scored above the distress cut-score, whereas impairment prevalence varied substantially, from 3.7% in the UK and 6.1% in Australia to 10.6% in the US and 33% in South Africa. Individuals above the distress cut-score consistently reported greater cognitive engagement, stronger social norms, more climate-related exposure, higher self-efficacy, greater pro-environmental behavior, and activism. In contrast, those above the impairment cut-score were more likely to report a mental health diagnosis and to express a strong preference for professional support across all four countries. In addition to the cut-scores, we developed two-item screeners for the distress and impairment subscales that demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance across countries (AUCs = .93–.98). These screeners provide a brief, valid, and scalable method for identifying individuals most psychologically affected by climate change. Our findings highlight the distinct profiles of high distress and high impairment and offer practical tools for the emerging field of affective climate science.

articles.title: Disentangling Negative Affectivity and General Psychopathology in Early Childhood: A Multi-Trait Multi-Method Approach to Validity and Informant Perspectives
articles.authors: Jordan L Harris; Isaac T. Petersen
articles.abstract:
Background
Children’s emotional and behavioral problems frequently co-occur, suggesting the existence of a general factor of psychopathology ("p factor") that accounts for the shared variance across internalizing and externalizing problems. Ongoing questions remain regarding the extent to which negative affectivity—a temperamental tendency to display observable manifestations likely reflecting negative emotions—and general psychopathology represent overlapping versus distinct constructs across early development. 

Methods
A community-based sample of 231 children aged 3 to 7 years participated in an accelerated longitudinal study, with assessments at four timepoints spaced nine months apart. Data were collected via multi-informant (mother, father, teacher/secondary caregiver) ratings, structured observational tasks, and standard questionnaires. This study evaluated the convergent and discriminant validity of negative affectivity and general psychopathology measures across informants and methods using multitrait-multimethod matrices while accounting for the unique perspective of the informant.

Results
Findings indicated that measures of negative affectivity and general psychopathology exhibited moderate convergent validity but also retained distinctiveness, supporting the discriminant validity in measures of these constructs. The association between the two was somewhat attenuated when controlling for informant type.

Conclusions
The results clarify that, although negative affectivity and general psychopathology are closely related in childhood, they are not redundant constructs. Additionally, the observed deflation in the association between negative affectivity and general psychopathology after accounting for the unique perspective of the informant highlights how measurement strategies—including informant source and method variance—can meaningfully alter interpretations of the associations between psychopathology and risk/protective factors. Together, these results emphasize the importance of both conceptual and methodological precision when studying the early indicators of psychopathology and suggest critical targets for early identification and intervention to promote mental health across development.

articles.title: Affective Valence and Temporal Framing: A Unified Generative Model of the Temporal Structure of Emotion
articles.authors: Manon JOB; Ben White; Mahault Albarracin
articles.abstract: Emotions are temporally structured: regret concerns what has happened, anxiety what will happen, joy what is happening now. Three strands of the active-inference literature each formalise one temporal face of affect: backward valence as the negative rate of change of variational free energy (Joffily and Coricelli 2013), present valence as reward prediction error (Pattisapu et al. 2025), and forward valence as the affective charge of policy revision (Hesp et al. 2021). Yet none alone spans the full temporal range, unifies these quantities into a taxonomy of emotion, or models how an agent actively selects the temporal orientation that dominates its own affect. We develop a single factored generative model in which a hidden temporal-frame state (past/present/future) redistributes precision across horizons, so that framing emerges from expected-free-energy minimisation. We motivate the architecture from the psychology of mental time travel, understood as the graded, cost-bounded regulation of how deeply memories and plans are unrolled, and show that a single depth regulator with two temporal faces reproduces the classical split between rumination (past-directed) and worry (future-directed). Affect here is a readout layer over a task-specific generative model, and the three channels are general operators on its inference dynamics. Driven by real experience-sampling sequences, the full model predicts next-moment affect out of sample better than linear autoregressive baselines, roughly doubling one-step skill where affect is volatile (held-out R² = 0.19 vs 0.09); the lead replicates in an independent second sample. On a static gamble it recovers the standard happiness equation (n = 14,803 held out) where each predecessor channel alone falls short, reaching that ceiling without expected value as a regressor: the forward channel supplies it by construction, a +30% gain over a reward-prediction-error channel. The same integration then supports capabilities the single-channel accounts lack: a latent temporal-frame state that tracks an independently measured symptom it is never shown (r = 0.17); counterfactual emotions with a behavioural signature a reward-only model cannot produce (regret drives choice-switching over and above one's own outcome, t = 10.4, replicated in a second dataset); and a mood layer whose diathesis-stress prediction holds in independent data, where a baseline vulnerability trait both lowers mood and amplifies affective stress-reactivity (vulnerability × stress, t = 4.2), a conjunction that in simulation collapses into a self-sustaining low-mood attractor. Throughout, we separate predictive claims (the channel integration) from generative ones (counterfactual and hedonic-asymmetry mechanisms).

articles.title: Preparing the University for Generation Alpha: A Research Agenda for the Digital Transformation of Higher Education
articles.authors: Sandra Grinschgl; Malte Elson; Tina Hascher; Andre Klostermann; Etna Rosa Krakenberger; Adrian Ritz; Thomas Christian Sauter; Amanda Zurkirchen; Michael Schulte-Mecklenbeck
articles.abstract: Generation Alpha, a cohort growing up with smartphones and generative AI as ordinary features of everyday life, will soon enter a higher education system that is itself undergoing profound digital transformation. We argue that the central challenge of this transformation is not technological alone but human and that it is shaped by three fundamental tensions: upskilling vs. deskilling, autonomy vs. dependence, and individualization vs. collaboration. Developed by an interdisciplinary Community of Practice at the University of Bern (UniBE), we introduce the BRIDGE model, which conceptualizes the university as an ecosystem of three interdependent groups: students, academic (researchers and lecturers) and organizational support staff whose psycho-social, health, well-being, and performance competencies must be understood across the trajectory from school to working life. Building on this model, we propose a two-phase research agenda: systematic identification of competencies, expectations, and institutional processes through a multi-year, longitudinal research program spanning all three groups, followed by collaborative transformation of higher education through empirically evaluated interventions. This agenda provides what digital transformation in higher education currently lacks: an empirical basis for deciding where digital tools strengthen learning, work, and well-being--and where they undermine them--and tested interventions to shift that balance. It thereby operationalizes UniBE's Digitalization Strategy 2030 and responds to national as well as international calls for evidence-based, human-centered digital transformation.

articles.title: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change
articles.authors: Douglas G. Lee; Giovanni Pezzulo
articles.abstract: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it. Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated. In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change. We focused on three factors that are especially informative for theory: choice difficulty, deliberation time, and the attribute structure of the options. First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices. Second, we showed that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, indicating that the relationship with deliberation time is not reducible to initial value difference alone. Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in terms of their attributes, with stronger effects for choices laden with tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance. Together, these results indicate that choice-induced preference change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a post hoc or artifactual revision of fixed values. The findings are compatible with both value-refinement and coherence-based reasoning accounts in some respects, but they also constrain both by showing that preference change depends jointly on difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.

articles.title: Self-Efficacy Predicts Differential Neuroticism Change in a Smartphone-Based Intervention
articles.authors: Michael Dominik Krämer; Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Johannes Zimmermann; Christoph Flückiger; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Self-guided, digital interventions can help people change their personality traits in desired directions, including becoming less neurotic. However, little is known about how and why people differ in intervention-related changes. Theoretical models state that intentional personality change must be perceived as feasible and that being motivated to change is not sufficient to elicit lasting trait changes. Using a German-speaking sample (N = 446; M_age = 25.88; 85% female; Residence: 47% Switzerland, 26% Germany, 26% Austria, 1% Other), we tested whether self-efficacy and growth mindset predict change in multiple neuroticism measures across a 6-week intervention and 2-month follow-up. To isolate temporal processes during the intervention, we examined co-development of weekly neuroticism and self-efficacy and their week-to-week temporal associations. We found evidence for self-efficacy predicting differential neuroticism change but not for growth mindset. Participants with higher self-efficacy showed greater pre-post decreases in self-reported neuroticism and greater pre-post increases in emotional resilience than those with lower self-efficacy. At follow-up, participants with higher self-efficacy continued to improve more in neuroticism and emotional resilience. Last, higher self-efficacy in one week predicted lower neuroticism in the following week, and vice versa, independent of participants’ overall trajectories. In contrast, there was no consistent evidence for between-person co-development of weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism across the intervention. Findings support theoretical expectations that perceived feasibility is a precondition for neuroticism change and suggest possible reinforcement mechanisms between weekly self-efficacy and neuroticism. We discuss implications for theory and future intervention studies.

articles.title: The Impact of Religiosity on Suicidality in the Autistic Population: The Mediating Role  of Perceived Stress
articles.authors: Aliya Navroz; Jan Wiener
articles.abstract: This study examined the relationship between religiosity and suicidality in autistic adults, with a particular focus on whether perceived stress mediates this relationship. Prior research suggests that autistic individuals are at increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, yet the mechanisms underlying this vulnerability are not fully understood. While religiosity has been identified as a potential protective factor in the general population, its role within autistic populations has received limited attention. A secondary data analysis was conducted on data from 127 autistic adults aged 19-73 years. Measures included self-reported religiosity, perceived stress, suicidality, and additional psychosocial variables such as loneliness, psychological distress, social anxiety, social support, and contextual stressors. Pearson correlation analyses, mediation analysis, and multiple regression were performed. The findings indicated that perceived stress did not significantly mediate the relationship between religiosity and suicidality. Furthermore, religiosity was not identified as a significant predictor of suicidality within this sample. However, other factors, including loneliness, psychological distress, and social anxiety, showed stronger associations with increased suicidality, while social support appeared to play a protective role. Moreover, psychological distress and treatment/health difficulties were found to be significant predictors of suicidality. These results suggest that, although religiosity may offer benefits for some individuals, it does not seem to play a central role in reducing suicide risk among autistic adults. Instead, interventions targeting emotional distress, social isolation, and stress management may be more effective. This study emphasises the importance of focusing on broader psychosocial factors to better understand and reduce suicidality in the autistic population.

articles.title: “It’s a form of survival”: Autistic transgender and nonbinary people’s experiences of disordered eating
articles.authors: Luka White; Hazel Marzetti; Fiona Duffy; Jonah Shehata; Karri Gillespie-Smith
articles.abstract:
Autistic transgender and/or nonbinary (TNB) people are a multiply marginalised group systematically impacted by high rates of disordered eating. Feminist scholarship has examined the role of systems of oppression in creating environments where disordered eating can flourish, particularly sexism, racism and weight stigma. We expand this conversation by taking an intersectional, minority stress lens to examine the roles of cis-heteronormativity and neuronormativity in disordered eating in Autistic TNB people. Twenty-one Autistic TNB participants (aged 19-51) with disordered eating were asked to take part in narrative online interviews that were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. 
Participants framed their disordered eating as a survival technique. In line with minority stress theory, disordered eating was articulated both as a direct response to systemic and interpersonal violence, and an indirect response to internalisation of queerphobic or anti-Autistic experiences. A struggle for belonging characterised participants’ intersectional experience. Queer communities provided a site of acceptance and improved disordered eating for some, yet were also places that could exacerbate unbelonging and disordered eating through intersecting ableism, racism and fatphobia and the communication of queer-specific appearance pressures. 
Findings demonstrate the utility of an intersectional minority stress lens to examine Autistic TNB health inequities. Beyond individualised neuro- and gender-affirming approaches for Autistic TNB people with disordered eating, researchers and clinicians must move towards an emancipatory approach which considers the systemic factors influencing the mental health of this multiple minoritised community.

articles.title: Impact of an Embodied Conversational Agent on Loneliness and Emotional States in Community Dwelling Older Adults: Initial Quantitative and Qualitative Evidence
articles.authors: Feliciano Villar; Rumen Manolov
articles.abstract: The current study explores the implementation of an embodied conversational agent called AiMA at home, for community-dwelling older adults and its impact on loneliness and emotional states of older adults. Seventeen community-dwelling older adults (12 women, 5 men) líving alone participated in the study. An embodied conversational agent was implemented in their homes for 15 days. The focus of the study is placed on both qualitative and quantitative aspects. In terms of the quantitative information, the amount of interaction (days, conversations, turns) was summarized, as well as the percentage of joy and sadness. Specifically, it was found that the most frequent transition from the initial to the final emotional state across interactions, for all participants, was from neutral to joy.  In qualitative terms, participants answered an open-ended interview in which positive aspects reported of using the device and areas of improvement, were included. Results show that participants engaged and tended to engage with the ECA in an anthropomorphic way, in some cases showing a ‘human’ bond with the device. Despite both emotional and cognitive benefits were mentioned, the emotional positive impact of the interaction with the ECA (reduction of loneliness, elicitation of positive emotions) as the most frequently mentioned one. When mentioning areas of improvement, one of the aspects that participants missed was the lack of proactivity. Findings showed that participants engaged in interactions with the conversational agent, which suggests that it could a useful tool to mitigate loneliness and enhance positive emotions among older adults living alone.

articles.title: Transdiagnostic efficacy of cognitive restructuring in adult populations from a gender perspective: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Joan Miquel Soldevilla-Alberti; Sandra Mateus-Gómez; Sonia Lorente
articles.abstract: Background: Psychological science has developed a higher sensitivity towards inclusion and diversity. In this regard, researchers have analysed the effects that certain social categories, such as gender, can have on clinical and health psychology. Maladaptive cognitions can be affected by gender-related differences and their intersection with sociocultural aspects, especially when considering transgender and gender non-conforming people. Cognitive restructuring (CR) is a frequently employed technique for reframing cognitive schemas. However, it is also possible that it may be susceptible to influences linked to gender diversity factors. With the review projected in this protocol, we aim to evaluate the effectiveness of CR in reducing the severity of psychological symptoms, taking gender-related differences into account. Method: Systematic review. Databases will include PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science CORE, and Google Scholar for grey literature. Data will be screened by two reviewers and discrepancies will be resolved through discussion or a third reviewer if necessary. Extracted data will include general information, methodological data, and sample general and clinical characteristics. Conclusions: The forthcoming results will explore the role of gender identity in different outcomes following CR interventions, examining its contributions to provide more tailored and effective interventions.

articles.title: Turn-Duration Burstiness as a Temporal Signature of Collective Cognitive Demand in Multidisciplinary Healthcare Team Meetings
articles.authors: Travis J. Wiltshire; Margo Janssens; Samantha C.P. van der Bruggen; Laurens Beerepoot; Roger Leenders
articles.abstract: Collective cognition in team settings is shaped not only by what is communicated, but by the temporal dynamics of how communication unfolds. Multidisciplinary team meetings (MDTMs) in oncological care offer a naturalistic window into collective decision-making under real-world constraints, where teams of medical clinicians must jointly process complex patient cases. In this study, we examine the temporal structure of speech turn durations in oncological MDTMs using burstiness, a measure of how irregularly communication is distributed over time, as a quantitative index of communicative temporal organization. We applied two complementary burstiness metrics, the burstiness parameter (B) and the length-normalized variant (Aₙ(r)), to meeting and case-level speech turn data, and used random intercept models to examine associations between burstiness, case complexity, and case processing time. Communication was predominantly bursty, exceeding levels expected under a random process. More complex cases were associated with higher burstiness, suggesting that irregular temporal communication structure has potential to serve as an observable marker of collective cognitive load. Growth curve modeling further revealed significant main effects of burstiness and case order on case processing time, as well as interactions moderated by MDT sample. These results indicate that temporal communication dynamics and case processing is context dependent varying systematically across meeting types and as meetings progress. These findings suggest that burstiness may reflect meaningful variation in the collective cognitive dynamics of MDTMs and may offer a promising foundation for real-time monitoring of team interactions and decision-making.

articles.title: Attitudes and Affect towards Statistics in First Year Psychology Studends - a Bayesian Approach
articles.authors: Christian Seida
articles.abstract:
Statistics is regarded as one of the most difficult and frightening subjects by psychology
students. The present study develops a Bayesian framework for a more comprehensive
understanding of students´ attitudes and affect towards statistics, their development and
predictors. Furthermore, an extensive collection of related constructs was raised and analysed
psychometrically. In a longitudinal design, data of first year psychology students was collected
via online surveys at the beginning of the lectures, midst-semester and after course completion.
Four Bayesian models were fitted to inspect response patterns, pairwise item correlations and
construct change over time. In a final multilevel generalized linear varying effects model, the
effects of Statistics Anxiety on Affective Behaviours towards statistics were analysed.
Psychometric analysis yielded surprising results, as most instruments revealed insufficient
properties in the present sample. Comparative analyses revealed that Affective Behaviours
increased over the course of the semester, and Statistics Anxiety decreased. The relationship
between Affective Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety was complex, as some subscales were
correlated positively against expectations. In conclusion, the present study developed a
Bayesian framework for comprehensive data analysis, presents preliminary results of Affective
Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety and discusses a potential reliability risk in the field due to
deficient reporting of psychometric analyses.

articles.title: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit: A Human and Machine Readable Standard for Coding Qualitative Data
articles.authors: Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Szilvia Zörgő
articles.abstract: The Reproducible Open Coding Kit (the ROCK) is a standard for human- and machine-readable qualitative (coded) data. It was designed to be accessible to researchers without dedicated software, while simultaneously offering enough structure to enable programmatic processing. Through this combination and a number of features tailored to these ends, the ROCK lends itself well to facilitate application of open science principles in qualitative research, to catalyse methodological innovation in qualitative research, and to progress towards machine-readability and interoperability of (coded) qualitative data, to ultimately enable truly Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) qualitative data. In this canonical reference, we lay out the ROCK standard v1.0. We hope this allows developers to implement the ROCK in existing free and open software, stimulates the development of additional applications, and ultimately, democratizes methodological innovation in qualitative research.

articles.title: Closed-book and open-book language model assessment  of employee experience.  A two-sample convergent validity study comparing  multi-stage retrieval and single-prompt approaches
articles.authors: Richard Justenhoven; Maximilian Endress; Achim Preuß
articles.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to produce quantitative judgements about organisations from publicly available text, yet such systems differ fundamentally in whether they consult external evidence at the point of judgement or draw only on knowledge encoded during training. This study compared two systems that estimate the same 24 dimensions of employee experience using the same base language model and differ only in how evidence is gathered: a multi-stage retrieval approach, assembling each score through staged web retrieval and sequential scoring over two to three hours per organisation, and a single-prompt approach, producing all dimensions in one call from parametric knowledge. Because the two share a base model, the comparison isolates the contribution of retrieval. Evidence came from two independent samples, comprising 35 large, well-known companies and 152 organisations spanning insurance, retail, healthcare, education and professional services. Both approaches proved reliable across repeated runs (ICC(A,1) = .84 to .97). Convergence between them was moderate, with per-dimension correlations averaging .79 and .63 in the two samples and rising to .81 and .72 after correction for attenuation, and was consistently stronger for an organisation's overall score than for individual dimensions (corrected r = .91 and .85). Performance varied systematically by dimension in both samples: agreement was highest on dimensions describing an organisation's public identity, such as brand, mission and rewards, and lowest on those describing internal working experience, such as the direct manager, career progression, and diversity and inclusion. Retrieval contributed most where public text carries least, suggesting that gathering evidence determines which parts of a construct can be measured rather than simply improving accuracy.

articles.title: Why Conventional Practices in Construct Validation Provide Limited Evidence of Construct Validity
articles.authors: Leon Patrick Wendt; Steffen Müller
articles.abstract: The construct validity of psychometric instruments is a foundation of psychological science, as instruments should measure the intended theoretical constructs rather than unintended ones. Yet it has been argued that conventional construct validation practices often produce weak, uninformative evidence and fall short of the strong, risk-bearing tests emphasized by validity theorists. Extant evidence often cannot support meaningful claims about construct validity. We introduce the EVE-CV framework, based on Meehl's logic of hypothesis testing, for evaluating the evidential value (or quality) of construct validation efforts. Evidential value refers to the extent to which conducting a test of construct validity is expected to shift confidence among the proposed construct interpretation and plausible alternative interpretations. The framework translates three logical requirements for evidential value into six practical criteria for designing and evaluating construct validation studies. We also use the framework to explain how three conventional validation practices contribute to low evidential value: using conceptual placeholders, overrelying on generic psychometric methods, and revising the nomological network based entirely on evidence generated by the measure under validation. We argue that these practices are commonly used to portray instruments as “validated”, while providing only nominal evidence of construct validity.

articles.title: Revisiting Long-Term Trends in Germany’s Upper Secondary Mathematics Achievement:  A Chain Linking Analysis from FIMS 1964 to TIMSS 1996
articles.authors: Carolin Rau; Alexander Robitzsch; Aiso Heinze; Tobias Rolfes
articles.abstract:
Public discourse in many countries reflects a persistent perception of declining educational achievement over the decades, particularly among upper secondary graduates in mathematics at the transition to higher education. Assessing such claims requires evidence of long-term trends. International large-scale assessments (ILSAs), including earlier study cycles, provide a key data source, especially where systematic monitoring is lacking. In Germany, participation in ILSAs has been discontinuous and upper secondary monitoring is absent. However, data from the First International Mathematics Study (FIMS, 1964) and the Third International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS, 1996) allow the reconstruction of achievement trends over more than three decades. This study therefore estimates trends in mathematics achievement among German upper secondary graduates between 1964 and 1996 through a secondary analysis of these data.
Item response theory was used to rescale the achievement data. FIMS Germany and TIMSS Germany were chain linked via Sweden across FIMS, the Second International Mathematics Study (SIMS, 1980-82), and TIMSS using Haberman linking. Subsequently, achievement distributions for 1964 and 1996 were transformed onto the TIMSS trend scale. Sampling and linking errors were computed to assess uncertainty.
The results indicate a non-significant gain of 22 points in achievement between 1964 and 1996. Subgroup analyses reveal a significant increase in achievement for students enrolled in advanced mathematics courses, whereas no significant changes are observed for basic course levels. The decomposition of uncertainty shows that linking error substantially exceeds sampling error, indicating that trend estimates are primarily driven by item-related uncertainty. At the same time, linking error was reduced relative to a previously reported joint linking approach.
The assumption of a substantial decline in mathematics achievement over the decades cannot be confirmed. Improvements were observed among students enrolled in advanced mathematics courses. The findings suggest that chain linking can improve the precision of trend estimates when item overlap is limited and may provide a valuable approach for reconstructing trends in data-sparse contexts lacking continuous monitoring. However, linking uncertainty remains substantial, underscoring the need for additional invariant link items and systematic monitoring at the upper secondary level to support robust trend evidence.

articles.title: Dialogical Emergence in Embodied Collaboration: A Micro-Analysis of How Dyads Co-Construct Insight from Conflicting Perceptions
articles.authors: NA; Xiyuan Li; Yan Song; Xiaoyan Wang; Ze Meng
articles.abstract:
In real-time embodied collaboration, partners occupying distinct vantage points capture only local projections of the system state. When these projections conflict—for instance, when one partner perceives “pushing” while the other perceives “being pulled”—both may mistake locally valid experience for complete truth, falling into a structural illusion. Whether and how collaborators can transcend these perspectival limits through dialogue, when physical repositioning and direct perceptual sharing are infeasible, remains theoretically under-addressed.
Using partnered dance as a model system, this multi-case qualitative study recruited four established dyads who completed a standardized task and participated in dyadic synchronized video-stimulated recall interviews. Grounded in a phenomenologically-dialogical epistemology, we employed a three-tiered analytical framework—thematic content, interaction process, and identity-narrative analysis—to analyze approximately 320 minutes of recorded interview data, with segments containing perceptual divergence (totaling ~58 minutes across 16 segments) subjected to full micro-level dialogical coding.
Four major findings emerged. First, perceptual divergence reflects each partner conflating a local projection with a complete system description, signaling temporary breakdown of pre-reflective intercorporeality. Second, partners exhibited two qualitatively distinct pathways: adversarial persistence, where dialogue stagnated in repetitive cycles of negation, and integrative co-construction, where partners collaboratively discovered the partiality of their perceptions and generated emergent understanding. Third, integrative co-construction followed a recurrent six-phase micro-structure: Divergence Exposure, Pause-and-Inquiry, Individual Retrospection, Difference Localization, Emergent Reframing, and New Consensus Formation. The Pause-and-Inquiry phase—marked by clarificatory questioning—emerged as the critical juncture determining whether dialogue stalled or pivoted toward co-construction. Fourth, cognitive advancement co-evolved with partnership identification: integrative co-construction simultaneously accomplished cognitive restructuring and psychological safety restoration through shared humor and the reframing of divergence from a “relational problem” to an “information differential.”
This study articulates the micro-mechanisms of dialogical emergence, revealing a transcendence paradigm of collaborative learning—a mode in which breakthrough arises from jointly discovering perspectival limits and generating new understanding within dialogical tension. We propose collaborative epistemic restructuring as a supplement to socially shared regulation of learning and advocate shifting shared mental models research from consensus-presupposition toward difference-management.

articles.title: Italian Adaptation and Validation of the ICAR-16 Sample Test
articles.authors: Eva Tolomeo; Leognano Ceraudo; Marco Balducci; Marco Tullio Liuzza
articles.abstract: The International Cognitive Ability Resource 16 (ICAR-16) is a public-domain measure of cognitive ability. However, no Italian validation currently exists. We translated and validated the ICAR-16 in a sample of 486 Italian adults (66% females), who completed the ICAR-16 and the long version of the Cognitive Reflection Test online. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the original hierarchical structure, with the Second-Order Latent Variable model (CFI=.98; TLI=.98) showing the best fit. Moreover, the ICAR-16 correlates strongly with the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) (ϕ= .81; 95% CI: .75, .86), confirming convergent validity. Internal consistency reliability was also adequate (ωt = .82; ωh = .59; α= .78). Measurement invariance analyses supported partial scalar invariance across sexes, with no further decrement in fit indexes for strict invariance. Only one item (MR47) exhibited uniform Differential Item Functioning. Overall, these findings support the Italian ICAR-16 as a reliable, freely available instrument for cognitive assessment in research.

articles.title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter: A Digital Decision Aid to Support the Selection of Communication Strategies to Overcome Language Barriers in General Practice
articles.authors: Brittany Ming Chu Chan; Julia van Weert; Hülya Ates; Jeanine Suurmond; Barbara C. Schouten
articles.abstract:
Objective: Migrant patients with limited proficiency in the host country's dominant language(s) often face difficulties in making informed decisions about selecting communication strategies to overcome language barriers. This study evaluated MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, an evidence-based digital decision aid developed through the Spiral Technology Action Research Model with migrant patients, usability experts, and healthcare providers, using an iterative process. This approach led to MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter, designed to empower patients to select appropriate communication strategies before language-discordant medical consultations, thereby facilitating shared decision-making with their healthcare providers (HCPs) during these consultations. 
Methods: A cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) was conducted in seven Dutch general practices, involving 18 participating HCPs and 75 Turkish-Dutch patients (31 in the control group and 44 in the intervention group; Mage = 61.79, SD = 12.40), all of whom had limited proficiency in Dutch. While questionnaires assessing HCPs’ demographics and perceived communication self-efficacy were administered once before the start of the trial, questionnaires were given to patients both before and after consultations. Control patients received standard care; intervention patients used MediLanguage’s Language Support Starter prior to their consultations.
