The chapter is complemented by selected artworks that symbolize key turning points in his journey and visually illustrate themes raised in the dialogue. Together, the narrative and visual materials illuminate how art–science collaborations can evolve, deepen, and open new directions for
research and creative practice.

articles.title: Science through an artistic lens: scientific aesthetics and aesthetic exhibition practices with kinetic art installations in science museums
articles.authors: Na Zhang; Priscilla Van Even; Huang Yaping
articles.abstract:
This chapter examines scientific aesthetics and the role of artistic mediation in contemporary science exhibitions, with a particular focus on kinetic art installations, a dynamic form of art that relies on movement and expressive motion. It situates aesthetic exhibition practices within the growing paradigm of experiential learning in science museums, which marks a shift from traditional top-down information transfer toward interactive exchange, as well as cognitive, sensorial, and aesthetic engagement of museum visitors through exhibition design. Rather than presenting science as static information to be passively absorbed, such exhibitions invite visitors to feel, reflect, and interpret through sensorial stimulation and meaningful cognitive engagement, reshaping how scientific knowledge is communicated, experienced, and understood.

Drawing on the vision of the Exploratorium, a museum of science, art, and human perception founded by Frank Oppenheimer, the chapter approaches art and science as complementary modes of revealing and exploring natural phenomena. Through a series of case studies in science museums where kinetic art installations function as artistic mediation, the chapter explores how these artworks communicate scientific ideas through metaphor, movement, and interaction. These examples demonstrate how artistic mediation can render complex processes tangible and participatory. Together, they show how aesthetic exhibition practices foster active meaning-making and position science as a dynamic, interpretative process.

articles.title: A practical guide to perform an Interdisciplinary Scoping Review
articles.authors: Jeroen Spijker
articles.abstract:
The growth of interdisciplinary research has brought with it an increasing demand for robust methods to map and synthesize diverse bodies of evidence. Among these, scoping reviews have emerged as a particularly valuable tool. They allow researchers to systematically explore complex, cross-cutting topics, clarify definitions, identify gaps, and build foundations for future inquiry.
This guide was developed to respond to that need. It provides a step-by-step framework for conducting an interdisciplinary scoping review, illustrated with the example of digitalisation and its effects on the physical health of older workers. By walking through each stage of the process—from formulating research questions to reporting and publishing findings—the guide aims to make the methodology transparent, practical, and replicable for researchers at different career stages and across disciplines.
The approach presented here is rooted in established frameworks and aligned with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to ensure rigour and clarity. At the same time, it reflects the lessons learned from my own experience conducting interdisciplinary reviews in practice.
I hope this guide encourages researchers to approach scoping reviews in a more systematic and transparent way, while also fostering collaboration across disciplines.

articles.title: Beyond technical thinking: revealing reflections on technology, media art, logocentrism, and epistemic diversity
articles.authors: Priscilla Van Even; Ief Spincemaille
articles.abstract:
This chapter examines art–science-technology interactions and epistemic diversity in a world
shaped by technological progress and scientific knowledge, which are deeply intertwined. While
technology is often understood as the use and development of instruments, a means to an end, it is
not only something we use; it also shapes how we understand and engage with reality. In this
technological ‘revealing’ of reality, the world increasingly presents itself as measurable,
controllable, and exploitable: as a resource. This chapter refers to this instrumentalization of reality
as technical thinking.

In this chapter, we first show that within artistic practice, the use of technology does not necessarily
lead to technical thinking. When engaged within artistic practice, it can open non-technical,
contemplative ways of relating to the world. The chapter then reverses this perspective by showing
that technical thinking can also operate without visible machines, particularly through logocentric
language in scientific practice, where articulation and description function as a technology of
ordering and control and become conditions for what counts as knowledge.

Ultimately, the chapter asks how artistic and other ways of knowing can enter scientific contexts
without being assimilated into technical thinking, and reflects on the conditions for sustaining
epistemic diversity in contemporary knowledge institutions.

articles.title: Meritocracy, Legitimation and Belonging on the University of Cambridge’s Foundation Year
articles.authors: Jacob Tuncel
articles.abstract: Widening participation spans the whole student lifecycle, from access through to success within higher education and progression beyond it, yet policy and evaluation have concentrated on the access stage alone. Far less is known about how students admitted through widened access routes come to understand the legitimacy of their place once inside an elite university. Reporting twenty-one (n=21) walking interviews with students who entered the University of Cambridge through its Foundation Year, a one-year pre-degree programme for applicants whose educational opportunities have been constrained by structural disadvantage, this article examines a tension at the heart of meritocracy. Participants recognized that admissions standards are shaped by unequal opportunity, though the recognition appeared not to weaken their commitment to meritocratic judgement, and they endeavored to suffuse their belonging with proof of deservingness. Such a pattern sits uneasily with Bourdieusian accounts of symbolic domination grounded in misrecognition, and points towards a compliance sustained through lucid perception of meritocracy and its ideological demands. Analysis of the walks suggests that the route organizes this tension by marking students publicly as different, by tying belonging to a competitive progression threshold, by collapsing heterogeneous experiences into a single administrative category, and by locating institutional judgement in everyday encounters with teaching staff. Belonging emerges less as a settled outcome of admission than as a conditional status that must be repeatedly earned. Widening access may therefore secure entry without securing the later stages of participation, so long as the legitimacy of membership continues to be organized through meritocratic evaluation that students simultaneously critique and reproduce.

articles.title: Cognitive and Proactive Building Operation: Current Status and an Eight-Gap Research Agenda
articles.authors: Matthias Huemmer
articles.abstract: Buildings dominate final energy demand, but operation remains reactive. This paper reviews cognitive and proactive building operation and derives a research agenda. Two questions guide the analysis: RQ1, the current status of seven constituent streams; RQ2, the gaps explaining the persistent distance between concept and practice. A critical review (July 2026) covers cognitive building concepts, MPC, RL/data-driven control, OCC, AFDD, cognitive digital twins with semantic infrastructure, and LLM-based agentic systems. Retrieval prioritised recent reviews and field deployments, with snowballing. An explicit evidence hierarchy and gap-derivation rule are stated, and bibliographic records were verified against metadata. An independent bibliometric strand uses a documented Web of Science query on cognitive, adaptive, cybernetic, and AI vocabulary, yielding 113 records (2011-2026). This corpus is profiled bibliometrically and mapped onto the gap taxonomy. The query string is reproduced verbatim, its retrieval behaviour is audited, and two artefacts materially affecting interpretation are discussed. The status pattern is consistent: conceptually rich, simulation-mature, field-poor. Bibliometrics sharpen this: 49% of records are from 2024-2026; a single 2020 review accounts for 49% of citations; only 20% are building-related (rest in software, manufacturing, general digital twins); cybernetic-building intersections contain only three records, the latest from 2015; co-word analysis reveals structural zeros, with cybernetics and self-adaptive systems never co-occurring. The query audit confirms: although the viable system model is named, exactly one of 113 records engages Beer's model, and it does not concern buildings. Outside the database, this organizing principle is applied in production management, software architecture, and agentic AI, but not in contemporary building operation. Eight gaps are derived: G1 definitional/theoretical, G2 reactive-to-proactive practice, G3 simulation-to-reality, G4 fragmentation, G5 architectural mechanism, G6 evaluation, G7 longevity/resilience, and G8 human factors/governance. G1-G4 and G6-G8 restate explicit deficits; G5 is an interpretive synthesis. The paper argues G5, the absence of an organizing principle for allocating sensing, computation, and actuation across subsystems, spatial scales, and time horizons, is structurally prior to several other gaps, and candidate principles are compared. Contributions include a cross-stream status consolidation, an evidence-anchored gap taxonomy with derivation rules, bibliometric quantitative support, and a defended keystone-gap argument. The review is evaluative rather than exhaustive and positions its findings as an evidence-based hypothesis set for a subsequent protocol-driven systematic review.

articles.title: Is Entrepreneurship Legitimate Where the State Is Not? Insights from Machine Learning Methods
articles.authors: Farhad Feizi
articles.abstract: Does the political environment influence people’s perceptions of entrepreneurship? Should there be any correlation between state legitimacy and that of entrepreneurship? These questions are crucial, as the success of any developmental tool, including entrepreneurship, depends on its public approval. To find the answers, the present paper examines Iran as an extreme case of a state facing recurring episodes of legitimacy crisis while simultaneously deeply involved in promoting entrepreneurship and penetrating the entrepreneurial ecosystem. The paper reveals that Iranians’ perceptions of entrepreneurship essentially mirror the polarized political atmosphere in society, divided between those who support the country’s entrepreneurial achievements and those who challenge them. Nonetheless, pragmatic reasons, rather than anti-state emotions, such as the state’s problematic intervention in the ecosystem, fueled these criticisms. More crucially, the paper contributes to the literature on institutional determinants of entrepreneurship legitimacy by demonstrating a direct and meaningful association between state and entrepreneurship legitimacy.

articles.title: Energy Security vs. Food Inflation: An Empirical Analysis of Crop-Substitution and Price Spillover Effects in India's E20 Ethanol Expansion
articles.authors: Abhay kumar chandarwal
articles.abstract: India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme has advanced from a marginal 1.14–1.53 per cent blending rate in 2013–14 to the statutory 20 per cent (E20) target by Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025–26, five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. This rapid scale-up has been accompanied by an equally rapid structural shift in feedstock composition: official data show the share of grain-based ethanol (maize, rice, and damaged food grain) rising from roughly 9 per cent of total procurement in ESY 2020–21 to nearly 60 per cent by early ESY 2024–25, with industry-association estimates placing maize's individual share alone at approximately 50 per cent by ESY 2024–25, up from 6.2 per cent two years earlier. This paper examines the resulting energy-security-versus-food-inflation trade-off using officially reported and peer-reviewed data. It synthesises the National Policy on Biofuels (2018, amended 2022), the NITI Aayog Roadmap for Ethanol Blending in India 2020–25, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) blending statistics, USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) maize market data, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and Ministry of Finance inflation reporting, and a 2026 peer-reviewed partial-equilibrium modelling study (published in PLOS One by researchers at the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, and the FABLE Consortium). The analysis finds credible evidence of crop-substitution pressure — a 14.7 per cent year-on-year decline in maize production coinciding with record consumption, an 84 per cent collapse in maize exports, and open-market maize prices exceeding the government's minimum support price by approximately 11 per cent in April 2024 — alongside documented cumulative energy-security gains of over ₹1.36–1.59 lakh crore in foreign exchange savings. However, the paper finds that a direct, India-specific econometric (VAR/Granger) estimate of ethanol-to-food-price transmission does not yet exist in the peer-reviewed literature; this study is accordingly framed as a literature- and data-grounded empirical synthesis rather than primary econometric estimation, and it explicitly flags this gap as a priority for future research. Policy recommendations centre on feedstock diversification toward 2G/cellulosic ethanol, protection of grain buffer stocks, and integration of food-price monitoring into the biofuel roadmap.

articles.title: Conveying the crisis: A corpus-assisted analysis of how left- and right-leaning UK newspapers frame the green energy transition
articles.authors: Yingnian Tao; Mark Ryan
articles.abstract: The green energy transition has recently become a hot topic in public and policy debates in the UK. This study employs corpus-assisted analysis to examine how the green energy transition is represented in left-leaning and right-leaning UK newspapers (2015-2024). Specifically, we identified the temporal changes in frequencies of emotional reporting and analysed and compared five group of strong emotion words (represented by crisis, damage, greenwashing, catastrophe, and wealth) through collocation analysis and concordance analysis. Our findings indicate that although the sentiment of coverage is more positive than negative, negative sentiment is gradually increasing over time. Both sides cover environmental and economic aspects of the transition; however, they differ in their priority area and the way they engage with these areas. Left-leaning newspapers emphasise environmental degradation, blame fossil fuels for the climate crisis, and call for urgent action. Right-leaning newspapers focus more on the economic impacts of transition, often framing policies as threats to jobs or prosperity while downplaying accountability for emissions. Across the spectrum, reporting tends to adopt a techno-optimist, business-as-usual stance that rarely challenges the idea of continuous economic growth. Implications for media, readers, and policymakers are discussed.

articles.title: Validation of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale and Autonomy Scale among People with Long-Term Care Needs
articles.authors: Takazumi Ono; Hiroko Costantini; Shinichiro Kumagaya; Ikuko Sugawara; Katsuya Iijima; Misato Nihei
articles.abstract: Social relationships with surrounding people and an individual's autonomy are fundamental components of age-friendly community and long-term care (LTC). The objective of the present study was to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale (TSS) and Autonomy Scales (AS) among people with LTC needs. We distributed a self-administered questionnaire to four daycare/day-services facilities and three home-visit nurse stations in Japan. The TSS consists of 20 items under 4 factors and the AS includes 20 items based on 3 factors. These scales were previously validated in the Japanese general population. 259 people participated in the survey. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated model fit for the TSS was good, whereas that for the AS was acceptable. In addition, explanatory factor analysis demonstrated that the AS had 2-factor structure specified for people with LTC. The regression coefficients for subjective well-being were 0.43 (95%CI 0.23, 0.62) and 0.73 (95%CI 0.50, 0.96), respectively. The alphas in the TSS and the AS ranged from 0.75 to 0.88, from 0.53 to 0.91, respectively. The alphas of the AS in first and second factors specified for people with LTC needs were 0.91 and 0.70, respectively. In conclusion, the TSS and the AS were valid and reliable in people with LTC needs. However, regarding the AS, different factor structures should be used (the structure in general population and that specified in people with LTC needs) depending on the purpose of the assessment. In addition, further studies to assess test-retest reliability and measurement error are needed.

articles.title: Tool or Trend? Workload, Confidence, and the Conditions for Generative AI Adoption in Research Administration
articles.authors: Claire Major; Sandeep Dhaliwal
articles.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly transforming white-collar work; however, little is known about its uptake in research administration, a specialized field of non-routine, judgement-dependent labour. This study reports the findings from a cross-sectional survey of researchers and research administrative staff at a large academic research hospital in Toronto, Canada (n = 119). Almost three-quarters of respondents (73%) reported using generative AI tools for research administrative work. Four outcome variables, Frequency, Effectiveness, Impact, and Quality of generative AI use, were strongly intercorrelated, indicating that respondents who used the tools more frequently also rated them more favourably across all three evaluative dimensions. Self-assessed confidence positively predicted evaluations of the tools, whereas job security concern was negatively associated with evaluations of generative AI. Respondents who iteratively refined outputs rated the tools more favourably than those who abandoned their attempts at using them, while heavier workloads were associated with less favourable quality perceptions. These findings suggest that realizing generative AI’s potential in administrative work depends on the user’s skills, confidence, and working conditions, rather than the tools themselves.

articles.title: Von Neumann’s Blurry Elephant: On The Need for Care and Clarity in Modeling Complex Social Systems
articles.authors: Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: Wildman and Shults have laid out an ambitious scope for their book, Modeling Religion: Simulating the Transformation of Worldviews, Lifeways, and Civilization. I laud their aims and echo their enthusiasm for modeling. However, I also believe that Wildman and Shults largely fail to achieve their goals. Their models are neither clear nor well justified, and so their results are not compelling. The book’s value is in the attempt, and in the discussions which are based more on interpretations of empirical data than on conclusions from the published models. I believe it will be instructive to explain why I think the goals of the book were not achieved. To do so, I will first explain a bit about how the models work. I will then discuss general guidelines for the use of formal models to understand complex social dynamics, and how Wildman Shults fail to meet them.

articles.title: Changing Partisanship Contributes Significantly to Rising Affective Polarization: Evidence from a Decomposition of Panel Data
articles.authors: Derek Edward Holliday
articles.abstract: Time-series cross-sectional surveys document a decades-long rise in American affective polarization. But the measure is defined only over partisans, and who counts as a partisan is itself dynamic. Using the three ANES panels spanning 1990--96 and 2016--24, I separate the measured rise into two channels: hardening, within-person change among those who keep their partisan label, and churn, turnover in who holds it. Churn accounts for almost a third of the within-panel rise, about 1.6 times movers' share of the sample. Those who change partisanship already lean toward their destination party, in affect and predicted partisanship, before they move: a prospective signature of sorting. Because movers are less polarized than stayers, the aggregate trend overstates how much partisan affect has changed and understates animosity among committed partisans---bearing on how we quantify partisan animosity, interpret its movement, and judge what reversal requires.

articles.title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Majority-Group Ties and Their Political Consequences
articles.authors: Sakeef M. Karim
articles.abstract: In this study, I highlight an underappreciated catalyst for political socialisation in immigrant societies—the intergenerational transmission of majority ties. Drawing on nine waves of German panel data from the Children of Immigrants Longitudinal Survey in Four European Countries (2011–2022), I demonstrate that the “Germanness” of parental networks shapes youth respondents’ majority- group ties in adolescence, and illustrate how these social inheritances influence the Germanness of adolescent networks during the transition to early adulthood. By Wave 9, when most respondents are in their late 20s, the Germanness of social networks is closely linked to political preferences: native majorities with more German-centric networks are less likely to support left-wing parties, while the inverse is true for most of their immigrant-origin peers. These patterns reflect distinct but complementary mechanisms: for immigrants and their descendants, majority ties signal structural assimilation into “mainstream” political culture and convergence with liberal-cosmopolitan norms; for natives, ethnically diverse social networks reinforce enculturation into progressive political communities. Overall, these findings show that political socialisation operates not only through the transmission of beliefs and cultural orientations, but through the concomitant reproduction of social environments.

articles.title: Resilience: Understand Breakdown, Foster Recovery, and Choose the Right Perspective
articles.authors: Frank Schweitzer
articles.abstract:
Resilience denotes the capacity of a system to withstand shocks and to recover from them. We distinguish between two different types of dynamics. The first allows for a separation between phases of normalcy and phases of rapid breakdown followed by slow recovery. The second applies to volatile organizations in which such phases are intertwined.
Breakdown is often self-inflicted. Situation awareness is impaired by psychological mechanisms that lead to incorrect expectations regarding societal dynamics. Through positive feedback, the failure of a few elements is amplified into a failure cascade. However, positive feedback can also be harnessed to enable recovery.
In volatile systems, resilience must be understood as an emergent property arising from the interaction of agents. This necessitates a data-driven approach to inform agent-based models, drawing on repositories, knowledge graphs, or tools from artificial intelligence. Such models help demonstrate that resilience represents a compromise between robustness and adaptivity. Maximizing performance frequently comes at the expense of resilience, and second-order solutions aimed at transforming the system prove more promising than attempts to reconstruct past conditions.

articles.title: Do polls underestimate support for right-wing parties? Assessing variation in polling error by party family
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Will Jennings; Jonathan Mellon; Christopher Prosser; Christopher Wlezien
articles.abstract: Pollsters have underestimated support for notable right-wing electoral outcomes, including Donald Trump’s vote share in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the UK Conservative Party in 2015 and 2024, and Leave in the 2016 EU referendum. Do these outcomes reflect isolated polling failures, or a persistent partisan asymmetry in polling error across democracies? We provide the first comparative analysis of partisan polling error. Drawing on over 38,500 election-poll-party observations across 32 countries and 372 elections between 1945 and 2025, we use a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to estimate latent election-party polling error. We find that, on average, support for parties on the left is overestimated, while support for parties on the right is underestimated. This pattern is evident across countries, party classifications, and vote intention polling dating to the 1940s. In spotlighting persistent partisan asymmetries, our findings contribute to understanding institutional and contextual correlates of pre-election polling accuracy.

articles.title: Wealth Poverty: Measurement, Prevalence, Determinants
articles.authors: Manuel Schechtl; Janet C. Gornick; Carolyn Fisher
articles.abstract: We review the emerging literature on wealth poverty, defined as the lack of sufficient assets to sustain minimally adequate living standards, buffer shocks, or meet basic needs. This condition appears under multiple labels, including asset poverty, liquid-asset poverty, or net-worth poverty, but the underlying question is shared: how much economic insecurity remains invisible when insufficient wealth is not taken into account? We synthesize scholarship on three issues. First, we examine how researchers define wealth, choose thresholds, and distinguish stock-based, annuitized, and multidimensional approaches. Second, we review evidence on prevalence, showing that wealth poverty is widespread, only partially overlaps with income poverty, and varies sharply by asset definition, household structure, and institutional context. Third, we assess micro- and macro-level determinants, highlighting how stratification and policy regimes jointly structure households’ capacity to accumulate and retain assets. We also provide practical guidelines for future research on how to conceptualize and operationalize wealth poverty. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

articles.title: Leaving Money on the Table: A Monte-Carlo Study Comparing Causal Forest and Standard Regression Models for Experiments
articles.authors: Sam Fuller; Jack T. Rametta
articles.abstract: Causal machine learning methods for experiments have proliferated, but adoption in political science is scarce. Are political scientists "leaving money on the table" by neglecting to apply these methods? To answer this question, we use over two million Monte-Carlo simulations to compare causal forest (CF) to standard regression techniques commonly used to estimate average and conditional average treatment effects. We find that CF outperforms standard methods in terms of statistical power, coverage, precision, bias, and the accurate detection and consequent estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. However, CF underperforms in edge cases where measured covariates are entirely uninformative and sample sizes are very small. Moreover, we find that standard approaches have large false-positive rates for conditional treatment effects: 9–24 times larger than rates for CF. Our results suggest that researchers who choose to use CF stand to benefit greatly across statistical power, coverage, precision, bias, and heterogeneity detection.

articles.title: Are Random Forests Still ‘Good Enough’? Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Predictive and Causal Tasks
articles.authors: Jack T. Rametta; Sam Fuller
articles.abstract: Are random forests, the workhorse of supervised machine learning methods in the social sciences, still “good enough” versus new methods that tout dramatic performance beneﬁts? In this article we present a large, diverse Monte Carlo study and existing real-world data benchmarks to compare tree-based methods with TabPFN, a new pretrained transformer foundation model that performs in-context learning over millions of synthetic datasets designed for tabular data. We compare tree-based methods with TabPFN in the popular R-learner framework for conditional average treatment effect estimation. This allows us to assess both predictive model performance and resulting gains for downstream inference. First, our simulations suggest that TabPFN does outperform random forest, achieving near-oracle results for conditional effect estimation. TabPFN’s improvements manifest in the most diﬃcult simulation setups, where the data generating process is complex and there are fewer observations. Second, in real-world data analyses TabPFN performs well, outperforming random forest in some cases, especially as sample dwindles and the number of predictive covariates increases. Our results suggest that tree-based methods are still well suited for social science data, but TabPFN speciﬁcally, and the prior data ﬁtted network approach generally, is a strong competitor worthy of consideration.

articles.title: Ethnicity, Support for Gender Equality, and the Justification for Intimate Partner Violence Against Women in Nigeria
articles.authors: Adaora Okwo
articles.abstract: A negative association between gender equality and intimate partner violence against women (IPVAW) is widely reported in the literature. But does this effect extend to when attitudes towards both gender equality and IPVAW, rather than their actual levels or occurrence, are being studied? Are people less likely to justify IPVAW when they support gender-equal opportunities? Also, does ethnicity moderate this relationship? This study addresses these questions using nationally representative Nigerian samples from the World Values Survey (n = 1,106). Bivariate analyses using ANOVA and Chi-square tests, and multivariate analysis using logistic regression, were performed to test relationships. Accounting for covariates, the findings only marginally supported the hypothesised negative effect of gender equality support on IPVAW justification (AME = -0.12, p = .058), partly because ethnicity moderates this effect. The probability of justifying IPVAW significantly reduced with increasing support for gender equality among the Yoruba (AME = -0.43, p < .001) and ethnic minority groups (AME = -0.45, p < .001), but not among the Igbo or Hausa/Fulani. When examined by gender, the negative relationship was significant only for women (AME = -0.22, p < .05); strengthened when the woman is Yoruba (AME= -0.62, p < .001) or ethnic minority (AME= -0.70, p < .001), and weakened when the woman is Igbo (AME= 0.38, p < .05). These results highlight the importance of considering culture as affecting the relationship between support for gender equality and IPVAW justification in Nigeria for targeted interventions in changing attitudes supporting IPVAW.

articles.title: The Changing Landscape of Democratic (Dis)Satisfaction: Results from the American National Election Study 1996–2024
articles.authors: Sam Fuller; Neil Williams; Jack T. Rametta
articles.abstract: What predicts democratic satisfaction in the United States? Using the 1996–2024 time series as well as the 2000–02–04 and 2016–20–24 panels from the American National Election Study, this article identifies the consistent and time-specific predictors of democratic satisfaction. We analyze satisfaction using 1) random forests to identify important predictors; 2) causal forests to test established predictors; and 3) doubly-robust difference-in-differences to identify the causal effect of winning elections. We find that 1) predictors have shifted significantly over time—affect toward big business dominates after 2016—but election efficacy and government responsiveness are consistently predictive; 2) established predictors, except affective polarization and participation, are all significant; and 3) winning elections significantly increases satisfaction, and effects in 2004 are double the size of the midterm and general elections in 2002 and 2020, respectively. These findings contextualize the United States in the broader comparative literature, opening avenues for future research on democratic satisfaction.

articles.title: Policy or Partisanship? How Polarization Biases Valence Evaluations in the U.S., U.K., and Taiwan
articles.authors: Sam Fuller; Tzu-Ping Liu
articles.abstract: How does affective and political polarization influence voters' evaluations of politicians? To answer this question, we use causal mediation analysis to examine three conjoint experiments fielded in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Taiwan that elicit respondents' evaluations of politicians' trustworthiness and governing competence. We find that political disagreement—differences in partisanship and/or policy preferences—influences evaluations, but the existence of direct effects and the size of total effects depends on whether partisanship serves as the dominant political social identity. In the U.S. and Taiwan, where partisanship serves as a clear social identity, co-partisanship has effects comparable to policy disagreement and exerts both direct and affect-mediated effects; whereas in the U.K., co-partisanship has weaker effects than policy disagreement, and only indirectly. These findings suggest that polarization influences valence evaluations generally, but operates either through partisanship or policy (dis)agreements depending upon a country's particular structure of political identities.

articles.title: Does more money help? The impact of the apprenticeship minimum wage on training offers and take-ups
articles.authors: Lina Tobler; Lukas Fervers; Annika Reiff
articles.abstract: We analyse the effect of the German minimum apprenticeship wage that was introduced in 2020 in response to increasing difficulties faced by firms in filling training positions. Theoretically, the impact on training activity is ambiguous: increased wages could potentially increase applicant numbers, while higher costs may reduce firms’ incentives to offer apprenticeships. We provide empirical evidence of the policy’s impact on offered training positions and actual take-ups. Using a difference-in-differences design with firm-level panel data, we find no evidence of a positive effect on either offered or filled trainings, but (if at all) negative effects.

articles.title: Breaking hearts and norms: How relationship and marriage beliefs change across relationship dissolution transitions in seven Eastern and Western European countries
articles.authors: Marie-Fleur Philipp; Pia Schober
articles.abstract: Cohort replacement and social diffusion have been emphasised as key mechanisms of observed large shifts towards greater acceptance of different relationship and family forms. Relationship dissolutions across the life course may contribute to changing partnership and marriage beliefs. Experiencing union dissolution violates individuals’ normative ideals of the life course, which may lead them to adjust their partnership and marriage expectations downward. This study explores changes in partnership and marriage beliefs across relationship dissolutions in seven European countries. We use fixed-effects panel data models and entropy balancing based on the German pairfam data (2008-2022, N=9,413 respondents) and the Generations and Gender Survey (2004-2015; N=38,033 respondents) for two additional Western and four Eastern European countries. In Germany, all types of union dissolutions were accompanied by more negative partnership beliefs, while widespread beliefs regarding the benefits of partnerships remained mostly unchanged, supporting a strong couple norm. Across all seven countries, beliefs regarding nonmarital cohabitation, the lifetime duration and the institution of marriage became substantially more liberal across marital dissolution. The liberalising changes of marriage beliefs across marital dissolution were smaller in Poland as a more religious Eastern European country, which was, however, largely accounted for by the greater selectivity of individuals who divorce in Poland. While our findings point to a strong couple norm and widespread approval of marriage in Europe, the latter is substantially weakened as individuals experience marital dissolution.

articles.title: Opinion Monitor Artificial Intelligence. Shaping the Use of AI in the Workplace –  Between Autonomous Use and Workload Reduction: Brief Report on a Conjoint Study
articles.authors: Marco Lünich; Birte Keller; Florian Kruse; Frank Marcinkowski
articles.abstract: This brief report presents key findings from a conjoint study conducted in May 2026 as part of the project Opinion Monitor Artificial Intelligence 3.0. The analysis examines the preferences of around 2,800 dependent employees in Germany regarding different design options for artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the workplace. The findings show that the assessment of AI systems is not determined solely by their technical performance. The strongest influence on preference formation is employees’ autonomy in AI use: respondents prefer systems that they can use at their own discretion, while mandatory use is clearly rejected. The effects on workload and the need for training are also important. Employees prefer AI systems that reduce workload or at least do not create additional work demands, and that are accompanied by practical, time-limited training. The quality of AI outputs, monitoring of AI use, and possible effects on social contacts also influence the choice between systems, but are less decisive in direct comparison. Overall, the findings show that introducing AI in the workplace is not only a technical task but also a matter of work and organizational design.

articles.title: Varieties of democratic vulnerability: a comparative study of checks and balances and popular acceptance of transgressions
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus; Magnus Feldmann; Giovanni D'Agostino
articles.abstract:
The recent wave of democratic backsliding has demonstrated that liberal democracies are vulnerable to subversion by authoritarian leaders. Research showed that democratically elected leaders remove checks and balances that constrain their power. One of the explanations why leaders can violate democratic rules focuses on the response of citizens who trade off democracy for partisan and policy gains. This article investigates cross-country differences in vulnerabilities to democratic backsliding by comparing democratic priority profiles of citizens and the patterns of approval for transgressions of democratic rules. 
We use observational evidence from online surveys with large quota-based samples of citizens in a two-party presidential system (USA, N > 1700), a multi-party parliamentary system based on proportional representation with some semi-presidential features (Poland, N >1800), and a consociational parliamentary system based on proportional representation (Netherlands, N = > 2100). To complement observational evidence, we test experimentally some of these aggregate-level differences: next to partisanship and policy gains, we also manipulate different democratic transgressions (protest rights and decree powers) and measure their effects on government approval in the three countries. 
Our results show that citizens of different countries have different democratic priority profiles and differ in their disapproval of specific transgressions. Although overall transgressions are not rewarded, and citizens are mostly vigilant and disapproving of violating democratic rules, we find both observational and experimental evidence indicating that liberal democracies can have different vulnerabilities that relate to the democratic attitudes of citizens.

articles.title: Event-level modelling of showering behaviour in German households: Triangulating smart-meter, in-situ survey and contextual public data
articles.authors: David Morizet; Pablo Pereira-Doel; Xavier Font; Caroline Bastide; Juliette Brun; Valérie Drey
articles.abstract: Residential water demand is strongly shaped by showering behaviour, yet quantifying drivers at the event level remains rare. We first explored and identified key patterns across 8,550 sensor-logged showering events from 319 German households. We then combined this high-resolution smart-meter data with time-stamped post-shower surveys to analyse shampoo-shower duration. The Gamma mixed model (14 predictors spanning demographics, context, in-shower behaviour and hair characteristics) explained 68.4% of deviance (AIC = 4281.6). Behavioural predictors showed the clearest associations: showers with two or more shampoo applications were 27% longer than those with one, while showers with three or more water pauses were 28% longer than those with one. Some contextual and demographic predictors also mattered: soft water areas were linked to 23% longer durations, and younger/mid-age adults had durations up to 31% longer than adults 50+. Other factors (gender, employment, household composition/size, home type, bills responsibility and most hair characteristics) showed small or uncertain effects after adjustment. Findings demonstrate how smart metering, event-level behavioural data and robust modelling can reveal actionable levers for demand-side management, behavioural interventions and product design.

articles.title: The Politics of Military Force: Antimilitarism, Ideational Change and Post-War German Security Discourse
articles.authors: Frank A. Stengel
articles.abstract: The Politics of Military Force examines the dynamics of discursive change that made participation in military operations possible against the background of German antimilitarist culture. Once considered a strict taboo, so-called out-of-area operations have now become widely considered by German policymakers to be without alternative. The book argues that an understanding of how certain policies are made possible (in this case, military operations abroad and force transformation), one needs to focus on processes of discursive change that result in different policy options appearing rational, appropriate, feasible, or even self-evident. Drawing on Essex School discourse theory, the book develops a theoretical framework to understand how discursive change works, and elaborates on how discursive change makes once unthinkable policy options not only acceptable but even without alternative. Based on a detailed discourse analysis of more than 25 years of German parliamentary debates, The Politics of Military Force provides an explanation for: (1) the emergence of a new hegemonic discourse in German security policy after the end of the Cold War (discursive change), (2) the rearticulation of German antimilitarism in the process (ideational change/norm erosion) and (3) the resulting making-possible of military operations and force transformation (policy change). In doing so, the book also demonstrates the added value of a poststructuralist approach compared to the naive realism and linear conceptions of norm change so prominent in the study of German foreign policy and International Relations more generally.

articles.title: Feminist voices, partisan networks: gender and political communication by MEPs on social media
articles.authors: Ainara Larrondo-Ureta; Simón Peña-Fernández; Julen Orbegozo-Terradillos; Jordi Morales-i-Gras
articles.abstract: This article analyses whether gender shapes Members of the European Parliament’s communication on X/Twitter and whether equality-related and LGBTQ+ issues influence patterns of visibility, tone and interaction. Drawing on automated content, sentiment and network analysis of 122,972 tweets posted in 2022 by 620 MEPs, the study finds that women tweeted more frequently and were more visible in promotional content, while men favoured opinion-driven and news-focused messages. Equality and LGBTQ+ topics appeared more often in women’s tweets (8.6%) than in men’s (4.0%), and women’s posts showed a more positive tone. However, interaction patterns were only marginally shaped by gender; instead, networks largely reflected political-group affiliation and national delegation. Overall, the findings suggest that although female MEPs engage more with equality-related issues, their digital communication remains embedded in established political structures, indicating gradual discursive change rather than substantive structural transformation.

articles.title: Catch the Patient, Not the AI: Collective Sensemaking in an Online Health Community
articles.authors: Feng He
articles.abstract: Patients and caregivers increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical reports, weigh care decisions, and seek emotional support. Yet most research treats patient-facing AI as a private exchange between a user and a system, leaving open how AI-related content is taken up once users carry it back into the peer communities where they already make sense of illness. This study examines collective sensemaking around AI in House086, China's largest online community for lymphoma patients and caregivers. We identified roughly 400 publicly accessible discussion threads (2014 to 2026) through AI-related keyword searches and manual screening, extracted them into structured case profiles using a schema-prompted large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, deployed via AWS Bedrock), and conducted mixed-method analysis. After quality control, the verified analytic sample comprised 337 post-ChatGPT records focused on widespread conversational-AI use. Members most often reported using AI for informational support, followed by second opinions and psychosocial support. Although members often introduced AI favorably, roughly one in six described feeling overwhelmed by AI output. When other members responded, they frequently engaged the poster's underlying medical or emotional intent while leaving the AI dimension unaddressed. The tendency to bypass AI persisted even in threads seeking triangulation between AI output and other information sources, and when posters shared overwhelmed or unfavorable experiences with AI. On the occasions when members did discuss the AI, they were more often cautious than endorsing. Rather than auditing AI output for factual accuracy, the community more often worked to deflate the false certainty it produced, placing a single AI answer back among multiple sources of judgment. This study argues that AI does not replace the interpretive work of online health communities, nor is it systematically audited by them. Instead, it shifts the locus of sensemaking downstream, so that the community continues to catch the person even when it does not catch the AI, and the interpretive authority that follows does not settle in any single place. We discuss implications for CSCW theory, online-community norms, and patient-facing AI design.

articles.title: Promotion Strategy Based on the Effectiveness of Social Media, Outdoor Media, and Event Marketing on Students’ Decisions in Choosing a Private Higher Education Institution
articles.authors: Budi Setiawan
articles.abstract: The higher education sector is becoming increasingly competitive, requiring universities to implement effective promotion strategies to attract prospective students. This study analyzes the effectiveness of promotion strategies implemented by the studied private higher education institution through social media marketing, outdoor advertising, and event marketing, and identifies the main factors influencing students’ decisions to enroll. A quantitative descriptive approach was used with survey data collected from 207 respondents representing more than 93 schools. The results show that Instagram and TikTok are the most frequently used platforms among students, with usage rates of 87 percent and 82 percent. However, the conversion rate of social media video advertisements is relatively low, ranging from 21 percent to 29 percent. Outdoor advertising through billboards on Surya Kencana Street shows higher effectiveness with a conversion rate of 76 percent. Event marketing activities such as school presentations demonstrate moderate effectiveness, while programs such as institutional academic competition program, open stands, and the “institution Mengajar” show lower awareness levels. The main factors influencing students’ decisions include campus location, study program relevance, employment prospects, accreditation, and tuition fees. The study highlights the need for integrated promotional strategies combining digital engagement, offline visibility, and experiential marketing to improve recruitment effectiveness in private higher education institutions.

articles.title: Full Reporting in Empirical Asset Pricing: A Statistical Decision-Theoretic Approach
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: This study develops a full-reporting framework for empirical asset pricing grounded in statistical decision theory. In the abductive stage, simulated pseudo-factor model spaces are used to evaluate whether candidate test scores can distinguish valid from invalid model states through likelihood behavior, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and classification metrics. In the inductive stage, realized sample scores are mapped to likelihood ratios, error rates, and decision criteria, translating observed evidence into model-state predictions. Reporting this complete inferential chain enables test performance and realized evidence to be integrated into transparent assessments of factor-model validity.

articles.title: DA ORIGEM DO DECLÍNIO DO FUTEBOL BRASILEIRO POR MEIO DA ANÁLISE DE SUAS CAUSAS ESTRUTURAIS, OU A PRESERVAÇÃO DE VÍCIOS INSTITUCIONAIS NA LUTA PELO DESENVOLVIMENTO ESPORTIVO
articles.authors: Bruno Oliveira Costa Jimez
articles.abstract: Quando uma nação que se acostumou a tratar o futebol como atributo natural de sua gente é eliminada de uma Copa do Mundo nas oitavas de final, duas reações se apresentam de imediato: a busca do culpado e a busca do consolo. Ambas são compreensíveis; nenhuma é conhecimento. Esta obra nasce da recusa de ambas. O seu ponto de partida é um acontecimento datado — a derrota para a Noruega em 5 de julho de 2026 —, mas o seu objeto não é esse acontecimento: é o processo de longa duração de que ele é apenas a manifestação mais recente. O médico que confunde a febre com a doença trata o termômetro; o analista que confunde uma eliminação com o declínio troca o técnico. Este capítulo define o problema com a precisão necessária para que os tomos seguintes possam resolvê-lo.

articles.title: Advisor career stage and PhD advisee outcomes
articles.authors: Xi Hong; Jialin Liu; Chaoqun Ni
articles.abstract: PhD advisors are central to doctoral training, but their influence may vary across career stages. Early-, mid-, and late-career advisors may differ in research activity, mentoring capacity, professional networks and access to resources. However, little is known about how PhD advisor career stage is associated with PhD student development outcomes. Drawing on multiple large-scale datasets comprising 250,838 advisor-advisee pairs from 312 U.S. PhD-granting institutions, we examine the relationship between advisor career stage and PhD advisee outcomes in knowledge production, collaboration networks and academic career placement. We find that early-career PhD advisors are associated with advisees’ higher research productivity and citation performance, more opportunities to engage in direct and intensive research collaboration, and greater likelihood of securing a faculty position. Mid- and late-career faculty, by contrast, appear to have advantages in providing network capital which students can inherit after graduation, training PhD advisees to produce disruptive research, and supporting them in securing faculty positions at top institutions. This study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the reproduction of scientific talent by revealing the role of advisor career stage in shaping this process. These findings have implications for doctoral applicants’ decision-making and for institutional policymaking on PhD training, faculty support and faculty evaluation.

articles.title: When Does Anticorruption Pay off? Voter Support for Anticorruption Efforts in Latin America
articles.authors: Gustavo Guajardo
articles.abstract: While politicians commonly employ anticorruption appeals, the effectiveness of such appeals varies considerably. I argue that anticorruption appeals carry signals of authenticity and examine how voters use information on the context of corruption, the messenger, and the content of the policy in their evaluations. Drawing on two original survey experiments in Colombia and Mexico, I show that voters rely on these features to evaluate anticorruption action by politicians. Evaluations are more favorable in the absence of a recent corruption scandal, when the proposer is an opposition politician, and when the policy emphasizes punitiveness. However, political loyalties can dampen the effect of opposition membership. Remarkably, governing party legislators are rewarded for punitive action whereas opposition legislators are not---an effect that is strongest among respondents who did not support the incumbent president. These findings offer new insights into how voters evaluate the credibility of anticorruption appeals, showing how such appeals can boost electoral outcomes regardless of politicians’ intentions to follow through.

articles.title: Digital Green Signaling: Dual Pathways to Conspicuous Green  Consumption and eWOM
articles.authors: Senyo Obed Amponsah
articles.abstract: Sustainable marketing increasingly unfolds on social media, where green claims are not only read but also evaluated, liked, questioned, shared, and used for identity display. Yet research on green consumption often treats online green communication as a general stimulus and typically stops at purchase intention. This conceptual paper develops a digital green signaling framework explaining how engagement with online green content moves consumers toward conspicuous green consumption and green electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM). The framework argues that online green consumption is shaped by two complementary legitimacy routes. In the claim-legitimacy route, firm-generated green content builds perceived green brand authenticity and green trust when environmental claims are transparent, specific, and verifiable. In the social-validation route, user- and influencer-generated green content activates informational and normative social influence, particularly when social proof makes peer endorsement visible. Green trust and anticipated social approval then converge to make green consumption displayable, while green eWOM extends this display into digital advocacy. The paper contributes by reframing social media green consumption as a visibility, verification, and circulation problem; by differentiating firm-controlled and socially embedded routes without collapsing them into a single communication effect; and by positioning green eWOM as a continuation of public green identity signaling. A typology, propositions, boundary conditions, and an empirical research roadmap are developed to guide future sustainable marketing research.

articles.title: Mountain Development in Nepal: Settlements, Infrastructure, and Economic Transformation
articles.authors: Keshav Bhattarai; Ambika P. Adhikari
articles.abstract:
As Nepal urbanizes, expands infrastructure, strengthens local governments, and explores deeper connectivity with India and China, climate change is increasing floods, landslides, heat, and water insecurity. Rapid internal migration, rising disaster risks, youth outmigration, and dependence on remittances are also revealing the limits of conventional urban development, especially in the mountainous region. The central challenge for Nepal is no longer just to accommodate growing towns and cities, but to build settlements that are safe, productive, environmentally resilient, and capable of sustaining long-term prosperity.

This paper argues that Nepal's urban future must be guided by a new development paradigm centered on safe, smart, and resilient settlements. This is even more applicable for Nepal’s mountainous regions. This article presents an integrated framework that links risk-sensitive land use, climate-resilient infrastructure, ecological stewardship, productive local economies, digital technologies, and accountable governance to emerging opportunities in air, rail, and highway connectivity, data centers, medical tourism, higher education, and climate services. Rather than viewing urbanization as an inevitable consequence of rural-to-urban migration and economic growth, the article proposes that well-planned settlements should become Nepal's primary platform for reducing disaster risk, creating jobs, expanding exports, and strengthening national resilience in the twenty-first century.

articles.title: Economically Foreclosed-Choice Flexibility: How Maternal Remote Work is Miscounted as Voluntary
articles.authors: Maha Jehanzeb
articles.abstract: The existing literature on flexible and remote work treats ‘voluntariness’ as a condition that separates arrangements which protect employee wellbeing from those that harm it. The concept of voluntariness, itself, is traditionally measured as a worker’s reported choice over the practice; this measure cannot clearly distinguish a choice which is made freely from a choice which is made because no other option was financially possible. This article focuses on advancing a theory adaptation. Drawing from self-determination theory (SDT), more specifically the difference it establishes between autonomy as volition rather than mere independence, and between autonomous and controlled motivation, it re-specifies voluntariness in the field of flexible work. The paper introduces the concept of economically foreclosed-choice flexibility, which is defined as an objective condition of the household option set rather than by how a worker feels, and goes on to propose that economic foreclosure transforms a formally chosen arrangement into a controlled one. Thus, it breaks the autonomy mechanism with which voluntary remote work is said to confer its benefits. The paper will follow three propositions, with the last one stating that protective effect estimates of voluntary remote work are biased upwards because the results combine a benefitting volitional group with a non-benefitting foreclosed group. The core argument of the paper identifies a population that the current measure cannot see, and it points out where, and for whom, the field’s headline conclusions require qualification.

articles.title: Deepfakes in the Global South: Understanding Stakeholder Perceptions, Harms and Governance Challenges in Sri Lanka, India, and Bangladesh
articles.authors: Dilrukshi Gamage; Dilki Sewwandi; Sumaia Arefin; Dilaxshini Dunston; Kartik Joshi; Rashmi Gunawardena; Shreeti Shubham
articles.abstract:
With the rapid proliferation of AI-generated synthetic media
across South Asia, communities in Sri Lanka, India, and Bangladesh
face deepfake-related harms that existing Trust & Safety frameworks—
designed predominantly for Global North contexts—are ill-equipped to
address. Through three participatory workshops with 49 stakeholders
including journalists, lawyers, fact-checkers, feminist advocates, and civil
society practitioners, we investigate how deepfake harms are perceived,
experienced, and contested across these distinct yet interconnected
contexts. Our findings reveal four cross-cutting patterns: disproportionate
gendered targeting of women and marginalized communities; systematic
failure of platform moderation for South Asian languages; inaccessible
institutional recourse for victims; and strong community preference
for locally governed, participatory solutions over externally designed
technical fixes. We contribute empirical evidence of deepfake harm in
under-researched Global South contexts, a cross-country comparative
framework for Trust & Safety analysis, and a set of design and policy
implications that center community knowledge, survivor support, and
linguistic justice as foundations for a reimagined deepfake governance
paradigm.

articles.title: The Possibility of Bugs Bunny at Disneyland: A Reexamination of Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and Its Companion Studies
articles.authors: Thomas Kelly
articles.abstract:
Various studies report inducing false memories of meeting Bugs Bunny at Disney-owned theme
parks. Such claims have been influential in psychology– thought to substantiate broader claims
about false memories– and in the courtroom where the Bugs Bunny false memory research has
been used to question the credibility of those who report being witnesses or victims of serious
crime, including sexual assault. This paper examines Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and finds
multiple false claims of statistical significance, including its headline results that the authors
were able to increase the rate of false memories through doctored ads. This article discusses
other serious flaws in Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and its follow-up articles such as
impossible means, inaccurate p-values, apparent violation of random assignment, reported
survey instruments that were about generic theme park memories rather than Disney memories,
and a failure to screen out subjects who may have authentic memories of a Bugs Bunny
encounter due to the authors’ misunderstanding of the history of Warner Bros. characters in
theme parks.

articles.title: Age of Planetarity: A Deep Dive Assessment on Empire of Zombie Technologies
articles.authors: Florian Vidal; José Halloy
articles.abstract: This article analyses the contemporary international system through a pluridisciplinary lens integrating imperial history, complex systems theory, and Earth system science. Situated within the dynamics of the Anthropocene, it reconceptualizes contemporary great-power competition by examining socio-technical systems (STS) predicated on the intensive consumption of fossil fuels and mineral resources. We posit that the prevailing STS metabolic regime is unsustainable in the long term, owing to the significant constraints imposed by geological and planetary boundaries. These limitations will become increasingly pronounced as the effects of the systemic crisis intensify. This regime not only perpetuates imperialist logics, visible in rivalries over resources essential for technological dominance, but also generates a ‘zombified’ technosphere that actively disrupts Earth system processes and jeopardizes planetary habitability. The article consequently advocates for de-imperialism as an essential trajectory, requiring a shift to networked and systemic geopolitics via the active dismantling of imperial structures.

articles.title: Ten simple rules for creating and maintaining FAIR competency frameworks
articles.authors: Denise Bianco; Daria Sokolova; Matthew Forshaw; Clementina Ramirez Marengo; Emma Karoune; Kim T. Gurwitz; Vera Matser
articles.abstract: In a modern skills-based economy, competency frameworks are essential tools for workforce planning, career progression, and professional development. However, traditional frameworks often exist as static, isolated documents that lack digital connectivity and machine-readability. This paper introduces a strategic roadmap to modernise professional standards by applying the FAIR principles: making competency frameworks Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. We present the FAIR competency framework lifecycle, an iterative model centred on end-user engagement, and outline 10 simple rules to guide creators through every stage of development. These rules cover foundational definitions, clear language, persistent identifiers, permissive licensing, and robust governance. By transforming frameworks into machine-actionable digital objects, organisations can ensure their standards are easily discoverable, reusable, and ready for integration into broader learning management systems. Ultimately, adopting these guidelines promotes a more interconnected, transparent, and adaptable global skills landscape where professional expertise can be recognised and shared efficiently.

articles.title: Meinungsmonitor Künstliche Intelligenz – Die Gestaltung des KI-Einsatzes am Arbeitsplatz. Zwischen autonomer Nutzung und Arbeitsentlastung: Kurzbericht einer Conjoint-Studie
articles.authors: Marco Lünich; Birte Keller; Florian Kruse; Frank Marcinkowski
articles.abstract: Der Kurzbericht präsentiert zentrale Ergebnisse einer Conjoint-Studie des Projekts Meinungsmonitor Künstliche Intelligenz 3.0, die im Mai 2026 durchgeführt wurde. Analysiert werden Präferenzen von rund 2.800 abhängig Beschäftigten in Deutschland für unterschiedliche Gestaltungsformen von Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) am Arbeitsplatz. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass für die Bewertung von KI-Systemen nicht allein ihre technische Leistungsfähigkeit entscheidend ist. Am stärksten prägt die Autonomie bei der KI-Nutzung die Präferenzentscheidung: Beschäftigte bevorzugen Systeme, die sie nach eigenem Ermessen nutzen können, während eine verpflichtende Nutzung deutlich abgelehnt wird. Ebenfalls bedeutsam sind die Auswirkungen auf den Arbeitsumfang und der Weiterbildungsbedarf. Präferiert werden KI-Systeme, die Arbeit entlasten oder zumindest keine zusätzliche Arbeitsbelastung erzeugen und mit einer praxisnahen, zeitlich überschaubaren Qualifizierung verbunden sind. Die Qualität der KI-Ergebnisse, die Überwachung der KI-Nutzung und mögliche Auswirkungen auf soziale Kontakte beeinflussen die Auswahlentscheidung ebenfalls, sind im direkten Vergleich jedoch weniger ausschlaggebend. Insgesamt verdeutlichen die Befunde, dass die Einführung von KI am Arbeitsplatz nicht nur eine technische, sondern auch eine arbeits- und organisationspolitische Gestaltungsaufgabe ist.

articles.title: A mixed-methods study of University of Bristol researchers’ perceptions and attitudes towards sustainable research practices
articles.authors: Anne-Laure Donskoy; Daniel Major-Smith; Matthew Fackrell; Katie Major-Smith; Patricia Neville; Kate Tilling; Ava Lorenc
articles.abstract:
Objective: Universities are increasingly recognised as contributors to the climate crisis but there is little in-depth data on researchers’ understanding and practice. This project explores researcher knowledge and attitudes, barriers and drivers to embedding sustainability within research processes at a single institution, and how to improve the sustainability of research.

Design: Mixed-methods case study.

Setting: The University of Bristol (UoB), UK.

Data collection: Online survey (n=392) and five online qualitative focus groups (n=29). 

Participants: Staff and students involved in conducting or supporting research at the University. 

Results: Survey and qualitative results showed high concern about the climate impact of research (72% very or extremely worried about climate change; 57% believe very important to consider sustainability of research). However, barriers and trade-offs preventing engagement and capacity for change, including the complexity of sustainability, reflecting interconnected systemic problems and competing priorities (potential harms to research, limited funding and time and disproportionate effect on early career researchers). The perceived lack of institutional commitment and prioritisation of sustainability was troubling for participants, with accusations of hypocrisy, greenwashing and poor transparency. Survey data show low levels of training, knowledge and support from UoB (only 4% very or extremely familiar with UoB initiatives). Focus group participants were keen to challenge and disrupt research culture to promote more sustainable research practices, and for open, honest, meaningful conversations. 

Conclusions: Researchers at UoB who took part in our study were keen to make their research more sustainable, but face systemic barriers and competing priorities, and a troubling lack of institutional support, including funding, time, dialogue, sharing information. These issues are likely found across the wider UK university sector, perhaps globally. To achieve universities’ climate commitments - such as net-zero by 2050 - substantial and meaningful change is required. These findings have been integrated into UoB’s University Climate Action Plan to enact this change.

articles.title: Faker Island. Profiling misinformation sharers on the French Twittersphere using a matching procedure
articles.authors: Manon Berriche; Jean-Philippe Cointet; Anne-Sophie Hacquin; Sacha Altay; Béatrice Mazoyer; Benjamin Ooghe-Tabanou; Hugo Mercier; Dominique Cardon
articles.abstract: What are the distinctive characteristics of misinformation sharers? So far, most studies have focused on the U.S., a two-party system with a highly polarized media landscape, leaving open the question of what misinformation sharers look like in other socio-political contexts. Research has also prioritized testing causal links between cognitive or political variables and misinformation sharing, while paying less attention to fine-grained descriptions of who these users are. To address this gap, we analyze the French Twittersphere using ideological inference methods and a matching procedure. Drawing on four million tweets, we compare 1,907 users who shared at least one URL flagged as false or misleading by fact-checkers with 958 ideologically matched control users who did not. We show that misinformation sharers are more likely to be located at the extremes of the political spectrum, express hostility toward ruling elites and institutions, display political markers in their bios, use pseudonyms, share media content, engage in high-intensity and retweet-oriented activity, and express negative emotions. They also disproportionately circulate topics related to immigration, terrorism, and criticism of mainstream media. However, their language does not indicate lower analytical thinking. By shifting the focus from cognitive vulnerability alone to political self-presentation, anger, and amplification practices, this study contributes to ongoing theoretical debates and calls for further research on the activist practices and party affiliations of misinformation sharers.

articles.title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
articles.authors: Thijs Lindner; Willem de Koster; Jeroen van der Waal
articles.abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

articles.title: Accountability in action: Exploring ethical and legal risks in AI- supported employee relations in the UK railway industry
articles.authors: Daniel Grice-Lloyd
articles.abstract:
HR practitioners increasingly deploy Artificial Intelligence [AI] in employee relations [ER] activity that is high-stakes, procedurally sensitive, and legally bounded, yet empirical research into how they navigate the associated ethical and legal risks remains limited. This study gathered practitioner insight into those risks and developed theory- and practice-based recommendations for this nascent field. Semi-structured interviews with 11 senior HR practitioners in the UK railway industry were analysed within an interpretivist approach using NVivo, with reflexivity maintained throughout as the researcher is employed by the same organisation.

Coding developed four themes: professional judgement at the human-AI boundary; ethical and legal risks and guardrails; strategic oversight and digital maturity; and tensions across system ownership, governance, and accountability. From these, four empirical and four conceptual contributions were advanced. The empirical contributions are an accountability gradient between tactical and strategic practitioners; the passive positioning of HR in AI governance; context-sensitive anthropomorphisation; and information-flooding as a pathway to weakened meaningful human involvement and increased Art. 22 GDPR exposure. The conceptual contributions are a three-axis framework [kind/wicked × simple/complex × AI/human], a four-domain nexus, the alignment of kind/wicked rulesets with the jagged frontier, and an ER-specific case-law synthesis reinforcing substantive Human-in-the-Loop [HITL].

Findings suggest variation in senior practitioners' technical understanding, which may constrain their ability to retain meaningful ethical accountability for ER decision-making, with HITL frequently symbolic rather than substantive. HR must shift from passive policy recipient to active contributor in AI governance.

This appears to be among the first empirical studies focused specifically on AI-supported Employee Relations practice, and no directly comparable study within the UK railway industry was identified by the author. Generative AI use is disclosed in full in the Declarations section [editorial/grammar support only; see section 4.5 and Appendix E for the reflexivity comparator methodology].

articles.title: Benchmarking of national policies for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Eva Seyfarth; Carmen Klinger; Peter von Philipsborn
articles.abstract:
Introduction
Each year, approximately 18 million people die prematurely from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) worldwide, many of which could be prevented through effective policies targeting modifiable risk factors. Despite strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of policies, major gaps remain in their adoption and implementation. Benchmarking national policies against international standards helps identify implementation gaps and opportunities for improvement. This study systematically reviewed existing benchmarking initiatives assessing and comparing national policies to reduce modifiable risk factors for NCDs.

Methods
We conducted a scoping review in accordance with the recommendations by the Joanna Briggs Institute and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist. We applied a multi-stage search strategy, including a citation search based on literature known to the authors and identified through expert consultation (April-June 2025), a complementing AI-assisted search (July 2025), and a targeted search via PubMed (February 2026).

Results
A total of 243 full texts were screened, and 89 reports representing 16 benchmarking initiatives were included. Six initiatives assessed strategies to reduce harmful alcohol use, while three initiatives each focused on tobacco use, unhealthy diets, and physical inactivity. Only the World Health Organization’s NCD Progress Monitor addressed all four major risk factors. It comprises eleven indicators and is based on government self-reports supplemented by data from the World Health Organization. None of the identified initiatives enabled a comprehensive benchmarking and ranking of national strategies across all four major NCD risk factors based on objective data.

Conclusions
This scoping review provides a more nuanced understanding of current benchmarking efforts in NCD prevention and serves as a foundation for the development of a comprehensive, overarching NCD prevention index.

articles.title: From Coal to Cloud: Infrastructural Enclosure and the Politics of Land in West Virginia's AI Buildout
articles.authors: Justin Kollar
articles.abstract: Beneath the dramatic expansion of AI computing and digital systems across the world, data centers and energy systems are being constructed within inherited land and property institutions. Because of this, the consequences of this buildout—including resource strain and environmental and health impacts—are unevenly distributed, particularly in rural areas like Appalachia long structured by concentrated land ownership and extractive power relations. Recent discourse has focused on the implications of AI and digital systems for governance, as well as the immense resource demands of computing infrastructure. This article seeks to link these concerns by examining the unequal power relations involved in the production of computing infrastructure, including “powered land,” through which non-tech entities assemble land and entitlements as an asset for sale or rent to operators and AI labs. Within the historically extractive landscape of West Virginia, I examine the mechanisms of infrastructural enclosure that enable and sustain this asset against local resistance, including the passage of HB 2014 and HB 2002, which aim to remove local land-use authority, divert fiscal resources, and protect consequential information about proposed projects. A critical component of this process is asymmetric legibility, through which project details are made coherent for those within the development network but intentionally fragmented and obscured for affected communities. Infrastructural enclosure extends accumulation by dispossession beyond the appropriation of land and resources to encompass the historically aligned regimes that legitimize dispossession and erode democracy and collective place identity.

articles.title: La zona del franco CFA: ¿estabilidad para quién? La incidencia sectorial del anclaje del franco CFA al euro en la UEMOA y la CEMAC / Exposición cambiaria de importaciones y exportaciones
articles.authors: Armand Salouo-Mvondo
